project.title: daily-weather-slack
project.summary: A self-hosted n8n project that fetches the Bengaluru weather forecast every morning at 09:00 IST using the Open-Meteo API (no API key needed). It shapes the data, branches on rain chance and posts a summary to Slack. docker-compose.yml and .env.example run n8n so schedules keep firing with the editor closed, and the workflow JSON shows Schedule and Manual triggers, HTTP Request, Edit Fields (Set), IF and pinned test data. import.sh loads the workflow, and the README covers testing and activation.
project.run:
cp .env.example .env   # then edit N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY and SLACK_CHANNEL
docker compose up -d
./scripts/import.sh
# open http://localhost:5678, add a Slack credential to 'Post to Slack', test with Manual Trigger, then activate/publish the workflow

files.code:
# Self-hosted n8n. 'restart: unless-stopped' keeps it running after reboots,
# so the Schedule Trigger fires without anyone opening the editor.
services:
  n8n:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:latest   # pin a version tag for real production
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "5678:5678"                          # editor UI and webhook port
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      - GENERIC_TIMEZONE=${GENERIC_TIMEZONE}  # timezone used by Schedule Trigger
      - TZ=${GENERIC_TIMEZONE}                # container clock (logs, dates)
      - N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=${N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY} # encrypts saved credentials
      - N8N_BLOCK_ENV_ACCESS_IN_NODE=false    # lets expressions read $env.SLACK_CHANNEL
      - SLACK_CHANNEL=${SLACK_CHANNEL}
      - WEBHOOK_URL=${WEBHOOK_URL}            # public base URL for Webhook nodes later
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n              # workflows, credentials, executions
      - ./workflows:/workflows:ro             # exported JSON for the import script

volumes:
  n8n_data:

# Copy to .env and fill in. Never commit the real .env.

# Schedule Trigger uses this timezone. 09:00 means 09:00 IST.
GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata

# Long random string. Keep it safe: losing it makes saved credentials unreadable.
# Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32
N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=change-me-to-a-long-random-string

# Slack channel the summary is posted to (bot must be invited to it).
SLACK_CHANNEL=#daily-weather

# Base URL n8n shows for Webhook nodes. Use your public HTTPS URL in production.
WEBHOOK_URL=http://localhost:5678/

{
  "name": "Daily weather to Slack",
  "active": false,
  "settings": { "executionOrder": "v1", "timezone": "Asia/Kolkata" },
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "a1", "name": "Every day 9am", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.scheduleTrigger", "typeVersion": 1.2, "position": [0, 0],
      "parameters": { "rule": { "interval": [ { "field": "cronExpression", "expression": "0 9 * * *" } ] } } },
    { "id": "a2", "name": "Test manually", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.manualTrigger", "typeVersion": 1, "position": [0, 200], "parameters": {} },
    { "id": "a3", "name": "Fetch forecast", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.httpRequest", "typeVersion": 4.2, "position": [220, 100],
      "parameters": { "url": "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast", "sendQuery": true,
        "queryParameters": { "parameters": [
          { "name": "latitude", "value": "12.97" }, { "name": "longitude", "value": "77.59" },
          { "name": "daily", "value": "temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min,precipitation_probability_max" },
          { "name": "timezone", "value": "Asia/Kolkata" }, { "name": "forecast_days", "value": "1" } ] }, "options": {} } },
    { "id": "a4", "name": "Shape summary", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.set", "typeVersion": 3.4, "position": [440, 100],
      "parameters": { "assignments": { "assignments": [
        { "id": "f1", "name": "date", "type": "string", "value": "={{ $json.daily.time[0] }}" },
        { "id": "f2", "name": "maxC", "type": "number", "value": "={{ $json.daily.temperature_2m_max[0] }}" },
        { "id": "f3", "name": "minC", "type": "number", "value": "={{ $json.daily.temperature_2m_min[0] }}" },
        { "id": "f4", "name": "rainChance", "type": "number", "value": "={{ $json.daily.precipitation_probability_max[0] }}" } ] }, "options": {} } },
    { "id": "a5", "name": "Rain likely?", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.if", "typeVersion": 2.2, "position": [660, 100],
      "parameters": { "conditions": { "options": { "caseSensitive": true, "leftValue": "", "typeValidation": "strict", "version": 2 },
        "conditions": [ { "id": "c1", "leftValue": "={{ $json.rainChance }}", "rightValue": 50, "operator": { "type": "number", "operation": "gte" } } ],
        "combinator": "and" }, "options": {} } },
    { "id": "a6", "name": "Rain message", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.set", "typeVersion": 3.4, "position": [880, 0],
      "parameters": { "assignments": { "assignments": [ { "id": "m1", "name": "message", "type": "string",
        "value": "=:umbrella: Bengaluru {{ $json.date }}: {{ $json.rainChance }}% rain chance, {{ $json.minC }}-{{ $json.maxC }}°C. Carry an umbrella." } ] }, "options": {} } },
    { "id": "a7", "name": "Clear message", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.set", "typeVersion": 3.4, "position": [880, 200],
      "parameters": { "assignments": { "assignments": [ { "id": "m2", "name": "message", "type": "string",
        "value": "=:sunny: Bengaluru {{ $json.date }}: only {{ $json.rainChance }}% rain chance, {{ $json.minC }}-{{ $json.maxC }}°C." } ] }, "options": {} } },
    { "id": "a8", "name": "Post to Slack", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.slack", "typeVersion": 2.2, "position": [1100, 100],
      "parameters": { "select": "channel", "channelId": { "__rl": true, "mode": "name", "value": "={{ $env.SLACK_CHANNEL }}" },
        "text": "={{ $json.message }}", "otherOptions": { "includeLinkToWorkflow": false } } }
  ],
  "connections": {
    "Every day 9am": { "main": [ [ { "node": "Fetch forecast", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ] ] },
    "Test manually": { "main": [ [ { "node": "Fetch forecast", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ] ] },
    "Fetch forecast": { "main": [ [ { "node": "Shape summary", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ] ] },
    "Shape summary": { "main": [ [ { "node": "Rain likely?", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ] ] },
    "Rain likely?": { "main": [ [ { "node": "Rain message", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ], [ { "node": "Clear message", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ] ] },
    "Rain message": { "main": [ [ { "node": "Post to Slack", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ] ] },
    "Clear message": { "main": [ [ { "node": "Post to Slack", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ] ] }
  },
  "pinData": {
    "Fetch forecast": [ { "json": { "daily": { "time": ["2026-01-15"], "temperature_2m_max": [29.4],
      "temperature_2m_min": [17.8], "precipitation_probability_max": [65] } } } ]
  }
}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Imports the exported workflow into the running n8n container.
# Usage: ./scripts/import.sh   (run from the project root after 'docker compose up -d')
set -euo pipefail

WORKFLOW_FILE="/workflows/daily-weather-slack.json"   # path inside the container (see volumes)

# Wait until the n8n editor answers on port 5678.
echo "Waiting for n8n on http://localhost:5678 ..."
until curl -sf http://localhost:5678/healthz > /dev/null; do
  sleep 2
done

# The n8n CLI ships inside the image. Import creates the workflow as inactive.
docker compose exec -T n8n n8n import:workflow --input="$WORKFLOW_FILE"

echo "Imported. Next steps:"
echo "  1. Open http://localhost:5678 and open 'Daily weather to Slack'."
echo "  2. Select or create a Slack credential on the 'Post to Slack' node."
echo "  3. Click 'Execute workflow' (uses pinned data), then activate/publish it."

# daily-weather-slack

Step 2 hands-on task: a scheduled workflow that calls an API and posts a summary to Slack.

## Flow
Every day 9am (Schedule Trigger) / Test manually (Manual Trigger)
-> Fetch forecast (HTTP Request, Open-Meteo, no key)
-> Shape summary (Edit Fields / Set: date, maxC, minC, rainChance)
-> Rain likely? (IF rainChance >= 50)
-> true: Rain message | false: Clear message (Edit Fields)
-> Post to Slack (both branches feed one node; no Merge needed here)

## Key ideas from the lesson
- A workflow starts at a trigger node. Manual is for testing; Schedule runs only when the workflow is active.
- Each node runs once per item. The API returns one item, so Slack gets one message.
- Expressions such as `{{ $json.rainChance }}` read fields from the incoming item.
- IF has two outputs (true/false). Use Switch for more than two routes.
- Use Merge when you must wait for and combine two branches into one item list.
- Pinned data: the export pins a sample response on 'Fetch forecast'. Manual test runs use the pin and do not call the API. Production runs ignore pinned data. Unpin it to test against the live API.

## Run
1. `cp .env.example .env` and set N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY and SLACK_CHANNEL.
2. `docker compose up -d`, then `./scripts/import.sh`.
3. Create a Slack app with the `chat:write` bot scope. Invite the bot to the channel. Add it as a Slack credential on 'Post to Slack'.
4. Click 'Execute workflow' to test. Change the pinned rain value to see both branches.
5. Activate the workflow. Newer n8n versions call this Publish.

## Checkpoint
Close the browser. At 09:00 IST a message appears in Slack. Check it under Executions (mode: trigger).
For a quick check, temporarily change the cron to `*/5 * * * *`, then change it back.

revision.examFocus: This step covers the n8n Course Level 1 basics: triggers, core nodes, testing and activating workflows. Level 2 builds on it with data structure, Merge and item handling. The knowledge checks are mostly scenario questions. They ask why a workflow did not run on its own, which node fits a branching need, which Merge mode gives a given output, and why a test run and a production run behave differently.

compare.difference: Manual Trigger fires only when you click to execute in the editor. Schedule Trigger fires by itself on an interval or cron, but only after the workflow is activated (published).
compare.chooseA: Pick Manual Trigger to build and debug a workflow that does not need to run unattended yet.
compare.chooseB: Pick Schedule Trigger when the workflow must run at fixed times with nobody watching, such as a daily 8 AM IST report.

compare.difference: The Test URL receives one call only while the editor is listening, and the data shows on the canvas. The Production URL receives calls any time the workflow is active, and runs are logged in Executions.
compare.chooseA: Use the Test URL for a one-off call you trigger yourself, with 'Listen for test event' switched on.
compare.chooseB: Use the Production URL in any external system's settings, such as a form tool, payment gateway or GitHub.

compare.difference: IF always gives exactly two paths (true/false). Switch routes each item to one of many outputs based on rules or an expression, and can add a fallback output for unmatched items.
compare.chooseA: Choose IF for a yes/no decision, such as 'status equals 200' or 'amount > 1000'.
compare.chooseB: Choose Switch when a single field has three or more values that each need their own path, such as priority high/medium/low.

compare.difference: Append stacks all items from Input 1 and then Input 2, with no matching. Combine by matching fields joins items that share a key value, such as email or id, into single items, like a database join.
compare.chooseA: Choose Append when the two branches carry the same kind of record and you just want one list.
compare.chooseB: Choose Combine by matching fields when you need to enrich records from one source with data from another using a common key.

compare.difference: Pinned output replaces the node's real call during editor test runs only. Production runs always call the real API or service.
compare.chooseA: Pin data when an API is slow, rate-limited or costs money, so you can build downstream nodes without calling it again.
compare.chooseB: Rely on live data, and test once with pins removed, before you trust that production will work.

cues.cue: Works when I click Test workflow but never runs overnight
cues.pick: Missing Schedule/app trigger, or workflow not activated (published)
cues.why: Manual Trigger and unpublished workflows never fire unattended.

cues.cue: External service gets 404 from the webhook after I closed the editor
cues.pick: They were given the Test URL; switch to the Production URL and activate
cues.why: The Test URL only listens during a test session.

cues.cue: Report arrives at 2:30 PM / wrong hour
cues.pick: Set the workflow timezone to Asia/Kolkata in Workflow Settings (or GENERIC_TIMEZONE on self-hosted)
cues.why: The schedule is read in the workflow or instance timezone, not your laptop's clock.

cues.cue: Slack got 20 messages instead of one
cues.pick: Aggregate (or Summarize/Code) before Slack, or enable 'Execute Once' on the Slack node
cues.why: Nodes run once per incoming item by default.

cues.cue: Avoid calling the paid API on every test
cues.pick: Pin the HTTP Request node's output
cues.why: Pinned data is reused in test runs without a new request.

cues.cue: Route by many categories, plus a catch-all
cues.pick: Switch with fallback output
cues.why: IF cannot give more than two branches.

cues.cue: Join customer list with order list on customer_id
cues.pick: Merge, Combine by matching fields
cues.why: Matching needs a shared key; Append would just stack the lists.

cues.cue: Prove the job ran at 8 AM yesterday
cues.pick: Executions list (production executions)
cues.why: Scheduled and production runs are logged there, not on the editor canvas.

scenario.situation: A team builds a workflow: Manual Trigger, then HTTP Request to a weather API, then Slack. They pin the API response while building. It posts perfectly when tested. They then swap in a Schedule Trigger set to 'every day at 08:00', save, and leave. Next morning nothing arrives in Slack and the Executions list is empty. What is the most likely fix?
reasoning: An empty Executions list means the trigger never fired. So the API, the pinned data and Slack are not the first suspects.
A timezone mistake would still create an execution, just at the wrong hour. So timezone alone does not explain an empty list.
Pinned data only affects test runs. It cannot stop a scheduled run from starting.
The only thing that stops all unattended runs is a workflow that is not activated (published). Saving does not activate it.
scenario.answer: Activate (publish) the workflow so the Schedule Trigger is registered. Then set the workflow timezone to Asia/Kolkata and unpin data to confirm the live API call works. Only the active or published version runs on triggers.

memoryAids: TAPE before you leave: Trigger is unattended (not Manual), Activate/publish, Pins removed or tested live, Executions checked next day.
IF = 2 doors, Switch = many doors plus a back door (fallback).
Append = stack the plates; Combine = match the pairs (needs a key).
cheatSheet: Only Schedule, Webhook, app triggers (and similar event triggers) run unattended; Manual Trigger is for the editor only.
Save is not the same as publish. Every trigger change needs a save and then a publish or re-activation to reach production.
Webhook: Test URL is for the editor while listening; Production URL is for other systems and needs an active workflow.
Schedule timezone: Workflow Settings first, otherwise the instance default (GENERIC_TIMEZONE). Use Asia/Kolkata for IST.
Schedule Trigger supports intervals (minutes, hours, days, weeks, months) and custom cron expressions.
n8n passes data as items (a list of JSON objects). Each node runs once per item unless 'Execute Once' is on.
Use Aggregate or Summarize to turn many items into one before sending a single message or email.
Edit Fields (Set) adds, renames or keeps only chosen fields. Use it to shape data before branching or sending.
HTTP Request: set method, URL, auth (prefer saved credentials) and query/body. It returns items to downstream nodes.
Merge modes: Append, Combine (by matching fields, by position, all combinations), SQL Query, Choose Branch.
Pins are for editor tests only. Production always uses live data, so test once unpinned.
Debug production in the Executions list; you can load a past execution into the editor to inspect it.
selfCheck: I can explain why a workflow that works with Manual Trigger does not run on its own, and fix it in two steps.
I can tell which Webhook URL goes into an external system and when the Test URL stops responding.
I can set a schedule to fire at 8 AM IST and confirm it ran using the Executions list.
I can turn a 20-item API response into a single Slack or email summary in two different ways.
I can choose between IF and Switch, and between Merge Append and Combine by matching fields, for a given requirement.
I can say exactly what pinned data does and does not affect.

objective.question: You built a workflow that starts with a Manual Trigger. It fetches sales data and emails a report. You publish the workflow and expect a report every morning. Nothing arrives. What is the most likely cause?
options: The Manual Trigger needs a cron expression to run in production
The email node must be pinned before production runs
Manual Trigger workflows run only on n8n Cloud, not self-hosted
The Manual Trigger runs only when you click to execute it in the editor, so it never fires unattended
objective.explanation: The Manual Trigger exists only for testing in the editor and never runs in production. For unattended runs you need a Schedule Trigger, a Webhook or an app trigger. The other options describe features that do not exist.

objective.question: A developer tests a Webhook node, copies the URL shown in the node and gives it to a payment provider. Calls work during testing. The next day every call from the provider fails. What is the most likely reason?
options: Webhook nodes stop working after 24 hours unless re-created
The payment provider must use the GET method only
They shared the Test URL, which only works while the editor is listening for a test event
The webhook needs basic authentication enabled before production
objective.explanation: The Test URL is active only while the editor is waiting for a test event. External systems should get the Production URL, which works when the workflow is active or published. Authentication and HTTP method are not the cause here.

objective.question: A Schedule Trigger is set to run at 09:00. The team in Bengaluru sees it run at 14:30 IST every day. What should you fix first?
options: Set the workflow timezone to Asia/Kolkata in Workflow Settings (or set the instance timezone)
Pin the trigger output so it uses IST
Replace the Schedule Trigger with a Webhook
Change the trigger to run every 5.5 hours
objective.explanation: The run is 5 hours 30 minutes late, which matches a UTC timezone. The Schedule Trigger uses the workflow timezone, or the instance timezone if none is set. Setting Asia/Kolkata fixes it. Pinning and interval changes do not fix timezone.

objective.question: You change a published workflow's schedule from 09:00 to 08:00 in the editor. The next day it still runs at 09:00. What most likely happened?
options: The Schedule Trigger ignores hour changes after the first run
The change was not saved and published again, so production still uses the old version
n8n always rounds schedules to the nearest hour
Schedule changes take a week to apply
objective.explanation: Unsaved or unpublished trigger changes do not apply to production. You must save the workflow and publish it again. The other options are not real n8n behaviour.

objective.question: An HTTP Request node returns 25 items. The next node is a Slack node that posts a message. Slack receives 25 separate messages but you wanted one summary. What is the best fix?
options: Use a Switch node to split items into 25 outputs
Change the Schedule Trigger to run once a day
Pin the HTTP Request output
Add an Aggregate node (or a Code node) before Slack to combine the items into one
objective.explanation: Nodes run once per input item by default, so 25 items give 25 messages. Combining items into one with Aggregate or Code gives a single summary. Switch, pinning and schedule changes do not reduce the item count.

objective.question: How many outputs does the IF node have?
options: Exactly two: true and false
Two, plus an optional fallback output
As many as the rules you define
One output, plus an error output
objective.explanation: The IF node has exactly two outputs, true and false. Multiple outputs with an optional fallback describe the Switch node.

objective.question: You route support tickets by priority with a Switch node: High, Medium and Low. Some tickets arrive with an empty priority field and silently disappear. What should you do?
options: Pin the data so empty priorities get a default
Use a Merge node before the Switch
Enable the Switch node's fallback output and connect it to a handling branch
Replace the Switch with an IF node
objective.explanation: Items that match no rule are dropped unless you use the fallback output. Turning it on and connecting it catches unmatched items. IF only has two outputs and pinning affects test runs only.

objective.question: You pinned the output of an HTTP Request node while building a workflow. You then publish the workflow on a schedule. What data does the scheduled production run use?
options: The pinned data for the first run only
No data; pinned nodes are skipped in production
Live data fetched by the HTTP Request node
The pinned data, until you unpin it
objective.explanation: Pinned data affects test runs in the editor only. Production executions always run the node and fetch live data.

objective.question: Your manager asks for proof that last night's scheduled run actually happened, without you running it again. Where do you look?
options: The pinned data panel
The Schedule Trigger's parameter panel
The workflow's version history
The Executions list for the workflow
objective.explanation: Production executions are recorded in the Executions list with time and status. Pinned data and parameters show configuration, not run history.

objective.question: One branch gives customer records and another gives order records. Both have a customer_id field. You want one item per customer with their order details added. Which node fits best?
options: Merge node, combining by matching fields
Schedule Trigger
Switch node
IF node
objective.explanation: The Merge node can combine items from two inputs by matching a field such as customer_id. IF and Switch route items; they do not join data.

objective.question: An API returns items with 30 fields. You need only name, email and a new field status = "new" before sending to a CRM. Which approach is cleanest?
options: Use Merge in Append mode
Use Edit Fields (Set) to set the three fields and keep only the set fields
Pin the data with only the three fields
Use a Switch node with three outputs
objective.explanation: Edit Fields (Set) can add or change fields and drop all others. Switch and Merge do not reshape fields, and pinning only affects tests.

objective.question: In an Edit Fields node, you want a field to hold the value of the "title" field from the current input item. Which expression is correct?
options: {{ $input.title }}
{{ $json.title }}
{{ $node.title }}
{{ title }}
objective.explanation: $json refers to the JSON of the current item, so {{ $json.title }} reads its title field. The other forms are not valid ways to read the current item's field.

objective.question: A workflow with a Webhook node is published. An external system calls a URL containing "/webhook-test/" and gets an error saying the webhook is not registered. The workflow itself is fine. What is the fix?
options: Click 'Listen for test event' and leave the editor open permanently
Change the HTTP method to POST
Unpublish and republish the workflow
Give the external system the Production URL, which uses a different path
objective.explanation: The "/webhook-test/" path is the Test URL, which works only while the editor listens. A published workflow is reached through the Production URL. Keeping the editor open is not a production solution.

objective.question: On a self-hosted n8n instance with no workflow timezone set, which setting decides the timezone the Schedule Trigger uses?
options: The instance timezone, set with the GENERIC_TIMEZONE environment variable
Always UTC, with no way to change it
The timezone of the API you call
The browser's timezone of whoever saved the workflow
objective.explanation: If the workflow has no timezone in Workflow Settings, n8n uses the instance timezone, set by GENERIC_TIMEZONE on self-hosted. Browser and API timezones do not control the schedule.

objective.question: You want a workflow to run whenever a new issue is opened in a GitHub repository, without writing your own webhook handling. What should you use as the trigger?
options: Schedule Trigger every second
An HTTP Request node at the start
The GitHub app trigger node for that event
Manual Trigger
objective.explanation: App trigger nodes start a workflow on events in a service, such as a new GitHub issue. Manual Trigger does not run in production, and HTTP Request is not a trigger.

objective.question: A Webhook node is published with HTTP Method set to GET. A form provider sends POST requests to the Production URL. Every call fails with a 404 saying the webhook is not registered for POST. The workflow is active. What is the fix?
options: Change the Webhook node's HTTP Method to POST and publish again
Add an HTTP Request node after the webhook to accept POST
Turn on Retry On Fail in the Webhook node settings
Switch the provider to the Test URL
objective.explanation: A webhook registers only for the HTTP method set in the node, so a POST to a GET webhook is rejected. The Test URL only works while you listen in the editor. Retry and extra nodes cannot change how the incoming request is matched.

objective.question: A Webhook node receives a JSON POST body like {"email": "a@b.com"}. In the next node, which expression returns the email?
options: {{ $json.body.email }}
{{ $json.query.email }}
{{ $body.email }}
{{ $json.email }}
objective.explanation: The Webhook node puts headers, params, query and body in separate keys, so the POST payload sits under body. $json.email is undefined. $body is not a built-in variable. query holds URL query parameters, not the POST body.

objective.question: A Schedule Trigger uses the Custom (Cron) interval with the expression below. When does the workflow run?
options: At 09:00 on every day of the month from the 1st to the 5th
At 09:00 Monday to Friday, in the workflow's timezone
At 00:09 every weekday
Every 9 minutes, Monday to Friday
objective.explanation: The five fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. So minute 0, hour 9, weekdays 1–5, which is 09:00 Monday to Friday in the configured timezone. The other options read the fields in the wrong order or treat day-of-week as day-of-month.

objective.question: An Edit Fields node outputs 10 items. The next HTTP Request node calls a reporting API. You expected 1 call, but the API logs show 10. You only need one call, whatever the input. What is the simplest fix?
options: Replace the HTTP Request node with a Webhook node
Set the HTTP Request node to Always Output Data
Pin the Edit Fields output
Enable the Execute Once setting on the HTTP Request node
objective.explanation: n8n runs most nodes once per input item. Execute Once makes the node run a single time, using only the first item. Pinning only affects manual testing. Always Output Data controls empty outputs, not how many times the node runs.

objective.question: An IF node checks whether the field amount is greater than 1000 using the Number comparison. The API returns amount as the string "1500". The node errors with a wrong-type message. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Turn on the IF node's option to convert types where required (loose type validation)
Use a Switch node, because it ignores types
Pin the data with amount as a number
Change the operator to String > equals
objective.explanation: The IF node checks types strictly by default. Loose type validation ('Convert types where required') converts "1500" to a number before comparing. A string equals check cannot test 'greater than'. Switch also validates types. Pinning fixes only test data, not production.

objective.question: A Switch node in Rules mode has two rules: 'amount > 1000' goes to Output 0 and 'country = IN' goes to Output 1. An Indian order worth 5000 appears only in Output 0. You need it in both outputs. What should you do?
options: Add a Merge node before the Switch
Enable the fallback output
Enable the option to send data to all matching outputs
Reorder the rules so country comes first
objective.explanation: By default the Switch node sends an item only to the first rule it matches. The 'Send data to all matching outputs' option sends it to every matching output. Reordering only changes which single output wins. The fallback output is only for items that match no rule.

objective.question: An HTTP Request node must enrich 500 items. The API allows about 10 requests per second. The node fails with HTTP 429 errors. Which built-in setting best solves this?
options: Execute Once
Pinning the HTTP Request output
Raising the Timeout option
The Batching option, with a set number of items per batch and a batch interval
objective.explanation: Batching sends requests in groups with a delay between groups, so you stay under the rate limit. Execute Once would process only the first item. A longer timeout does not reduce the request rate. Pinning does nothing for production runs.

objective.question: Branch A returns 3 lead items from a form tool. Branch B returns 4 lead items from a CRM export. Both have the same fields. You want one list of 7 items for de-duplication later. Which Merge mode fits?
options: Combine by Position
Choose Branch
Append
Combine by Matching Fields
objective.explanation: Append outputs the items from input 1 followed by the items from input 2, which gives 7 items. Combine by Matching Fields and Combine by Position join items together into fewer records. Choose Branch outputs data from only one input.

objective.question: The workflow runs Fetch Orders (HTTP Request), then Edit Fields, then Slack. Edit Fields kept only total. In the Slack node you need the orderId from the matching Fetch Orders item. Which expression is correct?

code.code:
// Slack message text
Order {{ ???? }} total {{ $json.total }}

options: {{ $('Fetch Orders').item.json.orderId }}
{{ $node.orderId }}
{{ $('Fetch Orders').json.orderId }}
{{ $json.orderId }}
objective.explanation: $('Node name').item uses item pairing to find the item in that earlier node linked to the current item. $json only sees the previous node's output, which no longer has orderId. The other two forms are not valid ways to read a field from a node's item.

subjective.question: Explain the main trigger types in n8n and when you would use each one.
subjective.answer: Every workflow starts with a trigger node. The Manual Trigger lets me run the workflow by clicking in the editor. I use it only for building and testing, because it never runs in production. The Schedule Trigger runs the workflow at fixed times or intervals, for example every day at 9 AM IST. I use it for reports, syncs and clean-up jobs. The Webhook node gives a URL that an external system can call, so the workflow runs the moment an event happens, such as a form submission. App trigger nodes, like those for GitHub, Gmail or Google Sheets, start the workflow on events inside a specific service without me building the webhook logic. For any unattended run, I need Schedule, Webhook or an app trigger, and the workflow must be active or published.
keyPoints: Manual Trigger is for testing only and never runs in production
Schedule Trigger for time-based jobs
Webhook for event-driven calls from external systems
App triggers for service-specific events
Unattended runs need an active or published workflow

subjective.question: What is the difference between the Webhook Test URL and Production URL? Describe a bug this difference causes.
subjective.answer: A Webhook node shows two URLs. The Test URL works only while the editor is listening for a test event, after I click to listen. It lets me send a sample request and see the data in the editor. The Production URL works only when the workflow is active or published, and it runs without the editor open. The two URLs have different paths, so they are not interchangeable. A common bug is copying the Test URL into an external system like a payment gateway or form tool. It works while I am testing, so it looks fine. Later, when the editor is closed, every call fails. The fix is to publish the workflow and give the external system the Production URL. I check this every time I hand a webhook to another team.
keyPoints: Test URL works only while the editor is listening
Production URL works only when the workflow is active or published
The two URLs are different
Common bug: giving the Test URL to an external system
Fix: publish and share the Production URL

subjective.question: How does n8n process items between nodes, and why does it matter when building workflows?
subjective.answer: Data moves between nodes as a list of items. Each item is a JSON object. By default, a node runs once for each input item. So if an HTTP Request node returns 50 records, the next node processes 50 items. For a Slack or email node, this means 50 messages. This is useful when I want per-record actions, such as creating one CRM contact per row. It is a problem when I want a single summary. In that case I combine the items first, using an Aggregate node, a Code node, or Edit Fields with suitable expressions, so only one item reaches the sending node. Understanding items also helps with expressions: $json refers to the current item. Many beginner bugs, like duplicate messages, come from forgetting per-item execution.
keyPoints: Data flows as a list of JSON items
Nodes run once per input item by default
Many items into Slack or email means many messages
Use Aggregate, Code or Edit Fields to build one summary
$json refers to the current item

subjective.question: Walk through how you would build a scheduled workflow that fetches data from an API and posts a daily summary to Slack.
subjective.answer: I start with a Schedule Trigger set to, say, every day at 9:00, and I set the workflow timezone to Asia/Kolkata in Workflow Settings. Next, an HTTP Request node calls the API, with authentication stored in a credential, not hard-coded. I run it once and pin the output so I can build the rest without calling the API again. Then I use Edit Fields to keep only the fields I need. Because the API returns many items, I add an Aggregate or Code node to combine them into one item with a summary text. Then a Slack node posts that text to a channel. An IF node can skip posting when there is no data. Finally, I save and publish the workflow, and check the Executions list the next day to confirm it ran on schedule without me opening the editor.
keyPoints: Schedule Trigger with correct timezone
HTTP Request with stored credentials
Pin data while building
Combine items into one summary before Slack
Save, publish, and verify in Executions

subjective.question: A scheduled workflow runs at the wrong time. How do you troubleshoot it?
subjective.answer: First I compare the expected and actual times. If the gap is 5 hours 30 minutes, it is almost certainly a UTC versus IST problem. I open Workflow Settings and check the timezone. If none is set, n8n uses the instance timezone, which on self-hosted comes from the GENERIC_TIMEZONE environment variable. I set the workflow timezone to Asia/Kolkata if the team expects IST. Second, I check that the trigger settings are what I think, such as the hour, the interval or the cron expression. Third, I make sure the change was saved and the workflow published again, because unsaved trigger changes do not reach production. Finally, I look at the Executions list to see actual run times after the fix, so I have evidence that the schedule is correct.
keyPoints: 5h30m gap suggests UTC vs IST
Workflow timezone overrides instance timezone
GENERIC_TIMEZONE on self-hosted
Save and republish after changes
Confirm in the Executions list

subjective.question: Compare the IF node and the Switch node. When would you choose each?
subjective.answer: Both nodes route items based on conditions. The IF node has exactly two outputs: true and false. Each item goes down one of them. I use IF for simple yes or no decisions, such as 'is the amount above 10,000' or 'is the list empty'. The Switch node can have many outputs, one per rule or value, plus an optional fallback output for items that match no rule. I use Switch when there are three or more paths, such as routing tickets by High, Medium and Low priority, or by country. Chaining many IF nodes for this becomes hard to read. With Switch, I turn on the fallback output so unexpected values, like an empty priority, are handled instead of silently dropped. Choosing the right one keeps workflows readable and safe.
keyPoints: IF has exactly two outputs: true and false
Switch has many outputs
Switch has an optional fallback output
Use IF for binary decisions, Switch for multiple routes
Fallback prevents silently dropped items

subjective.question: What does the Merge node do, and give two practical uses.
subjective.answer: The Merge node takes items from two or more inputs and brings them together into one stream. It has different modes. The simplest is appending, where items from all inputs are listed one after another. Another is combining, where items are joined, for example by matching a common field like customer_id, or by position. It can also wait for parallel branches and pass on data from one chosen branch. A first practical use: I fetch customers from a CRM and orders from a billing API in two branches, then merge by customer_id to get one item per customer with order details. A second use: after an IF node splits items into two paths for different processing, I merge both paths back so one Slack node sends the final result. I always check the item count after a merge.
keyPoints: Merge combines data from multiple inputs
Append mode lists items together
Combine mode joins by matching field or position
Use to join data from two sources
Use to rejoin branches after IF or Switch

subjective.question: What is data pinning in n8n? Explain its benefits and its limits.
subjective.answer: Pinning saves a node's output in the editor so later test runs reuse that data instead of executing the node again. I usually pin the trigger or an HTTP Request node after one good run. The benefits are clear: I do not call a paid or rate-limited API repeatedly, I get the same input each time, which makes debugging easier, and I can test webhook-based logic without sending a new request every time. I can also edit pinned data to test edge cases like an empty list. The key limit is that pinned data affects test runs only. Production executions always run the node and fetch live data. So a workflow that works with pinned data may still fail in production if the live data looks different. I test once with live data before publishing.
keyPoints: Pinning stores node output for reuse in test runs
Saves API calls and gives repeatable tests
Pinned data can be edited to test edge cases
Pinned data does not apply in production
Test with live data before publishing

subjective.question: What does activating or publishing a workflow mean, and how do you prove it is working in production?
subjective.answer: A workflow in the editor does not run on its own. To run on its trigger, such as a schedule, webhook or app event, it must be activated. In newer n8n versions, the old Active toggle became a Publish action, but the idea is the same: only the activated or published version runs on triggers. This also means that after I edit a trigger, I must save and publish again, or production keeps using the old version. The workflow also needs a production-capable trigger; a Manual Trigger will never fire. To prove it works, I close the editor and wait for the next scheduled time. Then I open the Executions list and check that a production execution appears with the right time and a success status. I also confirm the output, like the Slack message, actually arrived.
keyPoints: Only activated or published workflows run on triggers
Active toggle became Publish in newer versions
Save and republish after trigger changes
Manual Trigger never runs in production
Prove runs using the Executions list

subjective.question: What is the Edit Fields (Set) node used for? Give examples.
subjective.answer: Edit Fields, earlier called the Set node, adds, changes or removes fields on each item. It is the main tool for shaping data between nodes. For example, an API returns 30 fields but my CRM needs only name, email and phone. I set those fields and choose to keep only the set fields, so the rest is dropped. I can also add new fields, such as status set to 'new' or source set to 'website'. Values can be fixed or built with expressions, like {{ $json.first_name }} plus {{ $json.last_name }} to create a full name, or a formatted date. Shaping data early makes later nodes simpler and reduces errors from unexpected fields. It also makes the data easier to read when I debug in the editor. It still runs per item, so it does not combine items by itself.
keyPoints: Adds, changes or removes fields on items
Option to keep only set fields
Supports fixed values and expressions
Shapes data for downstream nodes
Runs per item; does not aggregate by default

subjective.question: How do you use the HTTP Request node safely and effectively in a production workflow?
subjective.answer: The HTTP Request node calls any REST API, so it covers services that have no dedicated node. I set the method, URL, query parameters, headers and body. For authentication, I use n8n credentials instead of pasting API keys into the node, so secrets stay out of the workflow JSON. If the API documentation gives a cURL command, I can import it to fill the node quickly. I check how the response is returned; a JSON array usually becomes many items, which affects the next nodes. For large APIs, I use the node's pagination options instead of building loops by hand, and I respect rate limits. I think about failures too: the node can be set to retry or continue on error, so one bad call does not silently break a daily report. Then I pin one good response for building.
keyPoints: Configure method, URL, parameters, headers and body
Store secrets in credentials
Import cURL to set up quickly
Arrays become multiple items
Use pagination, retries and error settings

subjective.question: A Webhook-triggered workflow needs to send back a custom response to the caller. What options does the Webhook node give for responding?
subjective.answer: The Webhook node has a setting that controls when and how it responds to the caller. It can respond immediately, which tells the caller the request was received while the workflow keeps running. This is good when the caller has a short timeout or does not need results. It can respond when the last node finishes, returning the data from the final node, which suits short, quick workflows. The third option is to respond using a separate Respond to Webhook node, which lets me choose exactly what to send back, such as a custom JSON body, status code or headers, at a specific point in the flow. For example, I can validate input with an IF node and send a 400 error on the false branch. I choose based on how long the workflow takes and what the caller expects.
keyPoints: Respond immediately for quick acknowledgement
Respond when last node finishes to return results
Respond to Webhook node for custom body, status and headers
Choose based on caller timeouts and needs
Can return errors from specific branches

subjective.question: Some app trigger nodes use webhooks and others poll. Explain the difference and why it matters.
subjective.answer: An app trigger can work in two ways. A webhook-based trigger registers a URL with the service, and the service calls n8n the moment the event happens, for example a new GitHub issue. This is fast and efficient. A polling trigger does not wait for a call; n8n checks the service on an interval, such as every minute or every hour, and starts the workflow if it finds new data. Some services do not offer webhooks, so polling is the only choice, for example certain spreadsheet or email triggers. This matters for design. Polling adds delay up to the interval and uses API calls even when nothing changed, which can hit rate limits. Webhook triggers are near real-time but need the n8n instance to be reachable from the internet, which matters for self-hosted setups behind a firewall.
keyPoints: Webhook triggers receive calls from the service
Polling triggers check on an interval
Polling adds delay and uses API calls
Some services only support polling
Webhooks need a publicly reachable instance

subjective.question: Your scheduled workflow did not run last night. Give a step-by-step troubleshooting checklist.
subjective.answer: First, I open the Executions list. If there is a failed execution, the schedule worked and I debug the failing node, often an HTTP Request error or an expired credential. If there is no execution at all, the trigger did not fire. Then I check that the workflow is active or published, and that my latest changes were saved and published, since unpublished edits do not apply. Next, I confirm the trigger is a Schedule Trigger and not a Manual Trigger. I check the timezone in Workflow Settings and the instance timezone, because the run may have happened at a different hour than expected. On self-hosted, I check that the n8n instance or container was actually running at that time. Finally, after fixing, I watch the next scheduled run in Executions to confirm.
keyPoints: Check Executions list first
Failed run versus no run tells you where to look
Confirm workflow is published with latest changes
Check trigger type and timezone
On self-hosted, confirm the instance was running

subjective.question: An API returns 40 records and you need one email containing a summary of all of them. How do you build this in n8n?
subjective.answer: Because nodes run once per input item, sending the 40 items straight to an email node would send 40 emails. So I combine them first. One option is the Aggregate node, which collects a field, or all item data, into a single item holding a list. After that, an Edit Fields node or an expression can turn the list into readable text, for example joining titles with line breaks. Another option is a Code node, where I loop over all input items in JavaScript and return one item with a formatted summary, such as counts and totals. Before combining, I usually use Edit Fields to keep only the fields I need. Then the email or Slack node receives one item and sends one message. I test with pinned data, then check one live production run.
keyPoints: Per-item execution would send 40 emails
Aggregate node combines items into one
Code node can build a custom summary
Format text with Edit Fields or expressions
Only one item should reach the send node

subjective.question: An API returns 100 records per page and gives a 'next' URL in each response. How do you fetch all pages in n8n with the HTTP Request node?
subjective.answer: I use the Pagination option built into the HTTP Request node rather than building a loop by hand. Under Options I add Pagination and pick the mode that matches the API. Here the response contains the next URL, so I choose that mode and set the next URL with an expression such as {{ $response.body.next }}. If the API used page numbers or offsets, I would use the mode that updates a parameter in each request, for example page = {{ $pageCount + 1 }}. Then I set 'Pagination Complete When', for example when the next field is empty or a specific status code comes back. I also set a maximum number of pages as a safety limit, so a buggy API cannot loop forever. I may add a short interval between requests to respect rate limits. Finally, I test with a small page size and check the total item count.
keyPoints: Use the HTTP Request node's built-in Pagination option
Choose a mode: next URL in response, or update a parameter
Use $response and $pageCount in expressions
Define a clear completion condition and a max page limit
Respect rate limits with an interval between requests

subjective.question: Your workflow calls a third-party API that sometimes fails with timeouts or 429/5xx errors. Which HTTP Request node and node settings help make it reliable?
subjective.answer: First, in the node Settings I turn on Retry On Fail. I set a sensible number of tries and a wait time between them, so short glitches recover on their own. Second, for many items I use the Batching option to control items per batch and the interval, which keeps me under the rate limit and avoids 429s. Third, I set a Timeout in Options, so a hanging call does not block the run. Fourth, I decide what should happen on failure with the On Error setting. 'Stop Workflow' is right when the data is critical. 'Continue' (using an error output) lets me route failed items to a logging or alert branch. I store credentials in n8n credentials, never in plain headers. Finally, I check failed runs in the Executions list and add an error workflow for alerts.
keyPoints: Retry On Fail with tries and wait time
Batching to respect rate limits
Timeout option for hanging calls
On Error setting: stop vs continue with error output
Credentials stored securely, failures monitored

subjective.question: Explain the difference between $json, $('Node').item, $('Node').first() and $input.all() in n8n expressions. When would you use each?
subjective.answer: $json is the JSON of the current input item, which comes from the node directly before. I use it for most field mappings. $('Node name').item reaches back to an earlier node. It uses item pairing to return the item linked to the current one, so it is right when a later node has dropped a field I still need, such as an ID. $('Node name').first() always returns the first item of that node, whatever the current item is. It suits single values like a token or a config row. $input.all() returns every input item as an array. I use it when one operation must see all items, for example building a summary text with map and join in a node set to Execute Once. The common mistake is using first() where item is needed, which gives every item the same value.
keyPoints: $json = current item from previous node
$('Node').item uses item pairing to earlier node
first() returns a fixed first item
$input.all() returns all items as an array
Wrong choice causes repeated or mismatched values

subjective.question: A public Webhook node will receive order events from a partner. How do you secure it?
subjective.answer: A production webhook URL is reachable by anyone who knows it, so I add several layers. First, I set Authentication on the Webhook node. Options are Basic Auth, Header Auth or JWT Auth, and a shared secret header is the usual choice with partners. Second, I set the HTTP Method to exactly what the partner sends, usually POST, so other methods are rejected. Third, if the partner publishes fixed IPs, I use the IP allowlist option. Fourth, if the partner signs payloads, I verify the signature in the workflow and stop invalid requests early with an IF node, returning an error response. I also use a hard-to-guess path, validate required fields before any writes, and never echo sensitive data back in the response. On self-hosted n8n, I put it behind HTTPS with a reverse proxy.
keyPoints: Webhook Authentication: Basic, Header or JWT
Restrict the HTTP method
IP allowlist where possible
Validate signatures and payloads early
Serve over HTTPS

subjective.question: What does this Slack message expression do, and which node setting must be on for it to send a single summary?

code.code:
Daily report: {{ $input.all().length }} tickets
{{ $input.all().map(i => `• ${i.json.title} (${i.json.priority})`).join('\n') }}

subjective.answer: The first line counts all items that reached the Slack node and prints, for example, 'Daily report: 12 tickets'. The second line takes every input item, turns each one into a bullet line with its title and priority, and joins them with newlines into one block of text. On its own, though, the Slack node still runs once per item. With 12 items you would get 12 identical full summaries. To send one message, I enable Execute Once in the Slack node settings. The expression still reads all items through $input.all(), but the node runs only once. Another option is to use an Aggregate or Code node before Slack to collapse the items into one. I would also handle empty results, for example with an IF on the count, so the team does not get an empty report.
keyPoints: $input.all() reads every input item
map and join build one multi-line text
Nodes run per item by default
Execute Once, or an Aggregate node first, gives one message
Handle the zero-items case

subjective.question: A company wants new rows in a SaaS tool to trigger processing. n8n has an app trigger for that tool, but you could also use a Schedule Trigger plus an HTTP Request. How do you choose?
subjective.answer: I prefer the app trigger when it covers the event I need. It handles authentication, registers webhooks or polls for me, and tracks what it has already seen, so I get only new records without writing de-duplication logic. A Schedule Trigger plus HTTP Request makes sense in other cases. Examples are when the app trigger does not offer the event or fields I need, when I need a fixed batch time such as a 9 AM digest, or when I want full control over the query, filters and pagination. The cost is that I must handle 'only new since last run' myself, for example by filtering on a timestamp or using the Remove Duplicates node's option to remove items processed in previous executions. I also weigh speed against batching. Webhook-based triggers are near real time, while schedules suit reports.
keyPoints: App triggers handle auth and new-item tracking
Schedule + HTTP gives control and fixed timing
Schedule approach needs your own de-duplication
Real-time events vs batch digests
Check whether the trigger exposes the needed event

subjective.question: Your scheduled workflow fetches 'recent orders' every hour and posts them to Slack. People complain the same orders appear in many posts. How do you fix it?
subjective.answer: The API returns a rolling window, so overlapping hours repeat records. There are two clean fixes. One is to ask only for new data: pass a time filter in the HTTP Request, for example created_after = {{ $now.minus({hours: 1}).toISO() }}, so it matches the schedule interval. This is simple but can miss or repeat records if a run is late. The more robust fix is to de-duplicate across runs. The Remove Duplicates node has an operation that removes items processed in previous executions, keyed on a value such as the order ID, so each order passes only once. I then send only the remaining items, often aggregated into one message with Execute Once. Finally, I make sure the IF or empty-result check skips posting when there are no new orders, and I review a few executions to confirm it works.
keyPoints: Rolling window causes overlap
Filter by time based on the schedule interval
Remove Duplicates across previous executions by unique ID
Aggregate into one message
Skip posting when nothing is new

subjective.question: An IF node's true branch ends in a Slack alert and the workflow then continues. On days when no item matches, later nodes never run. Why, and how do you handle it?
subjective.answer: In n8n, a node that receives zero items does not run, and nothing flows past it. If the true branch is empty, every node after it on that path is skipped. The run still shows as successful, which is why this is easy to miss. There are a few fixes. I can enable the Always Output Data setting on the node that may return nothing. It then outputs one empty item, so the chain continues, but downstream nodes must handle an empty item safely. Often a better design is to keep work that must always happen off the conditional branch. For example, place it before the IF, or run it from the false branch too. If I need to bring branches together again, I use a Merge node with the right mode. I test both cases with pinned data, one with matches and one without.
keyPoints: Zero input items means the node does not execute
Run can show success while steps are skipped
Always Output Data emits an empty item
Restructure so must-run steps are not conditional
Test both paths with pinned data

subjective.question: How would you use pinned data to test edge cases in a workflow that starts with a Webhook or a slow API call?
subjective.answer: First I run the trigger or the API node once with real data, then pin its output. Manual test runs then reuse that output, so I don't need to resend webhooks or wait for slow or rate-limited APIs. Pinned data is editable, so I change it to create edge cases: an empty field, a string instead of a number, a missing priority, a very long text, or zero items. With each version I run the workflow and check that the IF, Switch and Edit Fields nodes behave correctly. I keep the data free of real personal information. Pinned data applies only to manual executions in the editor; production runs always use live data. So before relying on the workflow I unpin and run a real test. After publishing, I check the first production executions to confirm real data matches what I pinned.
keyPoints: Pin real output once to avoid re-triggering
Edit pinned data to simulate edge cases
Covers empty, wrong-type and missing fields
Pinned data affects only manual runs, not production
Unpin and verify with live data before relying on it

steps.overview: This step explains how data moves through an n8n workflow. Data travels as a list of items, and each item holds JSON. You will learn to read that data with expressions, reshape it with looping, splitting and aggregating nodes, and drop into the Code node when no built-in node fits. Level 1 and Level 2 knowledge checks test these ideas heavily, and they are the base for every real workflow you build.
objectives: Describe the n8n item structure (an array of objects with a json key and an optional binary key) and how nodes process items.
Write expressions with {{ $json }} and $('Node Name') to reference fields from the current or any earlier node.
Choose between automatic per-item processing, Loop Over Items, Split Out, Aggregate and Summarize for a given data shape.
Write a Code node in 'Run Once for All Items' and 'Run Once for Each Item' modes that returns valid n8n items.
Transform a CSV of orders into per-customer totals using both a no-code path (Summarize) and a Code node path.

concepts.explanation: An item is the unit of data in n8n. Each node receives and outputs an array of items. Each item is an object with a json key for structured data and an optional binary key for files. For example, a CSV with 50 rows becomes 50 items after parsing.

Most nodes run once for every incoming item automatically. If 50 items reach a Gmail node, it sends 50 emails. This is why you rarely need a manual loop in n8n. The node setting 'Execute Once' forces a node to run only for the first item.

An expression is JavaScript written inside {{ }} in a parameter set to Expression mode. {{ $json.email }} reads a field from the current item of the node's direct input. Expressions can call methods such as {{ $json.name.toUpperCase() }}. They also support n8n helpers like $now and $today (Luxon dates) and $jmespath.

$('Node Name').item.json.field gets the item in that node that is linked to the current item, using paired items. $('Node Name').first(), .last() and .all() give fixed positions or every item. The older $node["Node Name"].json syntax still appears in old workflows. The current $() syntax is the one to learn.

n8n tracks which input item produced each output item. This tracking is what lets .item find the matching item in an earlier node. Built-in nodes keep the links for you. A Code node that builds brand-new items can break them, which causes paired-item errors downstream.

This node splits incoming items into batches of a set size. It sends each batch through the 'loop' output, and when all batches are done it sends the combined results through the 'done' output. Use it for rate limits, very large datasets, or nodes that only process the first item. Do not use it for normal per-item work.

Split Out turns an array field inside one item into many items. Aggregate does the opposite and collects field values from many items into one item. Summarize works like a pivot table: it groups by 'Fields to Split By' and calculates Sum, Count, Average, Min, Max and similar values.

The Code node runs JavaScript or Python when built-in nodes cannot express the logic. 'Run Once for All Items' (the default) gives you every item through $input.all(). 'Run Once for Each Item' runs the code per item and exposes $json. The node must return items, which means objects with a json key.

keyFacts: Data between nodes is always an array of items, and each item looks like { json: {...}, binary?: {...} }.
{{ $json.field }} reads only from the node directly connected before the current one. Use $('Node Name') to read from any earlier node.
$('Node').item uses item linking. Use .first(), .last() or .all() when you need a fixed position or every item.
Code node default mode is 'Run Once for All Items'. $json is only available in 'Run Once for Each Item' mode.
In the Code node, $input.all(), $input.first() and $input.item read the node's input data.
Loop Over Items has two outputs: 'loop' for each batch and 'done' after every batch has been processed.
The Extract From File node parses CSV, XLSX and JSON files from binary data into items. CSV values usually arrive as strings.
On self-hosted n8n, the Code node can use external npm modules or Node built-ins only if they are allowed through NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL or NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN.

example.caption: Code node (JavaScript, Run Once for All Items): per-customer order totals from parsed CSV items

pitfalls: Adding Loop Over Items for simple per-item work. Nodes already iterate over every item, so the extra loop only adds complexity.
Forgetting that CSV values are strings. Summing '120' and '80' gives '12080' unless you convert with Number() or set the field type in an Edit Fields (Set) node.
Using $json to read data from a node that is not the direct parent. It silently reads the wrong data; use $('Node Name').item.json instead.
Returning plain values or a single object from the Code node instead of an array of { json: {...} } items. This causes errors or unexpected output.
Building new items in a Code node and then using .item references downstream. This can raise paired-item errors; use .first() or .all(), or keep the item links intact.
Printing an object inside a text expression. It shows [object Object]; use JSON.stringify() or select a specific field.

workflow.title: CSV of orders to per-customer totals

steps.label: Trigger and load the file
steps.detail: Start with a Manual Trigger, then read the CSV with Read/Write Files from Disk (self-hosted), HTTP Request or a Google Drive download.

steps.label: Parse CSV into items

steps.label: Clean and type fields
