project.title: orders-to-customer-totals
project.summary: A self-hosted n8n project that reads a CSV of orders, turns each row into an item, cleans the fields with expressions, groups them per customer with Summarize, and ranks the results in a Code node. docker-compose.yml runs n8n with file access, data/orders.csv is the input, workflows/customer-totals.json is the importable workflow, src/rank-customers.js is the Code node source, and README.md explains how items, per-item execution, expressions and paired items work in each node.
project.run:
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec n8n n8n import:workflow --input=/workflows/customer-totals.json
# open http://localhost:5678, create the owner account, open 'Orders to Customer Totals', click 'Execute workflow'

files.code:
# Runs a single self-hosted n8n instance for this lesson
services:
  n8n:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:latest   # official n8n image
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "5678:5678"                          # editor UI at http://localhost:5678
    environment:
      - GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata        # timezone used by schedule nodes
      - TZ=Asia/Kolkata
      # Read/Write Files from Disk may only touch this folder
      - N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO=/files
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n             # credentials, workflows, settings
      - ./data:/files                        # orders.csv is read from here
      - ./workflows:/workflows               # used by the import:workflow CLI

volumes:
  n8n_data:

# orders-to-customer-totals

Step 3 hands-on task: turn a CSV of orders into per-customer totals.

## Run
1. `docker compose up -d`
2. `docker compose exec n8n n8n import:workflow --input=/workflows/customer-totals.json`
3. Open http://localhost:5678, set up the owner account, open the workflow, click **Execute workflow**.

## What each node teaches
| Node | Concept |
|------|---------|
| Read Orders CSV | Output is 1 item with binary data (`data`), not JSON rows yet |
| Extract CSV | 1 file becomes 10 items. Each item is `{ json: {...} }`, all values are strings |
| Clean Fields | Per-item execution: expressions run once per item. `$json.amount` is the current item. `$('Extract CSV').item` uses paired items to find the matching earlier item |
| Total per Customer | Summarize groups items by `customer`, giving `sum_amount` and `count_order_id` |
| Rank Customers | Code node for logic nodes cannot do: share %, rounding, sorting. Uses `$('Clean Fields').all()` to read an earlier node |

## Expected output (3 items)
| customer | orders | total | share_pct |
|----------|--------|-------|-----------|
| Kiran Foods | 3 | 3000 | 49.6 |
| Asha Traders | 4 | 2000 | 33.1 |
| Rahul Stores | 3 | 1049.25 | 17.3 |

`all_orders` is 10 on every row. Note " Asha Traders " was trimmed, so it joined the right group.

## Checkpoint exercises
- In Clean Fields add `source_row = {{ $('Extract CSV').item.json.order_id }}`. This is referencing an earlier node.
- Replace Summarize with Aggregate ("All Item Data") and see 1 item with an array.
- After Extract CSV add Loop Over Items (batch size 3) to process rows in batches, e.g. for rate-limited APIs.
- Use Split Out on the Aggregate array to get items back.

## Tips
- `$json` = current item. `$('Node').item` = paired item. `.first()`, `.last()`, `.all()` work on any earlier node.
- Code node must return an array of `{ json: {...} }` objects.

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the data-handling parts of the n8n Level 1 and Level 2 courses. It covers the item data structure, expressions, referencing earlier nodes, splitting, merging and aggregating items, and the Code node. The knowledge checks usually show a short workflow or a snippet of expression or code. You then pick the output, the correct syntax, or the node that fits the job. Read every expression carefully. A single wrong reference ($json vs $('Node')) or mode (all items vs each item) is often the whole question.

compare.difference: $json reads only the current input item from the directly connected parent node. $('Node Name').item follows item linking back to the matching item in any earlier node.
compare.chooseA: Pick $json when the field comes from the node wired straight into the current one.
compare.chooseB: Pick $('Node Name').item.json when the field lives two or more nodes back, or on a different branch that has already executed.

compare.difference: .item depends on paired-item links and gives the item that matches the current one. .first() and .all() ignore links and use fixed positions.
compare.chooseA: Use .item when each output item must line up with its own source item, such as the same order or the same row.
compare.chooseB: Use .first() for a single config or token item, and .all() when you need every item. Also use them when links were broken, for example after a Code node created new items.

compare.difference: Split Out turns one item that holds an array into many items. Aggregate combines many items into one item with an array field. Summarize groups items and calculates values such as sum, count, min, max or average, like a pivot table.
compare.chooseA: Choose Split Out when an API returns a list inside one item and you need to process each element.
compare.chooseB: n/a

cues.cue: field from a node that is not directly connected
cues.pick: $('Node Name').item.json.field
cues.why: $json only sees the direct parent's output, so it would silently read the wrong data.

cues.cue: total per customer / count per category / group by
cues.pick: Summarize node (Group By + Sum or Count)
cues.why: It does grouped calculations without code and returns one item per group.

cues.cue: API rate limit, process N records at a time, wait between calls
cues.pick: Loop Over Items with a batch size, plus a Wait node inside the loop
cues.why: This is the real use for batching. Plain per-item work needs no loop.

cues.cue: one item contains an array of line items
cues.pick: Split Out on that array field
cues.why: It turns array elements into separate items, so later nodes run once per element.

cues.cue: logic no built-in node can do, e.g. custom maths across all items
cues.pick: Code node in 'Run Once for All Items' mode
cues.why: You get every item through $input.all() and can return any number of new items.

cues.cue: output shows [object Object]
cues.pick: JSON.stringify() or a specific sub-field
cues.why: A text expression converts an object to a string unless you serialise it or pick one field.

cues.cue: sum looks like '12080' instead of 200
cues.pick: Number() or set the field type to Number in Edit Fields (Set)
cues.why: CSV values arrive as strings, and + joins strings together instead of adding them.

cues.cue: paired item / 'can't determine which item to use' error
cues.pick: Switch to .first() or .all(), or keep item links intact in the Code node
cues.why: .item needs links that new items built in code do not have.

scenario.situation: A shop uploads a daily orders CSV with columns order_id, customer_email and amount. You read the file and use Extract From File to get one item per row. The manager wants one result per customer with the total amount spent. A colleague's draft uses Loop Over Items around a Code node that adds amount values with +, and the totals look far too large. What is the simplest correct fix?
reasoning: Spot the string trap first. CSV amounts are strings, so + joins them together ('120' + '80' = '12080'). That explains the 'far too large' totals.
Drop Loop Over Items. There is no rate limit or batch need, and nodes already process every item.
Look for a built-in node before writing code. Grouping by customer and summing a field is exactly what Summarize does.
Make the amount numeric. Set its type to Number in an Edit Fields (Set) node, or confirm that Summarize treats it as a number.
Reject a per-item Code node. It sees one row at a time and cannot build totals across rows.
scenario.answer: Use Extract From File, then Edit Fields (Set) to make amount a Number, then Summarize with Group By customer_email and Sum of amount. This removes the needless loop, fixes the string-concatenation bug, and returns one item per customer without any code.

memoryAids: Neighbour vs Name: $json reads your direct neighbour. For anyone further back, call them by name with $('Node Name').
Split spreads, Aggregate gathers, Summarize counts. One-to-many, many-to-one, many-to-groups.
Loop only for Limits: use Loop Over Items only when rate Limits, batch Limits or nodes that handle one item at a time force you to.
cheatSheet: Every node receives and returns an array of items. Each item keeps its fields under json, and files go under binary.
Most nodes run once per input item automatically, so check this before adding any loop.
Use $json for the direct parent and $('Node Name').item.json for any earlier node.
Use .first(), .last() or .all() when item links are missing or you need a fixed item.
Choose Code node 'Run Once for All Items' for cross-item maths. Use 'Run Once for Each Item' (where $json works) for per-row edits.
The Code node must return an array of { json: {...} } objects, even when there is only one result.
Wrap a CSV string field in Number() before adding it, or set its type in Edit Fields (Set).
Summarize handles grouped totals, counts and averages without code.
Use Split Out when an array inside one item should become many items.
Loop Over Items has two outputs: 'loop' runs per batch, 'done' fires once at the end. Connect the last node in the loop back to its input.
Use JSON.stringify() to print a whole object in text, otherwise you get [object Object].
Self-hosted only: npm or built-in modules in the Code node need NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL or NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN.
selfCheck: I can write an expression that reads a field from a node three steps back, and explain why $json would fail there.
I can predict how many items each node outputs in a chain of Extract From File, Split Out, Summarize and Code.
I can write a Code node in 'Run Once for All Items' mode that returns correctly shaped items.
I can explain when Loop Over Items is truly needed and when it only adds complexity.
I can fix a paired-item error by choosing between .item, .first() and .all().
I can turn a CSV of orders into per-customer numeric totals without any string bugs.

objective.question: In n8n, what is the shape of the data that one node passes to the next?
options: An array of items, where each item has a 'json' key and an optional 'binary' key
A key-value map indexed by node name
A CSV string that the next node parses
A single JSON object with all fields merged
objective.explanation: n8n always passes an array of items, and each item looks like { json: {...}, binary?: {...} }. It is never a single merged object, a raw CSV string or a map keyed by node name.

objective.question: Your workflow is Webhook → HTTP Request → Slack. In the Slack node you write {{ $json.email }}, but email was only in the Webhook body. The result is empty. Why?
options: $json reads only from the node directly connected before the current one, which is HTTP Request
The Webhook node must be pinned before you can use its data
Slack nodes do not support expressions
Expressions cannot read webhook data
objective.explanation: $json refers to the current input item, which here comes from HTTP Request. To read the Webhook field, reference that node by name. Expressions do work in Slack, and pinning is not required.

objective.question: Which expression correctly reads the email field from the matching item of an earlier node called 'Webhook'?
options: {{ $node.Webhook.email }}
{{ $input.Webhook.json.email }}
{{ $('Webhook').item.json.email }}
{{ $json('Webhook').email }}
objective.explanation: $('Node Name').item uses item linking to find the item that matches the current one, and .json.email reads the field. The other forms are not valid n8n syntax for this purpose.

objective.question: A 'Get Settings' node returns one item that holds an API region. A later node processes 200 order items and every order needs that same region. What is the most reliable expression?
options: {{ $('Get Settings').first().json.region }}
{{ $json.region }}
{{ $('Get Settings').all().json.region }}
{{ $('Get Settings').item.json.region }}
objective.explanation: .first() always returns the first item at a fixed position, so all 200 orders get the same single setting. .item depends on item linking, which may not map 200 items to one. $json reads the wrong node. .all() returns an array, so it has no .json property.

objective.question: What is the default mode of the Code node when you add it to a workflow?
options: Run Once per Batch
Run Only on First Item
Run Once for All Items
Run Once for Each Item
objective.explanation: The Code node defaults to 'Run Once for All Items'. The only other mode is 'Run Once for Each Item'. The other two options are not real Code node modes.

objective.question: A learner pastes 'return { total: $json.price * $json.qty };' into a new Code node and it fails. What is the best fix?
options: Switch the mode to 'Run Once for Each Item', or rewrite the code to loop over $input.all()
Add a Loop Over Items node before the Code node
Use Python instead of JavaScript
Rename $json to $data
objective.explanation: $json only works in 'Run Once for Each Item' mode. In the default all-items mode you must read items with $input.all() and return an array. Adding a loop or changing the language does not fix the mode problem.

objective.question: In 'Run Once for All Items' mode, which return statement gives valid output?
options: return $json;
console.log($input.all());
return $input.all().map(i => ({ json: { id: i.json.id, ok: true } }));
return 'done';
objective.explanation: In all-items mode the node must return an array of items, each with a json object. A plain string is not valid. $json is not available in this mode. console.log returns nothing to the next node.

objective.question: The Loop Over Items node has two outputs. What do they do?
options: 'success' and 'error' for error handling
'first' for the first item and 'rest' for the others
'loop' gives each batch for processing; 'done' fires after every batch has been processed
'true' and 'false', like an IF node
objective.explanation: Loop Over Items sends each batch out of 'loop' and, once all batches are processed, sends the combined result out of 'done'. It has no true/false, success/error or first/rest outputs.

objective.question: An API accepts at most 50 records per request and rate-limits you. You have 1,000 items. Which design fits best?
options: Use Aggregate to put all 1,000 into one item
Use Split Out on the items
Use Loop Over Items with batch size 50, add HTTP Request plus a Wait node on the 'loop' branch, and connect them back to the loop
Send all 1,000 items to HTTP Request with no changes
objective.explanation: Loop Over Items processes controlled batches, and a Wait node spaces out the calls to respect the rate limit. Sending everything at once ignores the limit. Aggregate creates one huge payload. Split Out is for splitting arrays inside an item.

objective.question: Each order item has a lineItems array with several products. You need one item per product for the next node. Which node should you use?
options: Split Out
Merge
Summarize
Aggregate
objective.explanation: Split Out turns an array field inside an item into separate items. Aggregate and Summarize do the opposite and combine items. Merge joins data from two inputs.

objective.question: You have one item per order with customer and amount fields. You need total amount per customer with the least custom code. Which configuration is right?
options: Summarize with a Sum aggregation on amount and 'customer' in Fields to Split By
Split Out on customer
Loop Over Items with batch size 1
Aggregate with 'All Item Data'
objective.explanation: Summarize works like a pivot table. Sum on amount, grouped by customer through 'Fields to Split By', gives per-customer totals. Aggregate only collects items into one item without grouping. Split Out and Loop Over Items do not calculate totals.

objective.question: After Extract From File reads an orders CSV, your Code node does 'totals[c] = (totals[c] || 0) + item.json.amount' and returns '0120.5045'. What went wrong?
options: The Code node does not support decimals
JavaScript objects cannot use customer names as keys
CSV values usually arrive as strings, so + concatenated text instead of adding numbers
Extract From File rounds numbers
objective.explanation: CSV values usually arrive as strings, and in JavaScript 0 + '120.50' gives the string '0120.50'. Convert the value first, for example with Number(item.json.amount). The other options are false.

objective.question: An HTTP Request node downloads orders.csv as binary data. Which node turns it into one item per row?
options: Convert to File
Aggregate
Extract From File
Split Out
objective.explanation: Extract From File parses CSV, XLSX and JSON files from binary data into items. Convert to File does the reverse. Split Out and Aggregate work on JSON items, not binary files.

objective.question: On a self-hosted n8n instance, a Code node using require('lodash') fails with a 'module not allowed' type error. lodash is installed on the server. What must the admin do?
options: Add lodash to the NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL environment variable and restart n8n
Set NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN to lodash
Switch the Code node to Python
Enable the module in the workflow's Settings tab
objective.explanation: External npm modules are blocked unless listed in NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL. NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN is only for Node built-ins such as crypto. Workflow settings and changing language do not grant module access.

objective.question: Your Code node collapses 10 order items into 3 customer-total items. A later node uses {{ $('Orders Sheet').item.json.region }} and shows a paired item error. What is the most sensible fix?
options: Change $( ) to $json
Increase the batch size in Loop Over Items
The 3 new items do not link clearly to single original items, so use .first()/.all() or carry the region into the Code node output
Delete the Code node and use Split Out
objective.explanation: .item relies on item linking, and items created by grouping have no clear one-to-one link back to the source. Carry the field through, or use a fixed position or .all() logic. $json reads the wrong node, and batch size is unrelated.

objective.question: A CSV column header is 'Customer Name' (with a space). Which expression reads it correctly from the current item?
options: {{ $json["Customer Name"] }}
{{ $json.Customer_Name }}
{{ $json->'Customer Name' }}
{{ $json.Customer Name }}
objective.explanation: Field names with spaces or special characters need JavaScript bracket notation. Dot notation breaks at the space. n8n does not rename the field to Customer_Name, and -> is not valid expression syntax.

objective.question: A workflow reads 200 orders and ends with a Slack node that posts 'Daily orders processed'. The team gets 200 identical Slack messages. What is the simplest fix without changing the message?
options: Wrap the Slack node in a Loop Over Items node with batch size 1
Add {{ $json }} to the message text
Set the Slack node to 'Always Output Data'
Turn on the 'Execute Once' setting on the Slack node
objective.explanation: Execute Once makes the node run only once, using the first input item, so it sends one message. A loop still sends one message per item. Always Output Data only controls empty output, and adding $json just changes the text.

objective.question: This Code node runs in 'Run Once for Each Item' mode. The input is two items: {qty: 2, price: 50} and {qty: 1, price: 30}. What is the output?

code.code:
const j = $input.item.json;
return { json: { ...j, lineTotal: j.qty * j.price } };

options: Two items, each with its original fields plus lineTotal (100 and 30)
Two items holding only lineTotal, with the original fields removed
An error, because per-item mode must return an array
One item: {lineTotal: 130}
objective.explanation: In per-item mode the code runs once per item. Returning one object with a json key is valid. The spread copies the original fields and adds lineTotal. The node never sums across items.

objective.question: An earlier node 'Orders' output three items with amount 100, 250 and 50. What does this expression return in a later node?

code.code: {{ $('Orders').all().map(i => i.json.amount).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) }}

options: A paired item error, because .all() needs item linking
100, the amount of the paired item
objective.explanation: .all() returns every output item of the node, without using item pairing. map pulls the amounts into an array, and reduce sums them to 400. .item would return only the paired item.

objective.question: In 'Run Once for All Items' mode, a Code node builds new items from input items. Why might you add pairedItem to each returned item?
options: It tells n8n which input item each output came from, so later .item references to earlier nodes resolve correctly
It makes the node process items in parallel
It keeps binary data attached to each item
It is required, or the Code node fails to run
objective.explanation: pairedItem records item linking. Later nodes can then use $('Earlier Node').item and get the correct record. It is not mandatory, and it does not affect parallelism or binary data.

objective.question: A Filter node sometimes lets zero items through. The workflow then stops, and the final 'Log Run' node never executes. You want 'Log Run' to always run. What setting helps?
options: Set the workflow timeout to a higher value
Enable 'Retry On Fail' on the Filter node
Enable 'Execute Once' on the Log Run node
Enable 'Always Output Data' on the Filter node
objective.explanation: When a node outputs no items, downstream nodes do not run. Always Output Data makes the node emit one empty item, so the chain continues. Downstream logic must then handle that empty item.

objective.question: Three items each have an email field. You add an Aggregate node with 'Individual Fields' and choose the field email. What is the output?
options: One item with email set to an array of the three values
One item with a data field containing all full items
One item with email set to the count 3
Three items, unchanged
objective.explanation: Aggregate in Individual Fields mode collects the chosen field from all items into one array on a single item. 'All Item Data' would put whole items into a list. Counting is a Summarize operation.

objective.question: An HTTP Request node downloads a PDF invoice. Where does n8n keep the file inside the item?
options: In item.binary, under a property such as 'data', alongside item.json
Only on disk, with no reference in the item
In a separate execution called the binary run
As a base64 string inside item.json.file
objective.explanation: An item has a json part for structured data and an optional binary part for files. The binary part is keyed by a property name, 'data' by default. Metadata such as the file name and MIME type sits there, and json stays separate.

objective.question: You need today's date as 2026-03-15 in a file name. Which expression is correct?
options: {{ $now.toFormat('yyyy-MM-dd') }}
{{ $today('yyyy-MM-dd') }}
{{ new Date().toFormat('yyyy-MM-dd') }}
{{ $now.format('YYYY-MM-DD') }}
objective.explanation: $now is a Luxon DateTime, so you format it with toFormat and Luxon tokens (yyyy-MM-dd). format() with Moment tokens does not exist on it. A native Date has no toFormat, and $today is a value, not a function.

subjective.question: Explain how n8n passes data from one node to the next.
subjective.answer: n8n passes data as an array of items. Each item is an object with a json key that holds the fields, and an optional binary key for files such as PDFs, images or CSVs. A node receives this array, does its work, and outputs a new array of items for the next node. Even a single record is wrapped as an array with one item. This matters in practice. When I inspect a node's output in table, JSON or schema view, I am looking at those items. When I write expressions or Code node logic, I read item.json.field. If a node outputs zero items, the next nodes usually do not run. Thinking in items is the base for everything else in n8n.
keyPoints: Data is always an array of items
Each item is { json: {...}, binary?: {...} }
A single record is still an array of one item
Binary holds files; json holds fields
Zero output items usually stops the downstream nodes

subjective.question: What does per-item execution mean in n8n, and what mistake can it cause?
subjective.answer: Most n8n nodes run their operation once for every input item. If a Gmail node gets 25 items, it sends 25 emails, one per item, and each expression is evaluated using that item's data. This is powerful because you rarely need an explicit loop. It can also cause surprises. A common mistake is placing a 'send summary' Slack message after a node that outputs 100 rows, so the team gets 100 messages. The fix is to collapse items first with Aggregate or Summarize, or to turn on the node's 'Execute Once' setting, which uses only the first item. I always check the item count on a node's input before I add a node with side effects such as emails, payments or database writes.
keyPoints: Most nodes run once per input item
Expressions are evaluated per item
No explicit loop is usually needed
Risk of duplicate side effects such as 100 messages
Fix with Aggregate or Summarize, or the Execute Once setting

subjective.question: Compare {{ $json.field }} with {{ $('Node Name').item.json.field }}. When would you use each?
subjective.answer: $json is a shortcut to the current input item, which means the output of the node directly connected before the current node. It is the quickest option when the field I need comes from the previous step. $('Node Name') lets me reach any earlier node in the workflow by its name. Adding .item uses item linking to find the item in that node that corresponds to the item being processed now. For example, in Webhook → HTTP Request → Gmail, the Gmail node can read the API response with $json.status and read the customer's email with $('Webhook').item.json.email. One caution: if you rename a node, n8n updates references in the workflow, but it is still wise to give nodes clear names early.
keyPoints: $json reads only from the directly previous node
$('Node Name') reaches any earlier node
The .item accessor uses item linking
Combine both in a single node
Use clear node names

subjective.question: What are paired items (item linking) and why do they matter?
subjective.answer: Paired items are n8n's record of which input item produced each output item. When a node turns item 3 into a new item, n8n remembers that link. Then $('Earlier Node').item can trace back through the chain and return the matching earlier item, not just the first one. This is what lets a node use fields from several steps back for the correct record. Linking is clear for one-to-one nodes. It becomes unclear when items are merged, grouped, split or newly created, for example by a Code node that builds fresh items. Then you may see a paired item error or wrong data. Fixes include carrying needed fields forward, using .first(), .last() or .all(), or setting pairedItem in Code node output.
keyPoints: Tracks which input item produced each output item
Powers $('Node').item
Works cleanly for one-to-one transformations
Can break when grouping, merging or creating new items
Fix by carrying fields, using fixed positions, or setting pairedItem

subjective.question: When do you use .first(), .last() and .all() instead of .item on a node reference?
subjective.answer: I use .item when I want the earlier item that matches the current item through item linking. That suits record-by-record flows. I use .first() when the earlier node produces one item that every later item should share, such as a config lookup, an access token or a single settings row. .last() is useful when the final item matters, for example the latest page of a paginated result or the last status update. .all() returns every item from that node as an array. I use it when I need to count, search or sum, for example {{ $('Orders').all().length }}. Because .all() returns an array, I must map or index it. I cannot call .json on it directly.
keyPoints: .item follows item linking for the matching record
.first() for a single shared value such as config
.last() when the final item matters
.all() returns an array of all items
Do not call .json directly on the .all() result

subjective.question: Compare the two Code node modes and say how you read input in each.
subjective.answer: 'Run Once for All Items' is the default. The code runs a single time and sees every input item together. I read items with $input.all(), $input.first() or $input.last(), and I must return an array of items, each like { json: {...} }. This mode suits grouping, totals, de-duplication and sorting, because those need all the rows at once. 'Run Once for Each Item' runs the code separately for each item. Here I can use $json or $input.item.json, and I return one item object. It suits simple per-record changes such as building a full name or cleaning a phone number. A common error is using $json in all-items mode. It is not available there, so the code fails.
keyPoints: The default is Run Once for All Items
All-items mode: $input.all() and return an array
Each-item mode: $json or $input.item, return one item
Grouping needs all-items mode
$json is not available in all-items mode

subjective.question: When should you reach for the Code node, and when should you avoid it?
subjective.answer: I first try built-in nodes such as Edit Fields (Set), Filter, IF, Split Out, Aggregate, Summarize, Merge and Remove Duplicates. They are visible, easy for teammates to maintain, and keep item linking clean. I reach for the Code node when logic is hard to express with nodes. Examples are complex parsing, multi-condition grouping, custom sorting, building nested payloads, or calculations across many items. The Code node supports JavaScript and Python. The trade-offs are real. Code is harder for non-developers to read. Errors only appear when the workflow runs. New items can lose paired item links. On n8n Cloud you also cannot freely import external modules. My rule: use nodes first, and use code to fill the gaps, with short, commented blocks.
keyPoints: Prefer built-in nodes for clarity and maintenance
Use Code for logic nodes cannot express
Supports JavaScript and Python
Risks: readability and broken item linking
Keep code blocks short and commented

subjective.question: Explain how to wire Loop Over Items correctly and when it is actually needed.
subjective.answer: Most nodes already process every item, so I do not add Loop Over Items by default. I use it when I need control over batches. Typical cases are rate-limited APIs, services that accept a limited number of records per call, adding a Wait between calls, or nodes that only handle the first item. Wiring: set Batch Size, then connect the 'loop' output to the processing nodes, for example HTTP Request and then Wait. Connect the last processing node back into the Loop Over Items input. When every batch is done, the 'done' output fires with the combined results, and I continue the workflow from there. A common bug is forgetting the connection back to the loop, so only the first batch runs.
keyPoints: Not needed for normal per-item processing
Use it for rate limits, batch-size limits and adding waits
The 'loop' output goes to the processing nodes
The last node connects back to the loop input
The 'done' output continues after all batches

subjective.question: What is the difference between Split Out, Aggregate and Summarize? Give an example of each.
subjective.answer: Split Out takes an array field inside an item and makes one item per element. For example, one order with a lineItems array becomes one item per product. Aggregate does the opposite. It combines many items into a single item, either collecting specific fields into lists or putting all item data into one array. For example, it can gather 30 email addresses into one list for a single bulk API call. Summarize works like a spreadsheet pivot table. It calculates values such as count, sum, average, min or max, optionally grouped by fields to split by. For example, it can give the total order amount per customer. In short: Split Out expands, Aggregate collects, and Summarize calculates.
keyPoints: Split Out turns an array into many items
Aggregate turns many items into one item with lists
Summarize gives pivot-style counts and sums with grouping
Real example for each
Expand vs collect vs calculate

subjective.question: Walk through building the hands-on task: a CSV of orders transformed into per-customer totals.
subjective.answer: First, get the file. I use a trigger, then an HTTP Request node or a file-reading node, so the CSV arrives as binary data. Second, Extract From File, set to CSV, turns each row into an item with fields such as order_id, customer and amount. Third, I fix data types. CSV values usually arrive as strings, so I use Edit Fields to set amount as a number, for example {{ $json.amount.toNumber() }}, and I trim customer names. Fourth, a Summarize node with Sum on amount, split by customer, gives one item per customer. Finally, I check the output count against the number of unique customers and spot-check one total by hand. Then I send the result to a Google Sheet or Slack.
keyPoints: Get the CSV as binary data
Extract From File in CSV mode gives items
Convert strings to numbers and clean names
Summarize: Sum of amount split by customer
Verify counts and spot-check totals

subjective.question: Write the core of a Code node (JavaScript, default mode) that produces per-customer totals, and explain it.
subjective.answer: In 'Run Once for All Items' mode I would write: const totals = {}; for (const item of $input.all()) { const c = String(item.json.customer).trim(); const amt = Number(item.json.amount) || 0; totals[c] = (totals[c] || 0) + amt; } return Object.entries(totals).map(([customer, total]) => ({ json: { customer, total: Math.round(total * 100) / 100 } })); The loop reads every input item. Number() is essential because CSV values are strings, and without it + would join text. Trimming avoids treating 'Asha ' and 'Asha' as different customers. The return maps the totals object to an array of items, each with a json key, which is the format the next node expects. Rounding avoids floating-point noise in currency values.
keyPoints: Use default all-items mode with $input.all()
Convert amount with Number()
Normalise customer keys with trim
Return an array of { json: {...} } items
Round currency values

subjective.question: Why do data types matter when processing CSV data in n8n, and how do you handle them?
subjective.answer: Extract From File usually gives CSV values as strings, even when they look like numbers or dates. This causes quiet bugs. Adding strings joins them as text. Comparisons such as '100' > '20' compare text, not numbers. Filters on dates may fail. I handle this early, right after parsing. In Edit Fields I set the field type to Number or Boolean, or I use expressions such as {{ $json.amount.toNumber() }}. In a Code node I use Number() or parseFloat(). For dates I convert to a proper date, for example with Luxon's DateTime in expressions. I also watch for empty cells, commas inside numbers like '1,200', and currency symbols, and I clean these before converting.
keyPoints: CSV values usually arrive as strings
Risks: text joining and wrong comparisons
Convert early with Edit Fields or toNumber()
Use Number() or parseFloat() in code
Clean commas, symbols and empty cells

subjective.question: An expression referencing an earlier node returns the wrong record or a paired item error. How do you debug it?
subjective.answer: First, I check the item counts on each node between the source and the current node. If counts change, item linking may be unclear. Second, I open the expression editor and look at the live preview for several items, not only the first. Third, I look for nodes that create or reshape items, such as Code, Aggregate, Summarize or Merge, because they can break or blur paired items. Fixes depend on intent. If I need one shared value, I use .first(). If I need the correct record, I carry the field forward with Edit Fields before the reshaping node. In a Code node I can set pairedItem on the output items. Pinning test data helps me reproduce the issue quickly.
keyPoints: Compare item counts across nodes
Preview the expression for several items
Find nodes that reshape items
Use .first() or carry fields forward
Set pairedItem in Code output; pin test data

subjective.question: On self-hosted n8n, how do you allow the Code node to use npm modules or Node built-ins, and what are the risks?
subjective.answer: By default, the Code node cannot require external npm modules or most Node built-in modules. On self-hosted n8n, an admin enables them with environment variables. NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN lists built-ins such as crypto. NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL lists installed npm packages such as lodash or moment. The external modules must also be installed where n8n runs, for example in a custom Docker image. Then n8n is restarted. The risks are about security and stability. Any workflow editor can run code with those modules, so allowing everything with a wildcard gives broad access to the server. I allow only specific modules that are needed, pin their versions, and keep the list documented. On n8n Cloud this kind of server control is generally not available.
keyPoints: Blocked by default
NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN for Node built-ins
NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL for npm packages
Install the modules and restart n8n
Allow only what is needed; avoid wildcards

subjective.question: Explain n8n expression syntax and give practical examples, including referencing a field from any earlier node.
subjective.answer: Expressions sit inside double curly braces in a parameter set to Expression mode. They contain JavaScript, so I can use operators, string methods and ternaries. Examples: {{ $json.firstName + ' ' + $json.lastName }} joins names. For fields with spaces I use bracket notation: {{ $json['Customer Name'] }}. I can add defaults with {{ $json.city ?? 'Unknown' }}. For dates I use {{ $now.toFormat('yyyy-MM-dd') }}. To read from any earlier node I use {{ $('Webhook').item.json.body.orderId }} for the matching record, or {{ $('Settings').first().json.region }} for a single shared value. I always check the inline preview, and I drag fields from the input panel to avoid typos in paths.
keyPoints: {{ }} contains JavaScript
Bracket notation for fields with spaces
Defaults with ?? and dates with $now
$('Node').item or .first() for earlier nodes
Use the preview and drag-and-drop fields

subjective.question: The orders CSV stores amounts as text like '₹1,200.50' and some rows are blank. How would you clean this before summing per customer?
subjective.answer: Extract From File gives every value as a string, so I clean the data before any maths. In a Code node, or an Edit Fields expression, I remove the currency symbol and the thousands separators: String(v).replace(/[^0-9.-]/g, ''). Then I wrap the result in Number(). If the result is NaN or the field was empty, I decide on a rule. Usually I skip the row, or route it to an error branch with a Filter or IF node. Treating it as 0 silently is risky. I also trim and normalise the customer key, for example with trim() and toLowerCase(), so 'Asha ' and 'asha' fall into one group. Only then do I use Summarize or a reduce. I spot-check a few rows in the output panel to confirm the amounts are numbers, not strings.
keyPoints: CSV values arrive as strings
Strip symbols and commas, then use Number()
Handle blanks and NaN explicitly instead of silently
Normalise the grouping key
Verify the types in the output panel

subjective.question: When would you use the Edit Fields (Set) node instead of a Code node to reshape items?
subjective.answer: I use Edit Fields for most simple reshaping: renaming, adding computed fields with expressions, and dropping fields. It runs per item, and it is visual, so teammates can read it without knowing JavaScript. Its 'Include Other Input Fields' option controls whether you keep everything else or output only the fields you set. That makes it good for trimming payloads before an API call. It also keeps item pairing intact, because each output item maps to one input item. I switch to a Code node when I need logic across items, such as grouping, deduplicating with custom rules or complex parsing. I also switch when the expressions get so long they are unreadable. In short, Edit Fields handles per-item field work, and Code handles cross-item or algorithmic work.
keyPoints: Edit Fields handles rename, add and remove per item
Include Other Input Fields controls what passes through
It is readable and keeps pairing intact
Use Code for cross-item logic or complex parsing

subjective.question: A workflow is Schedule → Get Orders (sheet) → HTTP Request (fetch customer profile per order) → Email. The email must include the order ID and the customer's tier. How do you reference both, and why does it work?
subjective.answer: The HTTP Request node runs once per order item, so its output items stay paired with the order items. In the Email node, $json is the HTTP response, so I write {{ $json.tier }} for the tier. The order ID came from the sheet, so I write {{ $('Get Orders').item.json.orderId }}. That works because n8n follows the item links back from the current item to the matching order. The approach breaks if a node between them changes the item count without keeping links. Examples are an Aggregate, or a Code node that builds new items without pairedItem. In those cases I either carry orderId forward in the data or use a Merge node to join the data. I also check the HTTP node is not set to batch everything into a single request.
keyPoints: $json is the immediate previous node
$('Get Orders').item follows item linking
HTTP Request keeps 1:1 pairing per item
Count-changing nodes can break links
Carry fields forward or use Merge as a fallback

subjective.question: You must send a single summary email after processing 300 orders. Compare three ways to do it: Execute Once, Aggregate before the email, and .all() in the email expression.
subjective.answer: Execute Once makes the email node run once using only the first item. That is fine when the message is static, but you cannot list or total all orders from item data. Aggregate, or Summarize, collapses the 300 items into one item that holds an array or totals. The email node then runs once naturally, and the summary data is visible in the item. That makes debugging easy. Using {{ $('Orders').all() }} inside the email expression can also build a total or a list. But if the email node still receives 300 items, it will run 300 times unless Execute Once is also on. My preferred design is Summarize or Aggregate into one item, then email. It is explicit and testable.
keyPoints: Execute Once only uses the first item
Aggregate or Summarize yields one item with full data
With .all(), the node still runs per incoming item
Prefer collapsing to one item, then sending

subjective.question: Review this Code node (Run Once for All Items). It should return orders over 1000 with a flag. What is wrong, and how would you fix it?
subjective.answer: There are two issues. First, it pushes item.json, the plain object, into the array. The Code node expects items, so the safe form is out.push({ json: {...item.json, big: true} }). Current n8n versions often auto-wrap plain objects, but returning explicit items is clearer and portable. Second, it mutates the input item directly. That can confuse debugging and can affect references to earlier data, so I copy the object with spread instead. Also, amount from a CSV is probably a string. The string '999' compared with 1000 is coerced to a number by JavaScript, but a value like '1,200' becomes NaN and fails silently. So I use Number() after cleaning. Finally, the code drops rows, so I would add pairedItem if later nodes reference earlier ones with .item. A Filter node plus Edit Fields could replace this code entirely.
keyPoints: Return items shaped { json: {...} }
Avoid mutating input items
Convert string amounts explicitly
Add pairedItem when items are dropped or created
Consider Filter plus Edit Fields instead

subjective.question: Explain how binary data travels through an n8n workflow and how it relates to JSON.
subjective.answer: Every item has a json part and an optional binary part. Files are stored under a binary property name, 'data' by default. Examples are a downloaded CSV, an image or an email attachment. The property also holds metadata such as fileName, mimeType and fileExtension. Nodes that work on files, such as Extract From File, Write to Disk, Send Email attachments or HTTP Request uploads, ask for the binary property name. Expressions only see the JSON part, so you cannot read file contents with $json. You first convert the file, for example with Extract From File to turn CSV rows into JSON items. Some nodes drop binary data from their output, so you may need to keep it or re-reference it from the earlier node. On self-hosted setups, admins can configure binary data to be stored on the filesystem or external storage instead of in memory. This matters for large files.
keyPoints: An item has json plus binary
Binary data sits under a named property with metadata
Expressions read json, not file contents
Use Extract From File or Convert to File to switch formats
Storage mode matters for large files on self-hosted setups

subjective.question: A Filter node can return zero items, and the workflow then silently ends. How do you diagnose this, and what are the options and risks of fixing it?
subjective.answer: In the execution view, the workflow shows as successful, but the nodes after the Filter have no run. The Filter output panel shows 0 items. That is expected n8n behaviour, because nodes only run when they receive items. The options are these. First, enable Always Output Data on the Filter, so it emits one empty item and the chain continues. Second, use an IF node and handle the false branch explicitly. Third, keep the Filter's discarded-items output, if enabled, to log rejected rows. The risk with Always Output Data is that downstream nodes receive an empty item. They might send a blank email or write an empty row. I add an IF check such as {{ Object.keys($json).length > 0 }}, or a dedicated 'no data' branch. Explicit branching is usually clearer than relying on an empty item.
keyPoints: Zero items means downstream nodes do not run
Check the item counts in the execution view
Always Output Data emits one empty item
Guard against blank downstream actions
An IF node with explicit branches is often clearer

subjective.question: A CSV of orders is very large. Executions get slow or run out of memory. What design changes would you make in n8n?
subjective.answer: First, I reduce what each item carries. I use Edit Fields to keep only the needed columns early, and I avoid keeping large binary data after extraction. Second, I process in chunks. Loop Over Items with a sensible batch size can feed a sub-workflow through Execute Workflow. Each batch's data is then handled in a separate execution, and memory is not held for the whole file at once. Third, I push heavy aggregation to where it fits better. That might be a database query with GROUP BY, or a single efficient Code node reduce instead of many chained nodes. On self-hosted setups, I can also store binary data outside memory, raise the resources given to n8n, and use queue mode with workers. I also turn off saving full execution data for successful runs if it is not needed. I avoid quoting fixed limits, because they depend on the plan and the hardware.
keyPoints: Trim fields and binary data early
Batch and offload to sub-workflows
Push aggregation to a database or a single Code node
Self-hosted tuning: binary storage, resources, queue mode
Reduce saved execution data

subjective.question: What can you write inside {{ }} expressions, and when should logic move out of an expression?
subjective.answer: An expression is a single JavaScript expression evaluated per item. You can use operators, ternaries, string and array methods such as trim, split, map and join, and Luxon dates through $now and $today. You can also use n8n variables such as $json, $('Node'), $itemIndex and $execution. The examples here set a priority label, clean up a name, and compute a date seven days ago. Expressions cannot hold multi-statement logic such as loops with variables. A function wrapped in an IIFE is possible, but it becomes unreadable. I move logic out when the expression grows past one clear line, when it is repeated across many fields, or when it needs cross-item work. Then I use Edit Fields with simpler expressions, a Code node, or a Summarize or Aggregate node. I also guard against missing fields, for example $json.name ?? '', so the expression does not throw.
keyPoints: One JavaScript expression per field, evaluated per item
Ternaries, methods, Luxon and n8n variables are available
No multi-statement logic in practice
Move complex or cross-item logic to Code or other nodes
Guard against missing fields

steps.overview: This step takes you through the official n8n Course Level 1 on docs.n8n.io. You build a mini-workflow first, then the course's sample business workflow for the fictional company ABCorp: fetch orders, store them, filter, transform, summarise, notify the team and schedule the run. You then pass the final knowledge check to earn the Level 1 badge, which is the checkpoint for this step and the base for Level 2.
objectives: Navigate the n8n Editor UI: canvas, nodes panel, node details view, executions and workflow settings.
Build a multi-node workflow from a trigger through HTTP Request, Airtable, If, Edit Fields (Set), Code and Discord nodes.
Use credentials and expressions to pass data safely between nodes.
Schedule, activate, export and import a workflow as JSON.
Complete every course exercise and pass the final knowledge check to earn the Level 1 badge.

concepts.explanation: A trigger node starts a workflow. Examples are Manual Trigger, Schedule Trigger and Webhook. Action nodes do the work after the trigger, such as fetching, writing or sending data. A workflow that should run on its own needs a non-manual trigger and must be activated.

concepts.term: Items and the JSON data structure
concepts.explanation: Data moves between nodes as an array of items. Each item wraps its fields in a json key. A node usually runs once for each incoming item. So 30 orders entering a node means 30 runs, unless the node or Code mode processes all items together.

Double-click a node to open its NDV. It shows the input panel, the parameters and the output panel, and you can switch between Table, JSON and Schema views. You can drag fields from the input panel into a parameter to create an expression.

Expressions are written inside {{ }} and are evaluated for each item. For example, {{ $json.orderPrice }} reads a field from the current item. They let a node parameter use data from earlier nodes. The Discord message in the course uses expressions to insert the weekly totals.

Credentials store API keys, tokens or auth headers separately from the workflow, and they are encrypted. In the course you create credentials for the HTTP Request (header auth), Airtable and Discord. Credentials are not included when you export a workflow to JSON.
The If node checks a condition and sends each item to a true output or a false output. In the course it splits orders on orderStatus. Booked orders go one way and processing orders go the other.

This node adds, renames or keeps only selected fields. The course uses it to keep only fields such as orderID and employeeName for processing orders. You can set it to keep only the fields you define.

The Code node runs JavaScript or Python. In 'Run Once for All Items' mode you read every item with $input.all() and return an array of objects with a json key. The course uses it to count booked orders and sum their prices.

Use Test workflow or Test step to execute manually while you build. You can pin a node's output so later tests reuse it without calling the API again. Pinned data is used only in manual runs, never in production executions.

keyFacts: Course URL: docs.n8n.io → Courses → Level one. It is free and text-based. The badge is awarded after you pass the final quiz.
Sample workflow chain: Schedule Trigger → HTTP Request (get orders) → Airtable (insert) → If (orderStatus) → Edit Fields on one branch / Code (totals) → Discord (notify).
The course schedule is weekly: Mondays at 9:00.
A manual run does not make a workflow live. You must activate (publish) it before triggers like Schedule or Webhook fire in production.
Expression syntax is {{ }}. The current item is $json, and a named node's output is $('Node Name').item.json.
Code node output must be an array of objects, each with a json key. For example: return [{ json: { total: 5 } }].
An exported workflow is a JSON file containing nodes, connections and settings. Credentials are not included and must be re-created after import.
The If node has two outputs, true and false. Each output can connect to a different branch.
Workflow settings include the timezone. Schedule Trigger times follow the workflow or instance timezone.

example.caption: Code node ('Run Once for All Items') that counts booked orders and sums their value for the Discord message

pitfalls: Testing with the Manual Trigger and assuming the workflow is live. It only runs on schedule after you add the Schedule Trigger and activate it.
Leaving the Code node in 'Run Once for Each Item' mode. You then get one summary per order instead of a single total.
Returning plain values from the Code node instead of objects wrapped in a json key. This causes errors.
Hard-coding values that should be expressions, or referencing the wrong node name after renaming a node.
Pasting API keys into node parameters instead of using Credentials. Exported JSON can then leak secrets.
Forgetting that pinned data hides real API changes. Unpin before the final test.
