objective.question: You are building a shared alert workflow that should run whenever another workflow fails. Which node must this alert workflow start with?
options: Error Trigger
Execute Workflow Trigger
Schedule Trigger
Webhook
objective.explanation: An error workflow must begin with an Error Trigger node, which receives the failure data. The other triggers start workflows on HTTP calls, schedules or sub-workflow calls, not on failures.

objective.question: Your error workflow is set up correctly but is not activated. A production workflow that uses it fails on a schedule. What happens?
options: The error workflow runs, because it does not need to be activated
n8n activates the error workflow automatically and then runs it
The failed workflow retries three times instead
Nothing runs, because the error workflow is inactive
objective.explanation: An error workflow does not need to be activated to run. Activation is needed for trigger-based workflows like webhooks and schedules, not for the Error Trigger.

objective.question: You open a workflow in the editor, click Execute Workflow, and a node fails. Your error workflow does not send an alert. Why?
options: The Error Trigger must be pinned with test data first
The error workflow must be in the same folder
Manual runs always use Continue on error
Error workflows only run for automatic executions, not manual ones
objective.explanation: Error workflows run only for automatic executions, such as triggers and schedules. Manual runs from the editor show the error in the canvas instead.

objective.question: Where do you link a production workflow to your shared error workflow?
options: In the failing node's Settings tab
In the n8n environment variables only
In the production workflow's Workflow Settings, under Error Workflow
In the Error Trigger node parameters
objective.explanation: Each workflow chooses its error workflow in Workflow Settings. The Error Trigger does not list which workflows it watches.

objective.question: In your Slack alert you want to show which node failed. Which expression from the Error Trigger output should you use?
options: {{ $json.workflow.nodeName }}
{{ $json.error.node }}
{{ $execution.failedNode }}
{{ $json.execution.lastNodeExecuted }}
objective.explanation: The Error Trigger output includes execution.lastNodeExecuted, which is the node where the run stopped. The other paths are not part of the documented output.

objective.question: You want the on-call engineer to click once and open the failed run. Which field should you put in the alert?
options: execution.url
execution.mode
execution.retryOf
workflow.id
objective.explanation: execution.url is a direct link to the failed execution. workflow.id identifies the workflow, execution.mode shows how it ran, and retryOf is only set for retries.

objective.question: An order workflow receives a payload with a missing customer email. No node errors, but you want the run to be marked as failed and trigger the error workflow. What should you add?
options: A Stop and Error node on the invalid branch
Retry On Fail on the next node
A Wait node with a long timeout
A No Operation node
objective.explanation: Stop and Error deliberately throws an error with your message, so the execution fails and the error workflow runs. The other options do not fail the execution.

objective.question: You enable Retry On Fail on an HTTP Request node and do not change anything else. What are the defaults?
options: Max Tries 2, Wait Between Tries 500 ms
Max Tries 3, Wait Between Tries 0 ms
Max Tries 3, Wait Between Tries 1000 ms
Max Tries 5, Wait Between Tries 5000 ms
objective.explanation: The defaults are Max Tries 3 and Wait Between Tries 1000 ms. You can raise the wait for rate-limited APIs.

objective.question: A CRM update node sometimes fails for single records. You want failed items to go to a separate branch that logs them, while good items carry on. Which On Error setting fits?
options: Continue
Continue (using error output)
Retry On Fail with Max Tries 1
Stop Workflow
objective.explanation: Continue (using error output) adds an error output so you can route failed items to their own branch. Continue passes data on without a separate branch, and Stop Workflow halts the run.

objective.question: A node is set to On Error: Continue. It fails during a scheduled run. What is the most likely result?
options: The node retries forever
The workflow is deactivated
The workflow continues, and the error workflow does not run for that node failure
The execution stops and the error workflow runs
objective.explanation: With Continue, n8n carries on to the next node instead of failing the execution, so the error workflow is not triggered by that failure. Stop Workflow is the default behaviour that fails the run.

objective.question: A workflow sometimes hangs for hours because an external API never responds. Which setting best protects the instance at the workflow level?
options: Use the test webhook URL
Set On Error to Continue on the trigger
Turn on Always Output Data
Set a timeout in Workflow Settings so the execution is cancelled after a limit
objective.explanation: The workflow timeout setting stops executions that run past a set time. The other options do not limit run time.

objective.question: You built a reusable 'Send invoice' sub-workflow. You want only workflows in the same project to call it. Where do you control this?
options: Instance environment variables
The Error Trigger node
Sub-workflow's Workflow Settings > This workflow can be called by
Execute Workflow node > Options > Permissions
objective.explanation: The setting 'This workflow can be called by' in the sub-workflow's Workflow Settings controls which workflows may run it. The calling node has no permission setting.

objective.question: Your team worries that splitting a big workflow into sub-workflows will use up the plan's execution quota faster. What does n8n document?
options: Sub-workflow executions do not count toward the plan's execution limits
Sub-workflows count double
Only sub-workflows that fail are counted
Each sub-workflow run counts as a full execution
objective.explanation: n8n documents that sub-workflow executions do not count toward plan execution limits. Only the parent execution counts.

objective.question: A partner calls your production webhook URL and gets a 404 error, but the test URL works when you click 'Listen for test event'. What is the most likely cause?
options: Header Auth is missing
The Respond to Webhook node is missing
Retry On Fail is off
The workflow is not active
objective.explanation: Production webhook URLs only work when the workflow is active. Test URLs work only while the editor is listening.

objective.question: Your Webhook node uses Respond: 'Using Respond to Webhook Node'. On one IF branch there is no Respond to Webhook node. What happens when a request takes that branch?
options: The caller gets an error or waits, because no response node was reached
The webhook switches to the test URL
The request is retried on the other branch
n8n sends an empty 200 response automatically and silently
objective.explanation: With this option, the workflow must reach a Respond to Webhook node. If a branch skips it, the caller gets an error or waits for a response.

objective.question: Your alert workflow uses {{$json.execution.url}} to link to the failed run. For one failure the link is empty. The Error Trigger output for that failure is shown below. Why is the link empty?
options: The error happened in the trigger node, so n8n sends less data and there is no execution object
The workflow setting 'Save failed production executions' is off, which removes all error fields
The execution was a manual run from the editor, which never includes a URL
The error workflow was not activated, so n8n dropped the execution fields
objective.explanation: When the main workflow fails in its trigger node, the Error Trigger receives a smaller payload with a 'trigger' object and no execution ID or URL. Manual runs do not reach the error workflow at all, and the other options do not change the payload shape.

objective.question: An HTTP Request node calls a slow reporting API. Sometimes the API holds the connection open for many minutes. You want only this call to give up after 30 seconds so its error can be handled, while the rest of the workflow has no time limit. What should you configure?
options: Set the HTTP Request node option 'Timeout' to 30000 milliseconds
Add a Wait node set to 30 seconds before the HTTP Request node
Enable Retry On Fail with Wait Between Tries set to 30000 ms
Set the workflow setting 'Timeout Workflow' to 30 seconds
objective.explanation: The HTTP Request node has its own Timeout option in milliseconds that fails only that request. A workflow timeout would stop the whole run, Retry On Fail does not limit how long one attempt takes, and a Wait node only adds a delay.

objective.question: A payment API is down for 10 minutes. The 'Charge card' node below runs during that time. What happens?

code.code:
{
  "name": "Charge card",
  "type": "n8n-nodes-base.httpRequest",
  "retryOnFail": true,
  "maxTries": 4,
  "waitBetweenTries": 2000,
  "onError": "continueErrorOutput"
}

options: The node tries once, then sends the items to the error output, because the error output disables retries
The node tries 4 times, then stops the workflow and triggers the error workflow
The node retries every 2 seconds until the API comes back, because Retry On Fail has no limit
The node tries 4 times about 2 seconds apart, then sends the failed items to its error output and the run keeps going
objective.explanation: Retries happen first: up to Max Tries attempts with the configured wait. After the last failed attempt, 'Continue (using error output)' routes the items to the error branch instead of stopping the run, so the error workflow does not fire unless you fail the run later.

objective.question: A self-hosted n8n instance has the environment variables shown. A user opens a workflow's settings and wants a 15-minute timeout. What is true?

code.code:
EXECUTIONS_TIMEOUT=300
EXECUTIONS_TIMEOUT_MAX=600

options: The user can set 15 minutes, because workflow settings always override environment variables
Timeouts only apply to manual executions, so production runs are unaffected
Workflows with no timeout of their own stop after 5 minutes, and a workflow can be given at most 10 minutes, not 15
All workflows stop after 600 seconds, and per-workflow timeouts are ignored
objective.explanation: EXECUTIONS_TIMEOUT sets the default timeout in seconds for all workflows. EXECUTIONS_TIMEOUT_MAX caps what a user can set on a single workflow, so 15 minutes is above the 600-second limit.

objective.question: A Webhook node has Respond set to 'When Last Node Finishes' and Response Data set to 'First Entry JSON'. The last node outputs three items. What does the caller receive?
options: A JSON array with all three items
The JSON of the first item output by the last node that ran
The original request body sent back to the caller
An empty 200 response sent right away
objective.explanation: 'First Entry JSON' returns the JSON of the first item from the last executed node, after the workflow finishes. 'All Entries' would return every item, and 'Immediately' would reply before processing.

objective.question: You are building a 'Create customer' sub-workflow. You want the parent's Execute Workflow node to show named input fields (email, name, plan) so builders can map values without guessing. How should you set the sub-workflow trigger ('When Executed by Another Workflow')?
options: Add a Set node after the trigger that creates email, name and plan
Put the field names in the sub-workflow's description so the parent can read them
Input data mode: 'Define using fields below', and add email, name and plan
Input data mode: 'Accept all data'
objective.explanation: Defining the input fields on the sub-workflow trigger makes them appear as mappable inputs in the parent's Execute Workflow node. 'Accept all data' passes anything through with no visible contract, and a Set node or a description does not create inputs for the parent.

objective.question: A parent workflow passes 100 invoice items to an Execute Workflow node. The sub-workflow was written to handle one invoice per run, and you want a separate sub-workflow execution for each invoice. Which setting fits?
options: Mode: 'Run once for each item'
Turn off 'Wait For Sub-Workflow Completion'
Add a Loop Over Items node inside the sub-workflow
Mode: 'Run once with all items'
objective.explanation: 'Run once for each item' starts one sub-workflow execution per input item. 'Run once with all items' sends all 100 items to a single run, and turning off waiting only controls whether the parent waits for the result.

objective.question: A partner can only authenticate by sending a fixed API key in an 'X-API-Key' request header. Which Webhook node authentication should you choose?
options: JWT Auth
None, then check the IP(s) Whitelist option instead
Header Auth
Basic Auth
objective.explanation: Header Auth checks that a named header carries the expected value, which matches a static API key. Basic Auth expects a username and password, JWT Auth expects a signed token, and an IP allowlist does not check the key at all.

objective.question: A webhook workflow must reply to the caller within a few seconds. After replying, it calls a sub-workflow that takes 5 minutes to build a report. The parent does not need the report's output. Which Execute Workflow setting best fits?
options: Enable Retry On Fail on the Execute Workflow node
Set the workflow timeout of the parent to 5 minutes
Set Mode to 'Run once for each item'
Turn off 'Wait For Sub-Workflow Completion'
objective.explanation: With 'Wait For Sub-Workflow Completion' turned off, the parent starts the sub-workflow and carries on without waiting for its result. The other settings do not stop the parent from waiting.

subjective.question: What is an error workflow in n8n and how do you set one up?
subjective.answer: An error workflow is a separate workflow that runs when another workflow fails during an automatic execution. First, I create a new workflow that starts with an Error Trigger node. Then I add the alert steps, for example a Slack, email or Telegram node that sends the workflow name, the failing node, the error message and a link to the run. Next, I open each production workflow, go to Workflow Settings, and choose this workflow under Error Workflow. I save. The error workflow does not need to be activated. To test it, I add a Stop and Error node to a test workflow linked to it and run it through its trigger, not with the manual Execute button, because manual runs do not call the error workflow.
keyPoints: Starts with an Error Trigger node
Linked from each workflow's Workflow Settings
Does not need to be activated
Runs only for automatic executions

subjective.question: Describe the data the Error Trigger outputs and which fields you would use in an alert.
subjective.answer: The Error Trigger outputs one item describing the failure. It has an execution object and a workflow object. Under execution there are fields like id, url, lastNodeExecuted, mode, and an error object with message and stack. Under workflow there are id and name. In an alert I use workflow.name so people know which process broke, execution.lastNodeExecuted to show the failing node, execution.error.message for the reason, and execution.url so the engineer can open the failed run in one click. I may add execution.mode to show if it was a trigger or retry. One edge case: if the failure happens in the trigger node itself, the output has a trigger object instead of full execution details, so my alert expressions should handle missing fields without breaking.
keyPoints: execution and workflow objects
lastNodeExecuted for the failing node
error.message for the reason
execution.url links to the run
Trigger failures give a different shape

subjective.question: Why did your error workflow not fire when you tested it, and how would you test it properly?
subjective.answer: The most common reason is that I ran the workflow manually with Execute Workflow in the editor. Error workflows run only for automatic executions, so a manual failure shows in the canvas but sends no alert. Other reasons are that the failing workflow was not linked under Workflow Settings > Error Workflow, or that the failing node was set to Continue, so the run did not actually fail. To test properly, I create a small test workflow with a Schedule Trigger or a Webhook, add a Stop and Error node with a clear message like 'Forced failure test', link it to the error workflow, and activate it. Then I let the schedule fire or call the production webhook URL. I check that the alert arrives with the failing node name and execution link.
keyPoints: Manual runs do not trigger error workflows
Check the Error Workflow setting
Continue settings hide failures
Use Stop and Error plus an automatic trigger

subjective.question: When would you use the Stop and Error node?
subjective.answer: I use Stop and Error when the data is wrong even though no node has technically failed. For example, an order webhook arrives without an email, or an API returns status 200 but with a body saying 'failed'. Without Stop and Error, the workflow would finish as successful and nobody would know. I put an IF node to check the condition and, on the bad branch, a Stop and Error node with a clear message, such as 'Order 123 missing customer email'. This marks the execution as failed, so it appears in the execution list and triggers the error workflow. It is also the easiest way to force a failure when testing alerts. I can give a simple message or an error object with more detail.
keyPoints: Turns a business rule violation into a failure
Usually after an IF or Switch check
Triggers the error workflow
Useful for testing alerts

subjective.question: Explain Retry On Fail and when you would change its default values.
subjective.answer: Retry On Fail is a node setting. When enabled, if the node errors, n8n runs it again before giving up. The defaults are Max Tries 3 and Wait Between Tries 1000 ms. It is good for temporary problems such as a network glitch, a 502 or 503 from an API, or a short database lock. I change the defaults when the cause needs more time. For rate-limited APIs that return 429, I increase the wait to several seconds so I do not hit the limit again straight away. For a flaky but critical service, I may raise Max Tries. I do not rely on retries for permanent errors like bad credentials or invalid input, because retrying only delays the failure. If all tries fail, the On Error setting decides what happens next.
keyPoints: Defaults: 3 tries, 1000 ms wait
For temporary errors only
Increase wait for rate limits
On Error applies after retries are used up

subjective.question: Compare the three On Error options: Stop Workflow, Continue, and Continue (using error output).
subjective.answer: Stop Workflow is the default. If the node fails, the execution stops, is marked as failed, and the error workflow runs. I use it when later steps must not run on bad data. Continue lets the workflow go on to the next node as if the node had passed, carrying error information in the data. It is useful for optional steps, like enriching a lead from a third-party service, but it can hide failures because the run looks successful. Continue (using error output) adds a second output to the node. Successful items go out the normal output and failed items go out the error output. I use this for item-level handling, for example sending failed records to a Google Sheet or a retry queue while good records continue. It gives control without stopping the whole run.
keyPoints: Stop Workflow is default and triggers error workflow
Continue can hide failures
Error output splits good and failed items
Choose based on whether later steps depend on the node

subjective.question: How do timeouts help make workflows reliable in n8n?
subjective.answer: Timeouts stop a workflow or a request from running forever. At the workflow level, Workflow Settings has a timeout option. If I enable it and set a time, n8n cancels executions that run longer than that. This protects the instance from stuck runs that hold memory and workers, especially on self-hosted setups. At the node level, the HTTP Request node has a timeout option, so a call that hangs fails after a set time instead of waiting. Combined with Retry On Fail, a hung request fails fast, retries, and if it still fails, the error workflow alerts me. I set timeouts based on normal run times with some margin, so slow but valid runs are not killed. Self-hosted admins can also set instance-level limits on maximum timeout.
keyPoints: Workflow-level timeout in Workflow Settings
HTTP Request node timeout option
Prevents stuck runs using resources
Works with retries and error workflows

subjective.question: What are sub-workflows and why would you use them?
subjective.answer: A sub-workflow is a workflow called by another workflow using the Execute Workflow node (shown as Execute Sub-workflow in newer versions). The sub-workflow starts with the Execute Workflow Trigger, labelled 'When Executed by Another Workflow'. I use them for three reasons. First, reuse: logic like 'send invoice' or 'look up customer' is built once and called from many workflows. Second, maintainability: large workflows are split into smaller parts that are easier to read, test and fix. Third, performance: processing heavy data in a sub-workflow can reduce memory use in the parent. n8n also documents that sub-workflow executions do not count toward plan execution limits. I define the inputs the sub-workflow expects, so callers pass clean data, and the last node's output is returned to the parent.
keyPoints: Execute Workflow node calls it
Starts with Execute Workflow Trigger
Reuse, readability, memory
Does not count toward execution limits
Last node output returns to parent

subjective.question: How do you control who can call a sub-workflow, and why does it matter?
subjective.answer: In the sub-workflow I open Workflow Settings and use the option 'This workflow can be called by'. I can restrict it so no other workflows can call it, allow only workflows in the same project, or allow specific workflows by ID, depending on the version and plan. This matters for security and stability. A sub-workflow might send payments, delete records or use powerful credentials. If any workflow could call it, a careless or test workflow could trigger real actions. Restricting callers also makes changes safer, because I know exactly which parents depend on it. Before changing a sub-workflow's inputs, I check its callers so I do not break them. This is a simple control that is often missed in team instances.
keyPoints: Setting is in the sub-workflow's Workflow Settings
Restricts which workflows may call it
Protects sensitive actions and credentials
Helps track dependencies

subjective.question: How do errors behave between a parent workflow and a sub-workflow?
subjective.answer: When the parent waits for the sub-workflow to complete, which is the default, a failure inside the sub-workflow makes the Execute Workflow node in the parent fail. The parent then follows that node's settings. If On Error is Stop Workflow, the parent fails and its error workflow runs. I can also use Retry On Fail or the error output on the Execute Workflow node to handle the failure in the parent. The sub-workflow has its own Workflow Settings too, so it can have its own error workflow. I avoid double alerts by deciding where alerting happens, usually in the shared error workflow linked to both. If the parent does not wait for completion, the parent continues and will not see the sub-workflow's failure, so the sub-workflow's own error workflow becomes important.
keyPoints: Sub-workflow failure fails the calling node
Parent node settings decide next step
Sub-workflow can have own error workflow
Not waiting means parent will not see failure

subjective.question: Explain the difference between a webhook's test URL and production URL.
subjective.answer: Each Webhook node has two URLs. The test URL contains webhook-test in the path. It only works while the editor is listening, after I click 'Listen for test event' or execute the workflow. It shows the incoming data on the canvas, which is great for building and debugging, and it stops listening after one call or a timeout. The production URL uses webhook in the path. It only works when the workflow is active. Data does not appear live in the editor; I check it in the execution list. A common mistake is giving a partner the test URL, which then fails once I close the editor, or giving the production URL before activating, which returns a not found error. Only production executions are automatic, so only they trigger the error workflow.
keyPoints: Test URL needs editor listening
Production URL needs active workflow
Test shows data on canvas; production in executions
Only production runs trigger error workflows

subjective.question: How would you secure a public webhook in n8n?
subjective.answer: First, I set Authentication on the Webhook node. The options include Basic Auth, Header Auth and JWT Auth. Header Auth is common for server-to-server calls: the caller sends a secret header, such as an API key, and n8n rejects requests without it. I store the secret in an n8n credential, not in the workflow. Second, I restrict the HTTP method to the one expected, usually POST. Third, where supported, I use the IP allowlist option to accept only the sender's IPs. Fourth, for services that sign payloads, like payment gateways, I verify the signature in the workflow and use Stop and Error when it does not match. Finally, I validate the payload fields and keep the instance on HTTPS. Unauthenticated webhooks can be found and abused, so I never leave sensitive ones open.
keyPoints: Basic, Header or JWT authentication
Secrets stored as credentials
Restrict method and IPs
Verify signatures and validate payload

subjective.question: Describe the Respond options on the Webhook node and the main pitfall.
subjective.answer: The Webhook node's Respond setting decides when the caller gets a reply. 'Immediately' returns a response as soon as the request arrives, which suits fire-and-forget events. 'When Last Node Finishes' waits for the workflow to end and returns data from the last node, useful for simple APIs. 'Using Respond to Webhook Node' lets me control the reply myself: I place a Respond to Webhook node where I want and set the body, status code and headers. The pitfall is that the workflow must reach a Respond to Webhook node. If an IF branch or an error path skips it, the caller gets an error or waits until it times out. So I add a response on every branch, including error branches, for example returning 400 for invalid input. I also keep slow work after the response when callers have short timeouts.
keyPoints: Immediately, When Last Node Finishes, Respond to Webhook node
Respond node controls body, code, headers
Every branch must reach a response
Respond early when callers have short timeouts

subjective.question: Design a production-grade alert for failed workflows. What would the message contain and where would it go?
subjective.answer: I build one shared error workflow starting with an Error Trigger and link every production workflow to it. The message goes to a channel the team watches, like a Slack or Teams channel, plus email for critical workflows. It contains the workflow name from workflow.name, the failing node from execution.lastNodeExecuted, the error text from execution.error.message, the time, and a link from execution.url to open the run. I may add execution.mode and whether it was a retry using execution.retryOf. To avoid noise, I can use a Switch on workflow.name to route critical workflows to an on-call tool and others to a low-priority channel. I also make the error workflow simple and robust, because if it fails, nobody is alerted. I test it with a forced failure using Stop and Error on an active test workflow.
keyPoints: Shared error workflow for all production workflows
Name, failing node, message, link
Route by severity
Keep it simple and test it

subjective.question: A webhook-based order workflow calls a flaky payment API and a CRM. How would you combine this week's features to make it reliable?
subjective.answer: I start with the Webhook node using Header Auth and Respond 'Using Respond to Webhook Node'. After validating the payload with an IF node, I send a quick 202 response if the caller only needs acknowledgement, or a 400 with a Stop and Error on invalid data. For the payment API, I enable Retry On Fail and raise the wait to handle short outages, and set a timeout on the HTTP Request so it never hangs. The CRM update moves into a sub-workflow so other flows can reuse it; its 'This workflow can be called by' setting is restricted to the project. On the CRM node I use Continue (using error output) to log failed records without blocking orders. I set a workflow timeout and link the shared error workflow so any hard failure alerts us with the failing node and execution link.
keyPoints: Authenticated webhook with controlled responses
Retries and timeouts on flaky API
Reusable restricted sub-workflow
Error output for item-level failures
Error workflow for hard failures

subjective.question: A colleague wrote this Slack message text in the shared error workflow. Explain what it shows, then describe a situation where it breaks and how you would make it robust.
subjective.answer: The message shows the workflow name, the last node executed (usually the failing node), the error message, the execution mode, and a link to the failed run. It works for errors in normal nodes. It breaks when the failure is in the main workflow's trigger node. Then the Error Trigger sends a smaller payload with a 'trigger' object and no 'execution' object, so the node, URL and message lines come out empty. To make it robust, I would add an IF node that checks whether $json.execution exists. One branch sends the normal alert. The other sends a trigger-failure alert using $json.trigger.error.message and a link to the workflow built from $json.workflow.id. I could also use fallback values in the expression, for example the ?? operator, so an empty field reads 'n/a' instead of a blank. Finally, I would force both kinds of failure to confirm that each branch works.
keyPoints: Identifies the fields: workflow name, lastNodeExecuted, error message, mode, url
Trigger-node failures send a reduced payload with no execution object
Branch on whether execution exists, or use fallback values
Uses trigger.error.message for trigger failures
Tests both failure types

subjective.question: Your self-hosted n8n runs behind a reverse proxy at https://automation.example.in. Error alerts arrive, but the 'Open run' link points to http://localhost:5678/... and partners see localhost in webhook URLs. Diagnose and fix.
subjective.answer: n8n builds the links it shows from its own settings. Behind a reverse proxy, it does not know its public address unless you tell it, so it falls back to localhost and the internal port. The execution URL in the Error Trigger and the webhook URLs on the Webhook node both depend on this. The fix is to set the public URL in environment variables. WEBHOOK_URL should be https://automation.example.in/ so webhook test and production URLs are correct. N8N_EDITOR_BASE_URL should also point to the public address, so links into the editor, such as execution links, are correct. The proxy must also forward the right headers and support the paths n8n uses. After restarting n8n, I would check the Webhook node's URLs, then force a failure and click the alert link. I would also tell partners to update any URL they copied while it showed localhost.
keyPoints: n8n does not know its public URL behind a proxy by default
Set WEBHOOK_URL to the public HTTPS address
Set N8N_EDITOR_BASE_URL so editor and execution links are correct
Restart, then verify the webhook URLs and the alert link
Partners must update any wrong URLs they copied

subjective.question: You enabled Retry On Fail on a node that creates orders in an ERP. Finance now reports duplicate orders. What happened, and how do you make retries safe?
subjective.answer: Retry On Fail re-runs the node when it errors. But an error does not always mean the request failed on the server. A timeout or a dropped connection can happen after the ERP has already created the order. The retry then sends the same create request again, which makes a duplicate. To make retries safe, the operation must be idempotent. The best option is an idempotency key, if the API supports one. I would base it on something stable, such as the source order ID, so the ERP ignores repeat requests. If the API has no such feature, I would check first: search for an order with that external ID, and create it only if none exists. Or I would use an upsert endpoint. I would keep retries on read calls and safe updates, reduce Max Tries on create calls, and send real failures to an error output for review instead of blind retries.
keyPoints: An error can happen after the server already did the work
Retrying non-idempotent creates causes duplicates
Use idempotency keys based on a stable source ID
Otherwise check-then-create, or use upsert
Limit retries on create calls and route failures for review

subjective.question: An API you call returns HTTP 429 with a 'Retry-After: 60' header when you exceed its rate limit. Retry On Fail does not solve it. Why not, and how would you handle it in n8n?
subjective.answer: Retry On Fail waits a fixed time between tries, and that time has a low ceiling of a few seconds. It also ignores the Retry-After header. So all the retries hit the limit again and the node still fails. I would handle it in three ways. First, prevent most 429s: use the HTTP Request node's batching options, or Loop Over Items with a Wait node, to slow the request rate. Second, handle the 429 that still happens. I would set the node to 'Continue (using error output)', or turn on the option to always output the response, then check the status code with an IF node. On a 429, a Wait node pauses for the Retry-After value, then the flow loops back to try again. Third, I would add a counter so the loop stops after a few attempts and then fails the run with Stop and Error, so the error workflow alerts someone.
keyPoints: Retry On Fail uses a short fixed wait and ignores Retry-After
Throttle with batching or Loop Over Items plus Wait
Catch the 429 with the error output or the response status code
Wait for the Retry-After value, then loop back
Cap the attempts and escalate with Stop and Error

subjective.question: Explain what this design does and why it is better than letting the workflow fail on bad input.

code.code:
Webhook (POST /orders, Header Auth, Respond: Using 'Respond to Webhook' Node)
  -> IF  {{ $json.body.email }} is not empty AND {{ $json.body.amount }} > 0
       true  -> Respond to Webhook (Response Code 202, JSON {"status":"accepted"})
                -> Execute Workflow 'Process order'
       false -> Respond to Webhook (Response Code 400, JSON {"error":"email and positive amount required"})

subjective.answer: The Webhook node accepts POST requests on /orders only when the right auth header is present. It does not reply by itself. The reply comes from a Respond to Webhook node. The IF node checks the payload. If the email and amount are valid, the caller gets 202 Accepted at once, and then the order is processed in a sub-workflow. If not, the caller gets 400 with a clear message and no processing happens. This is better than failing because the caller learns exactly what was wrong and can fix it, instead of getting a generic 500 error or a timeout. Bad input is the caller's problem, not an incident, so it does not create noise in the error workflow. Replying 202 before the heavy work keeps the response fast. Every branch has a Respond to Webhook node, which avoids requests hanging without a reply.
keyPoints: Header Auth protects the endpoint
Validation is done with IF before any processing
202 for accepted, 400 with a clear message for bad input
Early reply keeps the caller fast; processing runs in a sub-workflow
Every branch responds, and bad input does not trigger false alerts

subjective.question: Your shared error workflow posts to Slack. One night a downstream API outage made a high-frequency workflow fail 400 times, and the channel flooded. How would you redesign alerting to avoid this?
subjective.answer: I would add grouping and throttling inside the error workflow. First, build a key from the workflow ID plus the failing node, or a short form of the error message. Then I would store the last alert time for each key, for example in a Data Table, a database or Redis. If the same key alerted within the last 15 minutes, the workflow only increases a counter and does not post. When the window ends, it sends one summary such as '400 failures in 15 minutes', with a link to the latest run. I would also route by severity. Critical workflows page the on-call person, and the rest go to a digest channel. At the source, the high-frequency workflow should handle known outage errors better, using retries and the error output, so one outage does not mean hundreds of failed runs. I would also check that the error workflow itself cannot fail silently.
keyPoints: Dedupe by a key such as workflow ID plus node or error
Store state outside the run (Data Table, database, Redis)
Throttle within a time window and send summary counts
Route by severity: page for critical, digest for the rest
Reduce failures at the source with retries and error outputs

subjective.question: A partner's system times out after 10 seconds, but your webhook workflow takes about 2 minutes to enrich and save each event. The partner keeps re-sending events. How would you redesign the webhook?
subjective.answer: The partner waits for a reply. When none comes within 10 seconds, it treats the request as failed and sends it again, which causes duplicates. I would acknowledge fast and process later. In the simplest form, I set the Webhook node to Respond: 'Immediately', or I use a Respond to Webhook node right after a quick validation step, returning 202 or 200. Then the slow work runs. It can stay in the same run, or I can hand it to a sub-workflow with 'Wait For Sub-Workflow Completion' turned off. For very high volume, the webhook could write the event to a queue or table, and a separate workflow processes it. Because partners may still re-send, I would store the partner's event ID and skip events I have already seen. Failures in the slow part go to the error workflow, since the partner has already received its reply.
keyPoints: The caller timeout causes re-sends and duplicates
Reply quickly: Respond Immediately or an early Respond to Webhook
Process asynchronously, for example a sub-workflow without waiting
Deduplicate on the partner's event ID
Alert on processing failures through the error workflow

subjective.question: A CRM sync processes 500 records. You use 'Continue (using error output)' so good records continue. But the ops team wants the run marked as failed and alerted if any record failed. How do you build this?
subjective.answer: I keep the error output so one bad record does not block the other 499. The error branch collects the failed items, with the record ID and the error message, and writes them to a log such as a sheet, a table or a database. At the end, I merge or aggregate this branch so I know how many failures there were. I make sure this check runs after the main branch finishes, so the whole batch is handled first. Then an IF node checks whether the failure count is greater than zero. If it is, a Stop and Error node fails the run with a clear message, for example '7 of 500 records failed, see log'. A custom error object can include the count and the log link. Because the run now ends with an error, the workflow's error workflow fires, and the alert shows the Stop and Error node and its message. If there were no failures, the run ends as successful.
keyPoints: Keep the error output so good items continue
Log failed items with their ID and error
Count the failures after the batch completes
IF count > 0, then Stop and Error with a clear message
The run is marked failed, so the error workflow alerts

subjective.question: A payment provider signs each webhook with an HMAC-SHA256 signature in a header, computed over the raw request body. The Webhook node has no built-in option for this. How would you verify it in n8n, and what self-hosting setting may you need?
subjective.answer: The signature is computed over the exact bytes that were sent, so I need the raw body, not re-serialised JSON. In the Webhook node I turn on the Raw Body option. Then a Code node computes the HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body with the shared secret, using Node's crypto module. It compares the result with the header value using a constant-time comparison, and checks the timestamp if the provider sends one, to block replay attacks. If they do not match, the flow goes to a Respond to Webhook node that returns 401, and nothing else runs. If they match, processing continues. On self-hosted n8n, the Code node blocks built-in modules by default, so I need to set NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN to include crypto. I keep the secret out of the workflow JSON, for example in a credential or an environment variable, and I use HTTPS.
keyPoints: Use the raw body because the signature is over exact bytes
Compute the HMAC in a Code node and compare in constant time
Reject with 401 via Respond to Webhook before any processing
Self-hosted: set NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN to allow crypto
Keep the secret out of the workflow JSON and check timestamps against replay

steps.overview: This step teaches you to build AI agent workflows in n8n. You will connect the AI Agent node to a chat model, memory and tools, and use RAG so the agent answers from your own documents. The official Level 1 and Level 2 courses focus on core workflow skills, so treat this as practical, interview-ready knowledge that builds on those skills, including error handling and sub-workflows.
objectives: Configure an AI Agent node with a chat model, a system message and a Chat Trigger.
Add conversation memory and keep sessions separate with a session ID.
Attach tools such as the HTTP Request Tool, Call n8n Workflow Tool and a vector store, and write clear tool descriptions.
Build a RAG pipeline that loads, splits, embeds, stores and retrieves documents.
Test that the agent answers from documents and calls a ticket tool only when it is needed.

concepts.explanation: The AI Agent is a cluster root node. It takes a user message, reasons with the connected chat model and decides which tools to call. Current versions work as a tools agent, which uses the model's native tool or function calling. It needs at least one chat model sub-node, and it will not run without one.

AI features in n8n are built as a root node with sub-nodes attached to typed connectors: Chat Model, Memory, Tool, Embeddings, Document Loader and Text Splitter. Sub-nodes do not run on their own. Expressions inside a sub-node resolve against the first item only, unlike normal nodes, which run once per item.

The 'When chat message received' trigger starts the workflow from n8n's built-in chat UI or from an embedded or hosted chat. It outputs chatInput, which is the user text, and sessionId. Memory nodes use sessionId by default to keep each conversation separate.

Simple Memory (formerly Window Buffer Memory) keeps the last N interactions inside the n8n instance and suits testing. Postgres Chat Memory and Redis Chat Memory store history externally, so it survives restarts and works in queue mode. Context Window Length controls how many past interactions are sent back to the model.

A tool is a sub-node the agent may call, for example the HTTP Request Tool, the Call n8n Workflow Tool, app tools such as Notion or Gmail, or a vector store tool. The model picks a tool based on its name and description, so the description is effectively your routing logic. Write clearly when the tool should be used and when it should not.

$fromAI('key', 'description', 'type') lets the model fill a tool parameter at run time, for example a ticket title or priority. You can also click the 'Let the model define this parameter' button on a tool field. This replaces hard-coded values and avoids extra placeholder setup.

RAG grounds answers in your data. At ingest time, documents are loaded with the Default Data Loader, split with the Recursive Character Text Splitter, turned into vectors by an Embeddings node and inserted into a vector store. At query time, the user question is embedded and the top-K similar chunks are retrieved and passed to the model as context.

Supported stores include Simple Vector Store (in-memory), PGVector, Pinecone, Qdrant and Supabase. Each store has operation modes: insert documents, get many, retrieve documents for a chain or tool, and retrieve documents as a tool for the AI Agent. Ingest and query must use the same embedding model.

This tool lets the agent run another workflow that starts with 'When Executed by Another Workflow'. You define the input fields, and the model fills them. It is the cleanest way to wrap multi-step actions such as creating a ticket, with validation and error handling kept in a reusable sub-workflow.

keyFacts: An AI Agent must have a chat model connected. Memory and tools are optional, but without tools it is only a chatbot.
Agent Max Iterations defaults to 10. It caps tool-call loops so a confused agent cannot run forever.
The Chat Trigger supplies sessionId, and memory nodes read it by default. With a non-chat trigger you must define the session key yourself, for example with an expression.

Simple Memory and Simple Vector Store are held in instance memory. Their data is lost on restart and is not suitable for production or queue mode; use Postgres or Redis memory and PGVector, Qdrant or Pinecone instead.
Embedding dimensions must match the vector index. For example, OpenAI text-embedding-3-small gives 1536 dimensions. Changing the model means re-embedding all documents.
Use two flows for RAG: an ingest flow (manual or scheduled trigger, then load, split, embed, insert) and a query flow (chat, then agent, then a retrieve-as-tool vector store).
Chunk size and overlap in the text splitter affect retrieval quality. Overlap keeps context across chunk boundaries.
Sub-node expressions resolve only against the first input item.
Credentials for model providers (OpenAI, Anthropic and others) are set on the chat model and embeddings sub-nodes, not on the AI Agent node.

example.caption: Support agent wiring, system message and ticket tool parameters
example.code:
WORKFLOW A - Ingest (run once or on a schedule)
Manual Trigger -> Google Drive / Read Files -> PGVector Store [Insert Documents]
   PGVector sub-nodes: Embeddings OpenAI (text-embedding-3-small)
                       Default Data Loader -> Recursive Character Text Splitter (chunk 1000, overlap 200)

WORKFLOW B - Support agent
When chat message received -> AI Agent
   Chat Model : Anthropic Chat Model
   Memory     : Postgres Chat Memory (session key = {{ $json.sessionId }}, window 10)
   Tool 1     : PGVector Store [Retrieve Documents (As Tool for AI Agent)]
                name: product_docs  topK: 4  + same Embeddings OpenAI model
                description: Search official product docs. Use for any how-to or policy question.
   Tool 2     : Call n8n Workflow Tool -> 'Create Ticket' sub-workflow
                name: create_ticket
                description: Create a support ticket ONLY if docs do not solve the issue
                             or the user explicitly asks for a human/ticket.
                inputs: title    = {{ $fromAI('title', 'Short issue summary', 'string') }}
                        priority = {{ $fromAI('priority', 'low, medium or high', 'string') }}
                        email    = {{ $fromAI('email', 'Customer email', 'string') }}

System message:
You are the support assistant for Acme. Always search product_docs first.
Answer only from retrieved content and cite the doc title.
If the docs do not cover it, say so and offer a ticket.
Call create_ticket only after the user agrees and gives an email.

WORKFLOW C - Create Ticket
When Executed by Another Workflow -> Notion [Create database page] -> Set {ticketId}

pitfalls: Using different embedding models for insert and retrieve. Similarity search returns rubbish or fails on a dimension mismatch.
Vague tool descriptions such as 'creates tickets'. The agent then opens tickets for simple questions. State the trigger conditions explicitly in the tool description and in the system message.
Relying on Simple Memory or Simple Vector Store in production. Data disappears on restart and is not shared across workers in queue mode.
Forgetting the session key when the workflow is not started by the Chat Trigger, for example a webhook or Telegram. All users then share one conversation history.
Putting all documents into the system prompt instead of using RAG. This wastes tokens, hits context limits and gets stale.
Not handling tool errors. Add error handling in the ticket sub-workflow and return a clear message so the agent can tell the user what happened instead of looping until Max Iterations.

project.title: support-agent-rag
project.summary: A self-hosted n8n support agent for a fictional product, CloudNotes. It answers questions from your own Markdown documents using RAG, and it calls a ticket tool only when the documents cannot solve the problem and the user agrees. docker-compose.yml and .env.example run n8n with a mock ticket API. docs/ holds the knowledge base. Workflow 1 loads, splits, embeds and stores the documents. Workflow 2 is the ticket tool, a sub-workflow that reads $fromAI() inputs and calls an HTTP API. Workflow 3 is the AI Agent root node, with a Chat Trigger and four sub-nodes: chat model, memory, vector store tool and Call n8n Workflow Tool.
project.run:
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec n8n n8n import:workflow --separate --input=/workflows
open http://localhost:5678  # create owner account, add OpenAI credential to the 4 OpenAI sub-nodes
# Run workflow '1 - Ingest support docs' once, then open '3 - Support agent' and click 'Open chat'

files.code:
# support-agent-rag (n8n Step 6: AI agents)

A support chatbot that answers ONLY from `docs/` and creates a ticket only when needed.

## What each part teaches
- **Chat Trigger**: gives the agent a chat window and a `sessionId` for memory.
- **AI Agent (root node)**: a cluster node. Sub-nodes plug into it:
  - Chat model (OpenAI `gpt-4o-mini`), which does the reasoning.
  - Simple Memory (window buffer), which keeps the last 10 messages per session.
  - Tool `search_docs`: an In-Memory Vector Store in *retrieve-as-tool* mode (RAG).
  - Tool `create_ticket`: a Call n8n Workflow Tool. Its inputs are filled by `$fromAI()`.
- **RAG pipeline** (workflow 1): Read files, then Default Data Loader, then Recursive Character Text Splitter, then OpenAI Embeddings, then insert into vector store key `support_docs`.
- **Tool descriptions** decide WHEN the model calls a tool. Read them in workflow 3.

## Setup
1. `cp .env.example .env` and set a long random `N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.
2. `docker compose up -d`, then import the workflows (see the run commands).
3. In the n8n UI, create one **OpenAI** credential. Select it on:
   - the Embeddings node in workflow 1;
   - the Embeddings node and the Chat Model node in workflow 3.
4. Run **1 - Ingest support docs** once.
   - The in-memory store is cleared on every n8n restart, so run it again after each restart.
   - For production, use Pinecone, Qdrant, PGVector or Supabase.
5. Activate or open **3 - Support agent** and click **Open chat**.

## Checkpoint tests
| Message | Expected |
|---|---|
| How long do refunds take? | Answer from docs, using `search_docs` only |
| How do I export notes to PDF? | Answer from docs, no ticket |
| My sync has failed for 3 days, nothing in docs helps | Agent asks for your email, confirms, then calls `create_ticket` |

Check **Executions**. Open a run and look at the agent's tool calls. `create_ticket` must appear only in the third case.

## Notes
- The mock ticket API is `httpbin` at `TICKET_API_URL=http://tickets/post`. It echoes the payload back.
- Workflow 3 calls workflow 2 by its fixed ID `createTicket0001`. That ID is set in the JSON, so the link survives import.
- `N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO` limits the Read Files node to `/data/docs`.

# n8n + a mock ticket API, all local
services:
  n8n:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "5678:5678"            # n8n editor + chat at http://localhost:5678
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      - N8N_RESTRICT_FILE_ACCESS_TO=/data/docs   # Read Files node may only read here
      - N8N_BLOCK_ENV_ACCESS_IN_NODE=false       # allow {{ $env.TICKET_API_URL }} in workflow 2
      - TICKET_API_URL=http://tickets/post       # used by the create-ticket sub-workflow
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n                 # credentials, workflows, executions
      - ./docs:/data/docs:ro                     # knowledge base for RAG
      - ./workflows:/workflows:ro                # exported JSON for n8n import:workflow
    depends_on:
      - tickets

  tickets:
    image: kennethreitz/httpbin                  # echoes POST /post, stands in for a helpdesk API
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  n8n_data:

# Copy to .env. Never commit the real file.
# Encrypts saved credentials (your OpenAI key). Keep it stable across restarts.
N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=replace-with-a-long-random-string

# Indian time for schedules and execution logs
GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata
TZ=Asia/Kolkata

# Editor URL used in links and webhook URLs
N8N_HOST=localhost
N8N_PORT=5678
N8N_PROTOCOL=http

# The OpenAI API key is NOT set here.
# Add it in the n8n UI as an 'OpenAI' credential, so it is stored encrypted.

# CloudNotes Support FAQ

## Refunds
- Refunds are allowed within 14 days of purchase for annual plans.
- Monthly plans are not refundable, but you can cancel any time.
- Approved refunds reach your bank or UPI account in 5 to 7 working days.

## Exporting notes
- Open a note, click the three-dot menu, choose Export, then PDF or Markdown.
- To export all notes, go to Settings > Data > Export workspace (ZIP file).

## Sync problems
- Check you are on the latest app version.
- Sign out and sign in again to refresh the sync token.
- Sync pauses when device storage is below 200 MB.
- If sync still fails after these steps, contact support. A ticket is needed.

## Account and billing
- Change your plan in Settings > Billing.
- GST invoices are emailed after each payment and are also in Settings > Billing > Invoices.
- Password reset: use 'Forgot password' on the login screen.

## Support hours
- Human support works Monday to Saturday, 9:00 to 18:00 IST.
- Tickets get a first reply within one working day.

revision.examFocus: The official n8n Level 1 and Level 2 text courses focus on core workflow skills such as nodes, expressions, data structures and error workflows. AI agents are covered mainly in n8n's Advanced AI documentation and are tested in practical builds and interviews. Expect two kinds of questions: which cluster sub-node to attach (model, memory, tool, vector store, embeddings), and why an agent misbehaves (wrong tool calls, lost memory, bad retrieval).

compare.b: Postgres or Redis Chat Memory / PGVector, Qdrant, Pinecone
compare.difference: The Simple nodes keep data in the n8n process's RAM. The external nodes persist data and share it across restarts and queue-mode workers.
compare.chooseA: Pick Simple nodes for a quick prototype or a demo on a single instance where losing data is acceptable.
compare.chooseB: Pick external stores whenever the question mentions production, restarts, scaling, multiple workers or queue mode.

compare.difference: The Workflow Tool runs a whole sub-workflow, so you get multiple steps, validation and error handling. The HTTP Request Tool makes one API call.
compare.chooseA: Pick the Workflow Tool when the action needs several steps, checks, logging or a friendly error message, such as creating a ticket.
compare.chooseB: Pick the HTTP Request Tool for one simple, read-only or low-risk API call, such as fetching order status.

compare.a: Vector store in 'retrieve as tool for AI Agent' mode
compare.difference: Retrieve mode is attached to the agent in the query flow. Insert mode sits in the ingest flow with a document loader, splitter and embeddings.
compare.chooseA: Choose retrieve-as-tool when the agent must look up knowledge during a chat.
compare.chooseB: Choose insert when loading or refreshing documents, on a manual or scheduled trigger.

compare.difference: The Chat Trigger supplies sessionId automatically. Other triggers need you to set the memory session key yourself.
compare.chooseA: Use the Chat Trigger for n8n's hosted or embedded chat, where memory works with default settings.
compare.chooseB: Use other triggers for external channels, and set the session key with an expression such as the chat ID or user ID.

compare.difference: The tool description tells the model what one tool does and when to call it. The system message sets overall role, rules and priority, for example 'search docs first'.
compare.chooseA: Fix the tool description when the agent calls the wrong tool, or calls a tool at the wrong time.
compare.chooseB: Fix the system message when the agent's overall behaviour, tone or order of steps is wrong.

cues.cue: agent opens tickets for simple questions
cues.pick: Rewrite the ticket tool description with explicit conditions, and add a matching rule in the system message
cues.why: The model decides tool use only from the descriptions and instructions it is given.

cues.cue: all users see each other's conversation
cues.pick: Set the memory session key with an expression based on the user or chat ID
cues.why: Without a unique key, every execution reads and writes one shared history.

cues.cue: similarity search returns irrelevant results or a dimension error
cues.pick: Use the same embedding model for insert and retrieve, then re-embed
cues.why: Vectors from different models or dimensions cannot be compared.

cues.cue: memory lost after restart / queue mode
cues.pick: Postgres or Redis Chat Memory
cues.why: Persistent stores survive restarts and are shared by all workers.

cues.cue: too many tokens / context limit / stale answers from a huge prompt
cues.pick: RAG with a vector store as a tool
cues.why: Only the relevant chunks are retrieved for each question.

cues.cue: answers miss information that sits across paragraphs
cues.pick: Tune chunk size and increase chunk overlap in the text splitter
cues.why: Overlap stops meaning being cut at chunk boundaries.

cues.cue: agent stops with max iterations reached
cues.pick: Make the tool return a clear success or error message; check tool descriptions
cues.why: Loops usually happen when tool output is empty, unclear or a failure the agent cannot interpret.

cues.cue: let the model fill in a tool parameter
cues.pick: $fromAI() in the tool's field
cues.why: It tells the agent to generate that value, using a key, a description and a type.

scenario.situation: A company runs n8n in queue mode with three workers. Its support agent is connected to a Telegram Trigger, an OpenAI chat model, Simple Memory, and a Simple Vector Store filled by a separate ingest workflow. Users complain that the bot forgets them, mixes up conversations, and sometimes says it has no documents. What is the best fix?
reasoning: Mixed-up conversations point to a missing or shared session key. The Telegram Trigger does not supply sessionId the way the Chat Trigger does.
Forgetting users and losing documents in queue mode point to in-memory nodes. Each worker has its own RAM, and restarts wipe it.
So adding more memory or a larger context window does not help. The storage is not shared, so that answer is wrong.
Changing the chat model does not fix storage or session problems either, so remove that option.
The correct fix has both parts: persistent shared stores plus a per-user session key.
scenario.answer: Replace Simple Memory with Postgres or Redis Chat Memory, keyed by an expression on the Telegram chat ID. Replace the Simple Vector Store with PGVector, Qdrant or Pinecone, and re-ingest the documents with the same embedding model.

memoryAids: Agent kit = M-M-T: Model (must have), Memory (optional), Tools (optional, but no tools means just a chatbot).
RAG ingest = L-S-E-I: Load, Split, Embed, Insert. RAG query = C-A-R: Chat, Agent, Retrieve-as-tool.
Same Model, Same Dimensions: embed and retrieve with one model, or re-embed everything.
cheatSheet: The AI Agent is a root node. Chat model, memory, tools and vector stores attach to it as sub-nodes.
API credentials go on the chat model or embeddings sub-node, never on the AI Agent node.
Max Iterations (default 10) is a safety cap on tool loops. It is not a fix for bad tools.
The Chat Trigger gives sessionId automatically. Any other trigger needs a session key expression.
Simple Memory and Simple Vector Store are for demos only. They are lost on restart and not shared across workers.
Keep ingest and query in separate workflows. Ingest runs on a manual or schedule trigger.
Changing the embedding model or its dimensions means rebuilding the index and re-embedding all documents.
Chunks too large give noisy matches. Chunks too small lose context. Overlap bridges the boundaries.
A good tool description states what the tool does, when to use it and when not to use it.
Use the Call n8n Workflow Tool for multi-step actions such as ticket creation, with error handling inside.
A tool sub-workflow should always return a clear text result, including on failure.
Sub-node expressions read only the first input item.
selfCheck: I can wire an AI Agent with a chat model, persistent memory, a retrieve-as-tool vector store and a ticket workflow tool.
I can build a separate ingest workflow that loads, splits, embeds and inserts documents with the same embedding model used for retrieval.
I can set a memory session key for a non-chat trigger such as Telegram or a webhook.
I can write a tool description and system message so the ticket tool runs only when the user asks for it or the documents cannot answer.
I can diagnose lost memory, shared conversations, irrelevant retrieval and max-iteration loops, and name the fix for each.
I can use $fromAI() to let the agent fill in ticket fields such as subject and priority.

objective.question: You add an AI Agent node to a new workflow. Which sub-node must you connect before the agent can run?
options: A Tool sub-node
An Output Parser sub-node
A Chat Model sub-node
A Memory sub-node
objective.explanation: The AI Agent needs a chat model to reason and reply, so the Chat Model connection is required. Memory, tools and output parsers are optional.

objective.question: An AI Agent has a chat model and Simple Memory connected but no tools. How does it behave?
options: It works as a chatbot that remembers the conversation but cannot take actions or fetch outside data
It calls any sub-workflow in the same project
It automatically uses the HTTP Request node to search the web
It fails validation and will not run
objective.explanation: Tools are optional, but without them the agent can only talk, using the model's knowledge and the conversation history. It cannot look up documents or create tickets.

objective.question: Your team is using OpenAI models. Where do you set the OpenAI credential in an agent workflow?
options: On the Chat Trigger node
On the OpenAI Chat Model sub-node and the Embeddings sub-node
In the workflow settings, once for all nodes
On the AI Agent node
objective.explanation: Provider credentials are set on the sub-nodes that call the provider, such as the chat model and embeddings sub-nodes. The AI Agent node has no provider credential of its own.

objective.question: During testing, a support agent keeps calling the same search tool again and again because the results never satisfy it. What setting stops this loop?
options: Max Iterations on the AI Agent node, which defaults to 10
Timeout on the Chat Trigger
Top K on the vector store
Context Window Length on the memory node
objective.explanation: Max Iterations caps how many reasoning and tool-call cycles the agent may run, with a default of 10. Context window length and Top K control memory size and the number of retrieved chunks, not loops.

objective.question: You replace the Chat Trigger with a Webhook trigger called by your website. Postgres Chat Memory now mixes up conversations between users. What is the fix?
options: Set the memory node's session key yourself, for example with an expression that reads the user or conversation ID from the webhook body
Increase Max Iterations
Add a second AI Agent node
Switch to Simple Memory
objective.explanation: The Chat Trigger supplies sessionId automatically, and memory reads it by default. With any other trigger you must define the session key yourself so that each conversation gets its own history.

objective.question: A self-hosted n8n instance runs in queue mode with several workers. The agent forgets earlier messages at random, and history disappears after restarts. It uses Simple Memory. What should you change?
options: Use Postgres Chat Memory or Redis Chat Memory
Turn off queue mode only for this workflow
Store the history in a Set node
Increase the context window length
objective.explanation: Simple Memory lives in the memory of one instance. It is not shared across workers and is lost on restart. Postgres or Redis memory persists outside n8n and works in production and in queue mode.

objective.question: You ingested documents into a Simple Vector Store. After the n8n server restarts, the agent says it cannot find any documents. Why?
options: Simple Vector Store keeps data in instance memory, so a restart erases it
The Chat Trigger session ended
Max Iterations was reached
The embeddings expired
objective.explanation: Simple Vector Store is in-memory and meant for testing. For persistent data use a real vector database such as PGVector, Qdrant or Pinecone.

objective.question: Your Qdrant collection was built with OpenAI text-embedding-3-small (1536 dimensions). You switch the embeddings sub-node to a model with a different dimension size, and inserts and queries fail. What is the correct fix?
options: Keep the old index and set Top K to 1
Change the chat model to match the embedding model
Create an index or collection that matches the new dimension size, then re-embed and re-insert all documents with the new model
Lower the chunk size in the text splitter
objective.explanation: Vector dimensions must match the index, and vectors from different models are not comparable. Changing the embedding model means you must re-embed the whole corpus into an index that matches the new size.

objective.question: What is the recommended structure for a RAG support bot in n8n?
options: A single Chat Trigger connected straight to the vector store with no agent
Embedding each user question and storing it as a document
An ingest flow (manual or scheduled trigger, load, split, embed, insert) and a separate query flow (Chat Trigger, AI Agent, vector store used as a retrieval tool)
One workflow that loads, embeds and inserts all documents on every chat message
objective.explanation: Ingestion is slow and runs only when documents change. Querying runs on every message. Keeping them in separate flows avoids re-embedding on every chat and keeps answers fast.

objective.question: Which vector store operation mode lets an AI Agent decide for itself when to search your documents?
options: Get Many
Retrieve Documents (As Tool for AI Agent)
Update Documents
Insert Documents
objective.explanation: In 'Retrieve Documents (As Tool for AI Agent)' mode, the vector store connects to the agent's Tool input. The agent then searches when its description fits the question. Insert is used for ingestion, and Get Many is for direct retrieval in a normal flow.

objective.question: Your agent creates support tickets even for simple questions that the documentation answers. What is the most effective first fix?
options: Write a clear tool description, for example 'Create a ticket only when the docs do not solve the issue or the user asks for a human', and support it in the system message
Raise Max Iterations to 50
Switch to a larger embedding model
Remove memory from the agent
objective.explanation: The agent chooses tools from their names and descriptions and from its system message. Clear rules about when to use, and when not to use, the ticket tool fix most wrong tool calls.

objective.question: In the ticket tool's 'Subject' field you write {{ $fromAI('subject', 'Short summary of the customer issue', 'string') }}. What does this do?
options: It lets the model generate the value for this parameter when it calls the tool
It encrypts the subject before sending it
It fetches the subject from the vector store
It reads the subject from the previous node's first item
objective.explanation: $fromAI() marks a tool parameter that the AI fills in at call time, using the key, description and type you give it. It does not read data from earlier nodes.

objective.question: You use the Call n8n Workflow Tool to run a 'Create Ticket' sub-workflow. How should that sub-workflow start?
options: With a Schedule Trigger
With a Webhook node set to POST
With the 'When Executed by Another Workflow' (Execute Workflow Trigger) node, defining the inputs it expects
With a Chat Trigger
objective.explanation: Sub-workflows called by the Call n8n Workflow Tool must start with the Execute Workflow Trigger. That node receives the inputs the agent passes to it.

objective.question: In the text splitter, what is the main purpose of chunk overlap?
options: It keeps context that crosses chunk boundaries, so a sentence or idea split between two chunks can still be retrieved meaningfully
It removes duplicate documents
It sets the vector dimension
It reduces the number of embeddings and the cost
objective.explanation: Overlap repeats some text between neighbouring chunks, so meaning is not cut at the boundary. It slightly increases the chunk count, so it does not reduce cost.

objective.question: Ten items flow into an AI Agent. A sub-node parameter uses {{ $json.customerId }}. What value does the sub-node use?
options: An array of all ten customerIds
The value is always empty
Only the customerId from the first input item
A different customerId for each of the ten items
objective.explanation: Sub-node expressions resolve only against the first input item, unlike normal nodes, which resolve per item. If each item needs its own value, process items one at a time, for example in a loop or a sub-workflow.

objective.question: Your AI Agent worked with the Chat Trigger. You replace the trigger with a Webhook node that receives {"message": "..."} in the request body. The agent now fails because it finds no prompt. What is the correct fix?
options: Rename the webhook body field to 'prompt' so the agent detects it automatically
Add a Simple Memory sub-node so the agent can read the incoming message
Enable 'Return Intermediate Steps' so the agent exposes the input text
Set the agent's prompt source to 'Define below' and map the prompt to {{ $json.body.message }}
objective.explanation: With the 'Connected Chat Trigger Node' prompt source, the agent expects the Chat Trigger's chatInput field. With any other trigger, you must define the prompt yourself and map it to the incoming data. Renaming fields, adding memory or exposing intermediate steps does not tell the agent where the user's text is.

objective.question: A support agent uses Simple Memory with Context Window Length set to 5. What does this setting control?
options: How many recent past interactions are sent to the model with each new message
How many minutes a conversation is kept before it expires
How many tool calls the agent may make per message
The maximum number of chat sessions the memory can hold at once
objective.explanation: Context Window Length limits how much recent history is passed to the chat model on each turn, which controls both context and token cost. It does not cap sessions, set an expiry time or limit tool calls. Tool calls are limited by Max Iterations.

objective.question: You set a Pinecone Vector Store node to the mode 'Retrieve Documents (As Vector Store for Chain/Tool)'. You want an AI Agent to use it for answering questions. How do you connect it?
options: Connect it to a Vector Store Question Answer Tool, then connect that tool to the agent
Connect it to the agent's Chat Model input in place of the LLM
Put it in the main flow before the agent so retrieved documents arrive as items
Connect the vector store directly to the agent's Memory input
objective.explanation: In this mode, the vector store feeds a chain or a tool such as the Vector Store Question Answer Tool. That tool then becomes one of the agent's tools. A vector store is not a memory or a chat model. Placing it in the main flow would retrieve documents once, not when the agent decides it needs them.

objective.question: While ingesting, you added a 'product' metadata field to every chunk with the Default Data Loader. Users of Product A sometimes get answers taken from Product B documents. What is the best fix?
options: Use a separate chat model for each product
Lower Max Iterations so the agent searches less often
Apply a metadata filter on product in the vector store retrieval options
Increase the chunk overlap so chunks carry more context
objective.explanation: A metadata filter limits similarity search to chunks that match a metadata value, such as product = A. Vector stores like PGVector, Qdrant and Pinecone support this. Overlap, model choice and iteration limits do not stop the search from returning chunks from the wrong product.

objective.question: An agent calls a 'Create Ticket' sub-workflow through the Call n8n Workflow Tool. What does the agent receive as the tool's result?
options: The data output by the last node that runs in the sub-workflow
Nothing; the tool runs asynchronously and returns immediately
The full execution log of the sub-workflow
Only a success or failure flag
objective.explanation: The tool returns the output of the sub-workflow's final node to the agent. Design that node to return something useful, such as the ticket ID and status, so the agent can confirm to the user. It does not return only a flag or the full execution log.

objective.question: A downstream node needs the agent's reply as JSON with the fields 'answer' and 'needsTicket'. Free-text prompting alone gives inconsistent output. What should you do?
options: Add a Code node after the agent that uses regex to extract the fields
Add a second memory sub-node that stores the JSON template
Set the chat model temperature to 0 and hope the format stays stable
Enable 'Require Specific Output Format' on the agent and connect a Structured Output Parser with the schema
objective.explanation: The output parser gives the model a schema and validates the agent's output against it, so you get reliable structured fields. Regex parsing and a low temperature are fragile. Memory has nothing to do with output format.

objective.question: An agent gives a wrong answer. You want to see which tools it called, with what inputs, and what each tool returned. Which option on the AI Agent node helps most?
options: Return Intermediate Steps
Context Window Length
Always Output Data
Max Iterations
objective.explanation: Return Intermediate Steps adds the agent's tool calls and observations to its output, so you can debug its reasoning path. The execution logs panel shows similar detail. Max Iterations and Context Window Length control behaviour, not visibility. Always Output Data is a general node setting.

objective.question: You made a Chat Trigger publicly available in Hosted Chat mode to demo the support bot. You realise anyone with the URL can use it and spend your LLM credits. Which built-in option restricts access without extra infrastructure?
options: Switch the vector store to insert mode
Rename the workflow so the URL changes
Lower the Simple Memory context window
Set the Chat Trigger's Authentication to Basic Auth or n8n User Auth
objective.explanation: The Chat Trigger has an Authentication option that supports Basic Auth and n8n User Auth. These restrict who can chat. Memory and vector store settings do not control access. A renamed workflow does not add any authentication.

objective.question: A ticket tool parameter contains the expression below. What is the role of the fourth argument, 'medium'?

code.code: {{ $fromAI('priority', 'Ticket priority: low, medium or high', 'string', 'medium') }}

options: It is a default value used when the model does not provide one
It tells the model to use a medium-sized chat model
It is the description shown to the user in the chat
It limits the model to producing at most a medium-length string
objective.explanation: The $fromAI() signature is key, description, type and defaultValue. The fourth argument is a fallback value used if the model does not supply that parameter. It does not control length, model choice or what the user sees.

subjective.question: Explain cluster nodes in n8n. How do the AI Agent root node and its sub-nodes relate to each other?
subjective.answer: In n8n, AI features are built as cluster nodes. A cluster has one root node and the sub-nodes plugged into it. The AI Agent is a root node. It controls the reasoning loop: it reads the input, decides what to do, calls tools and writes the final reply. Sub-nodes give it abilities. The Chat Model sub-node is required, because it is the brain. Memory sub-nodes keep the conversation history. Tool sub-nodes, such as the HTTP Request Tool, the Call n8n Workflow Tool or a vector store in tool mode, let the agent act and fetch data. An output parser can enforce structured output. Sub-nodes do not run on their own in the main flow; the root node calls them. Two details matter in practice. Credentials go on the sub-nodes, for example the chat model. Sub-node expressions resolve only against the first input item.
keyPoints: Cluster = one root node plus attached sub-nodes
AI Agent is the root and runs the reasoning and tool loop
Chat model is required; memory, tools and parsers are optional
Credentials are set on the sub-nodes
Sub-node expressions use the first item only

subjective.question: Walk me through how you would build a support agent in n8n that answers from company documents and can create a ticket.
subjective.answer: I build two workflows plus one sub-workflow. First comes the ingest flow. It has a manual or schedule trigger, then a node to fetch the files, for example from Google Drive. Next a vector store node in Insert Documents mode, with a Default Data Loader, a Recursive Character Text Splitter and an embeddings sub-node, stores everything in PGVector or Qdrant. Second comes the query flow. A Chat Trigger feeds an AI Agent. The agent gets a chat model, Postgres Chat Memory and two tools. One tool is the same vector store in 'Retrieve Documents (As Tool for AI Agent)' mode, using the same embedding model.
