The other is a Call n8n Workflow Tool that points to a 'Create Ticket' sub-workflow. That sub-workflow starts with the Execute Workflow Trigger and calls the helpdesk API. The system message tells the agent to answer only from the documents, and to create a ticket only when the documents do not solve the issue or the user asks for a human.
keyPoints: Separate ingest and query flows
Same embedding model for insert and retrieve
Vector store attached as a retrieval tool
Ticket action as a Call n8n Workflow Tool sub-workflow
System message and tool descriptions control behaviour

subjective.question: How does an AI Agent decide which tool to call? How do you make sure the ticket tool is used only when needed?
subjective.answer: The agent sends the model the user message, the system message, the memory and a list of the tools with their names, descriptions and parameter schemas. The model then decides whether to call a tool, which one, and with what arguments. So the tool description is effectively the instruction. For the ticket tool, I give it a clear name like 'create_support_ticket'. The description says when to use it and when not to: 'Use only after searching the knowledge base finds no answer, or when the user explicitly asks for a human. Do not use for general questions.' In the system message I repeat the order: search the docs first, answer if found, and offer or create a ticket only if not. I also give the knowledge base tool a clear description. Then I test with simple questions, questions the docs do not cover and explicit escalation requests. I check the execution log to see which tools were called.
keyPoints: The model chooses tools from name, description and schema
Descriptions should say when and when not to use the tool
System message sets the order: docs first, ticket last
Test with positive and negative cases
Check tool calls in the execution logs

subjective.question: How does conversation memory know which conversation it belongs to? What changes when you do not use the Chat Trigger?
subjective.answer: Memory nodes store history under a session key. When the workflow starts from the Chat Trigger, the trigger outputs a sessionId for each chat. Memory nodes read it by default, so every chat gets its own history with no extra setup. If I start the agent from a Webhook, a Telegram trigger or a form, there is no automatic sessionId. In the memory node I then change the session ID setting to define it myself, using an expression that points to a stable unique value. Examples are the Telegram chat ID, a user ID or a conversation ID sent by the website. If I get this wrong, for example by using a fixed value, all users share one history. That leaks context between customers and confuses the agent. I also choose a context window length that keeps enough recent turns without making prompts too long.
keyPoints: Memory is keyed by a session ID
Chat Trigger supplies sessionId automatically
Other triggers need a custom session key expression
A wrong key mixes users' histories
Context window length limits how much history is sent

subjective.question: Compare Simple Memory and Simple Vector Store with their production alternatives. When is each appropriate?
subjective.answer: Simple Memory and Simple Vector Store keep their data in the memory of the n8n instance. They need no setup, so they are great for learning, demos and quick tests. But the data is lost when n8n restarts. In queue mode, different executions may run on different workers that do not share that memory, so behaviour becomes unreliable. For production I use persistent stores. For chat history I use Postgres Chat Memory or Redis Chat Memory. Postgres suits teams that already run a database and want durable, queryable history. Redis is fast and suits short-lived sessions. For documents I use a real vector database: PGVector if we already run Postgres, Qdrant if we want a strong self-hostable option, or Pinecone if we prefer a managed service. Moving from test to production is mostly a matter of swapping the sub-nodes and adding credentials. The agent design stays the same.
keyPoints: Simple stores live in instance memory
Data is lost on restart and unreliable in queue mode
Use Postgres or Redis for chat memory
Use PGVector, Qdrant or Pinecone for vectors
Swapping sub-nodes keeps the agent design unchanged

subjective.question: Describe a production-ready RAG ingest flow in n8n and explain the role of each node.
subjective.answer: The ingest flow runs separately from the chat flow. It starts with a Schedule Trigger for regular syncs, or a manual trigger for one-off loads. A file event trigger such as a Google Drive trigger also works. Next, nodes fetch the source content, for example by downloading files or reading pages through HTTP. Then a vector store node, such as PGVector or Qdrant, in Insert Documents mode does the storing. Three sub-nodes attach to it. The Default Data Loader turns binary or JSON input into documents and can add metadata like source and title. The text splitter, usually the Recursive Character Text Splitter, breaks documents into chunks with a set size and overlap. The embeddings sub-node converts each chunk into a vector. I add metadata so I can filter results or cite the source later. I also plan for updates, for example by clearing the collection and re-inserting, or by deleting old chunks for a changed file, so I do not create duplicates.
keyPoints: Separate flow with a schedule or manual trigger
Fetch source data, then Insert Documents mode
Data loader, text splitter and embeddings sub-nodes
Add metadata for filtering and citations
Handle updates to avoid duplicate chunks

subjective.question: How do chunk size and chunk overlap affect retrieval quality? How would you tune them?
subjective.answer: Chunk size controls how much text each vector represents. Chunks that are too large mix several topics. Their embedding becomes vague, and they fill the model's context with irrelevant text. Chunks that are too small lose context; a single line may match the query but lack the surrounding explanation. Overlap repeats part of the previous chunk at the start of the next one. A sentence or step that crosses a boundary is then not cut in half. Overlap increases the number of chunks a little, which adds storage and embedding cost. To tune, I start with a moderate size and a small overlap. I build a test set of real support questions with known answers and check whether the correct chunks come back in the top results. Then I adjust the size, the overlap and the number of retrieved chunks. Structured documents like FAQs often work best when split on natural sections.
keyPoints: Large chunks give vague matches and waste context
Small chunks lose surrounding meaning
Overlap preserves context across boundaries
Overlap adds some cost through more chunks
Tune with a real question test set

subjective.question: Why must embedding dimensions match the vector index? What happens if you change the embedding model?
subjective.answer: An embedding model turns text into a vector with a fixed number of dimensions. OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, for example, produces 1536. A vector index or collection is created for one dimension size, and the database expects every vector to have exactly that length. If I insert or query with a model of a different size, the operation fails. Even if two models have the same size, their vectors live in different spaces. Comparing a query from one model with documents from another gives meaningless similarity scores. So the ingest flow and the query flow must use the same embedding model. If I change the model, I create a new index with the correct dimensions, re-embed and re-insert all documents, and only then switch the query flow to the new model. I usually keep the old index until the new one is tested, so I can roll back.
keyPoints: Index dimension is fixed, e.g. 1536 for text-embedding-3-small
A mismatched size causes errors
Different models' vectors are not comparable
Ingest and query must use the same model
Changing the model means re-embedding everything

subjective.question: What is $fromAI() and how would you use it in a ticket-creation tool?
subjective.answer: $fromAI() is an n8n expression function used in tool parameters. It tells n8n that the AI model should provide this value when it calls the tool. I give it a key, a description, and optionally a type and a default value. For a ticket tool, say an HTTP Request Tool calling our helpdesk API, I might set the subject to $fromAI('subject', 'One-line summary of the issue', 'string'). The description would be $fromAI('description', 'Full details including steps already tried', 'string'), and the priority would be $fromAI('priority', 'low, medium or high based on business impact', 'string'). The model sees these keys and descriptions as the tool's input schema and fills them from the conversation. Fixed values such as the API key, the queue ID or the requester source stay hard-coded, so the model cannot change them. Clear descriptions give cleaner, more consistent tickets.
keyPoints: Marks a parameter for the model to fill at call time
Takes a key, description, optional type and default
Becomes part of the tool's input schema
Keep secrets and fixed values hard-coded
Good descriptions improve argument quality

subjective.question: When would you use the Call n8n Workflow Tool rather than the HTTP Request Tool for creating tickets?
subjective.answer: The HTTP Request Tool is fine when a single API call does the job and the request is simple. The agent fills in a few parameters and n8n sends the call. I prefer the Call n8n Workflow Tool when ticket creation needs more logic. Examples: looking up the customer in the CRM, checking for an existing open ticket, setting priority rules, creating the ticket, posting to Slack and returning a clean confirmation. The sub-workflow starts with the Execute Workflow Trigger, which defines the inputs the agent must pass. It can use normal nodes, error handling and retries, and its last node's output goes back to the agent as the tool result. This keeps the agent simple and the business logic testable on its own. The sub-workflow can also be reused by other workflows. The sub-workflow also controls exactly which fields reach the helpdesk.
keyPoints: HTTP Request Tool for simple single API calls
Workflow Tool for multi-step logic and checks
Sub-workflow starts with Execute Workflow Trigger
The last node's output returns to the agent
Testable, reusable and supports error handling

subjective.question: What does Max Iterations do on the AI Agent node? How would you debug an agent that hits the limit?
subjective.answer: Max Iterations caps how many reasoning and tool-call cycles the agent can run for one input. The default is 10. It is a safety net: if the agent gets confused, it cannot loop forever, burn tokens or hammer an API. If an agent hits the limit, I open the execution and look at the agent's logs to see each tool call, its inputs and its outputs. Common causes are these. A tool returns an error or empty result, so the agent keeps retrying. Two tools have overlapping descriptions, so the agent swaps between them. The system message asks for something no tool can give. The retrieval tool returns irrelevant chunks, so the agent keeps searching. I fix the root cause: clearer tool descriptions, better tool outputs with useful error messages, better retrieval settings, or an instruction to stop and escalate. I raise the limit only when a task truly needs more steps.
keyPoints: Caps agent loop cycles; default 10
Prevents runaway cost and API abuse
Inspect agent logs for each tool call
Common causes: tool errors, vague descriptions, poor retrieval
Fix the root cause before raising the limit

subjective.question: Your support agent sometimes gives answers that are not in the documents. How do you make it stay grounded?
subjective.answer: First I check whether retrieval works at all. I look in the execution log to see whether the agent called the knowledge base tool, and what chunks came back. If it skipped the tool, I make the tool description clearer and add a rule to the system message: 'Always search the knowledge base before answering product questions. Answer only from the retrieved content. If the answer is not there, say so and offer to create a ticket.' If the tool ran but returned weak chunks, I fix the ingest side: chunk size and overlap, metadata, the number of results returned, and making sure the same embedding model is used. I can ask the agent to mention the source document, which makes guessing easier to spot. A lower model temperature also helps reduce creative answers. Finally, I test with questions that are deliberately out of scope and confirm the agent declines instead of inventing answers.
keyPoints: Check in the logs whether the retrieval tool was called
A strict system message: answer only from retrieved content
Fix retrieval quality on the ingest side
Ask for sources; lower the temperature
Test with out-of-scope questions

subjective.question: Explain the 'first item only' behaviour of sub-node expressions and how to work around it.
subjective.answer: Normal n8n nodes run once per input item, so an expression like {{ $json.email }} gets a different value for each item. Sub-nodes are different. Expressions in sub-nodes, such as a memory session key, a tool URL or a vector store filter, resolve only against the first input item. If ten items reach an AI Agent and the memory session key uses $json.userId, all ten use the first user's ID. That can mix histories or send wrong data. The workaround is to make sure each agent run sees one relevant item at a time. I can use Loop Over Items with a batch size of one before the agent. Or I can move the agent into a sub-workflow called once per item. In chat use cases this rarely matters, because the Chat Trigger sends one message per execution. It matters a lot in batch jobs, such as classifying many emails with an agent.
keyPoints: Normal nodes resolve expressions per item
Sub-node expressions use only the first item
Risk: wrong session keys, filters or URLs in batches
Workaround: Loop Over Items or a per-item sub-workflow
Mostly a concern in batch, not chat, workflows

subjective.question: How would you choose between PGVector, Qdrant and Pinecone for a self-hosted n8n support bot?
subjective.answer: All three work as vector store nodes in n8n, so the choice is mostly operational. PGVector is a Postgres extension. If we already run Postgres, for example as the n8n database or for chat memory, it adds no new system. Backups and access control are familiar. It suits small to medium document sets. Qdrant is a dedicated vector database that can be self-hosted easily with Docker. It offers good performance and metadata filtering, and data stays on our own servers, which helps with data residency requirements for Indian clients. Pinecone is fully managed, so there is nothing to run. It suits teams that want minimal operations and accept a cloud service and its pricing. Whatever I pick, I avoid Simple Vector Store in production, especially in queue mode. I make sure the index dimension matches the embedding model, and I plan re-indexing when documents or models change.
keyPoints: PGVector reuses existing Postgres; simple operations
Qdrant is self-hostable with strong filtering and data control
Pinecone is managed with low operational effort
Never use Simple Vector Store in production
Index dimension must match the embedding model

subjective.question: How would you test the checkpoint: the agent answers from documents and calls the ticket tool only when needed?
subjective.answer: I prepare a small test set with three groups. Group one: questions clearly answered in the documents. I expect the knowledge base tool to be called, a correct answer and no ticket. Group two: questions the documents do not cover. I expect the agent to say it could not find the answer and then offer or create a ticket. Group three: explicit requests like 'I want to talk to a human'. I expect a ticket with sensible fields. I run each through the Chat panel. In the execution view I check the agent logs: which tools ran, in what order, and with what arguments, including the $fromAI values. I confirm that the ticket sub-workflow ran only in groups two and three, and that tickets actually appear in the helpdesk. I also test follow-up messages, to check that memory carries context within the same session. I rerun the set after any prompt, tool description or chunking change.
keyPoints: Test set: covered, uncovered and escalation cases
Verify tool calls and order in the execution logs
Ticket tool runs only for uncovered or escalation cases
Check ticket fields and helpdesk records
Retest after any prompt or retrieval change

subjective.question: Review this system message for a support agent. What would you improve, and why?

code.code:
You are a helpful assistant. Answer any question the user asks.
Use your tools if you want. Be creative.

subjective.answer: This prompt invites hallucination and random tool use. 'Answer any question' and 'be creative' push the model to invent answers. 'Use your tools if you want' gives no rule for when to search or create a ticket. I would define a clear role: a support agent for our product. I would give it an explicit order of steps. First, always search the knowledge base tool for product questions. Answer only from the retrieved content. If nothing relevant is found, say so. Create a ticket only when the user reports a problem the documents cannot solve, or asks for a human. Before creating a ticket, collect the required details and confirm with the user. I would also add tone, a scope limit (refuse unrelated topics) and the output style. The tool descriptions should match these rules.
keyPoints: Remove wording that invites invented answers
Give an explicit rule: search documents first and stay grounded
Define precise conditions for creating a ticket and confirm first
Set scope, refusal behaviour and tone
Keep the prompt consistent with the tool descriptions

subjective.question: Explain the options for exposing an n8n chat agent to users through the Chat Trigger: hosted versus embedded chat, authentication and response modes.
subjective.answer: The Chat Trigger can be made publicly available. In Hosted Chat mode, n8n serves a ready-made chat page at the trigger's URL. This is good for demos and internal users. In Embedded Chat mode, you build your own interface or use n8n's chat widget on your website, and it calls the trigger's URL. For access control, the trigger supports Authentication options such as Basic Auth and n8n User Auth. The embedded widget should only be allowed from your own domains. For the reply, the default is to respond when the last node finishes. You can instead use response nodes to control exactly what is sent back. Recent versions also support streaming the agent's reply as it is generated. The session ID from the trigger links the chat to memory. Remember that the workflow must be active for the production URL to work.
keyPoints: Hosted Chat gives a ready page; Embedded Chat is for your own site or widget
Use the Authentication options to restrict access
Choose a response mode: last node finishes, response nodes or streaming
The session ID links the chat to memory
Activate the workflow to use the production URL

subjective.question: Design the 'Create Ticket' sub-workflow called by the agent so that it is safe and reliable. What inputs, checks and outputs would you include?
subjective.answer: The sub-workflow starts with the 'When Executed by Another Workflow' trigger. I define explicit input fields such as subject, description, priority and sessionId, so the agent's tool has a clear schema. Next, a validation step checks that required fields are present and that priority is one of the allowed values. If validation fails, it returns a clear error message so the agent can ask the user for the missing details. To avoid duplicates, I check whether an open ticket already exists for this session or user with a similar subject. Then I create the ticket in the helpdesk with a stored credential. I set Retry On Fail on that API call. The last node returns a small JSON object, such as ticketId, status and a short message. The agent reads this to confirm to the user. Errors are also logged or sent to an error workflow.
keyPoints: Use the 'When Executed by Another Workflow' trigger with defined inputs
Validate inputs and return readable errors to the agent
Check for duplicate tickets
Add retries and credential-based API calls
Return a concise result, such as ticket ID and status, from the final node

subjective.question: Documents were ingested successfully, but the agent keeps saying it cannot find relevant information. Give a structured troubleshooting checklist.
subjective.answer: First, I confirm the data exists. I run the vector store in Get Many mode, or check the database, to see chunks in the expected index, collection or table. Second, I check that the ingest and retrieval nodes point to the same index or collection name and namespace. Third, I confirm both sides use the same embedding model, because different models produce incompatible vectors. Fourth, I inspect the chunks. If they are too large, too small or full of noise, such as PDF headers, similarity search suffers. Fifth, I check the retrieval limit (top K) and any metadata filter that may exclude results. Sixth, I read the tool name and description. If the description is vague, the agent may not call the tool at all. I use the execution logs or intermediate steps to see whether the tool was called, with what query, and what came back. Finally, I test the same question directly against the vector store.
keyPoints: Verify the chunks actually exist in the target index or collection
Use the same index or namespace and the same embedding model on both sides
Inspect chunk quality and splitter settings
Check the limit and metadata filters
Confirm the agent calls the tool, using the logs, and test retrieval directly

subjective.question: Your product documentation changes every week. How would you keep the agent's knowledge base current in n8n without leaving stale answers?
subjective.answer: I would build a separate ingest workflow, triggered on a schedule or by a change event, such as a new file in Google Drive or a CMS webhook. Each chunk gets metadata such as document ID, source URL and version or updated date. When a document changes, I delete or replace all existing vectors for that document ID before inserting the new chunks. Otherwise, old and new versions both get retrieved and the agent contradicts itself. Not every vector store node supports deletion the same way, so I may need the store's API or SQL for PGVector. I process only changed documents to save embedding cost. I log each run and alert on failures. Including the source URL in the metadata also lets the agent cite where an answer came from, so users can check it.
keyPoints: Use a separate ingest workflow triggered by a schedule or change event
Add metadata with document ID, source and version
Remove old vectors before inserting the updated ones
Process only changed documents to control cost
Monitor runs, and use source metadata for citations

subjective.question: Your agent workflow is becoming expensive. Which n8n settings and design choices would you use to reduce token usage without hurting answer quality much?
subjective.answer: First, I look at what goes into each model call. Memory's Context Window Length controls how much history is sent, so I keep it small enough for the use case. Retrieval sends chunks to the model, so I tune chunk size and the vector store limit. A few focused chunks usually beat many large ones. I keep the system message concise and avoid long tool descriptions that repeat themselves. Max Iterations caps runaway tool loops, which can multiply cost. I choose a smaller, cheaper chat model for routine questions and reserve a stronger model for hard cases. I might route between them with an earlier classification step. For ingestion, I embed only new or changed documents. Finally, I review execution logs to see token-heavy runs and fix the prompts or tools that cause them.
keyPoints: Tune Context Window Length in memory
Tune chunk size and the retrieval limit
Keep prompts and tool descriptions concise
Cap loops with Max Iterations and choose the right model size
Avoid re-embedding unchanged documents and review the logs

subjective.question: What security risks come with a support agent that reads your documents and can create tickets, and how would you reduce them in n8n?
subjective.answer: The main risk is prompt injection. A user, or text inside a document, can tell the agent to ignore its rules, reveal its system prompt, or call tools with harmful inputs. Tools are where real damage happens, so I give each tool the least privilege it needs. The ticket tool can only create tickets, not delete or read other customers' data. Trusted values, such as the customer's ID or email, come from the authenticated session or the trigger data, not from $fromAI(). The sub-workflow validates every input. Credentials stay in n8n's credential store and are never placed in prompts. I secure the Chat Trigger with authentication and rate limits at the proxy. For high-impact actions, I add human approval. I also avoid ingesting confidential documents into a public bot, and I log tool calls for auditing.
keyPoints: Prompt injection from users or from document content
Give tools least privilege and validate their inputs
Take identity values from trusted data, not from the model
Protect credentials and the chat endpoint
Add human approval for risky actions and audit the logs

subjective.question: How do you handle errors in an n8n agent workflow, such as a failing helpdesk API, a model outage or a tool timeout?
subjective.answer: I handle errors at several layers. Inside tools, I set Retry On Fail on HTTP and helpdesk calls for transient errors. In sub-workflows, I catch failures and return a clear message, such as 'Ticket system unavailable, please try later'. The agent can then tell the user honestly instead of crashing or making up a ticket number. For the model, the AI Agent supports a fallback chat model, so a second provider can take over if the primary one fails. I set Max Iterations so the agent cannot loop forever on failing tools. At the workflow level, I attach an Error Workflow that alerts the team, for example on Slack or by email, with the execution details. For the chat user, I make sure some response is always returned, even on failure.
keyPoints: Retry On Fail for transient tool errors
Return readable error results to the agent instead of failing silently
A fallback chat model for provider outages
Max Iterations to stop loops
An Error Workflow for alerting, and always reply to the user

subjective.question: Review this HTTP Request tool configuration that an agent uses to create tickets. What is risky, and how would you fix it?
subjective.answer: There are three problems. First, the API key is hardcoded in the body. It should live in an n8n credential, such as Header Auth, so it is not exposed in the workflow JSON or in exports. Second, the customer email comes from $fromAI(). The model could invent an email or be tricked into using someone else's. Identity should come from trusted data, such as the authenticated session or trigger payload, mapped with a normal expression. Third, priority has no allowed values and no default. I would describe the allowed values, low, medium or high, give 'medium' as the default argument, and validate the value. Even better, I would move this logic into a sub-workflow called with the Call n8n Workflow Tool. That makes validation, duplicate checks and a clean ticket ID response easy. Only subject and description need to come from the model.
keyPoints: Move the hardcoded API key into n8n credentials
Take the customer identity from trusted data, not $fromAI()
Constrain priority with allowed values, a default and validation
Consider a sub-workflow for validation and a clean response
Let the model fill only the fields it should decide

steps.overview: This final step completes the official n8n Course Level 2 and moves one workflow from your laptop to a production instance. Level 2 tests how n8n handles data (items, JSON, binary), how to merge and split data, how to handle errors, and how to build a full business process. The production part covers environment variables, PostgreSQL, queue mode with Redis and workers, and moving workflows safely between environments.
objectives: Explain the n8n item structure and reshape data with Split Out, Aggregate, Merge and Loop Over Items
Build an error workflow with the Error Trigger node and use node-level retry and error outputs
Configure a self-hosted n8n instance with PostgreSQL and the correct environment variables
Deploy n8n in queue mode with Redis, a main instance and one or more workers
Move workflows between dev and production using Git-based source control or CLI export/import

concepts.explanation: Data passes between nodes as an array of items. Each item is an object with a json key and an optional binary key, for example [{ json: { name: 'Asha' } }]. Most nodes run once per item, so 10 input items usually produce 10 operations. The Code node can run once for all items or once for each item.

The Merge node joins data from two or more inputs. Append adds all items one after another. Combine by Matching Fields works like a SQL join (inner, left, outer and similar options). Combine by Position pairs item 1 with item 1, and so on. All Possible Combinations makes a cross join, and SQL Query lets you write a query over the inputs. Choose Branch outputs one input's data.

concepts.term: Split Out, Aggregate and Loop Over Items
concepts.explanation: Split Out turns an array inside one item into many items. Aggregate does the reverse: it collects field values from many items into one item. Loop Over Items (formerly Split In Batches) processes items in batches of a size you set. It is useful for rate-limited APIs or nodes that only handle the first item.

An error workflow starts with the Error Trigger node. You attach it to other workflows in Workflow Settings > Error Workflow. When a production execution fails, it receives details such as workflow name, failing node, error message and execution URL, and it can send an alert by email, Slack or Telegram. It does not fire for manual test runs, and it does not need to be active.

Each node's Settings tab has Retry On Fail, with Max Tries and Wait Between Tries. It also has On Error, with three choices: Stop Workflow (the default), Continue, or Continue (using error output). The error output adds a separate branch for failed items. The Stop and Error node deliberately fails a workflow with your own message, which then triggers the error workflow.

The Execute Workflow node calls another workflow. The called workflow starts with an Execute Workflow Trigger (shown in the UI as 'When Executed by Another Workflow'). Sub-workflows split a big business process into reusable, testable parts. Level 2's business-process lesson uses this modular style together with scheduling, merging and error handling.

By default n8n uses SQLite, stored in the ~/.n8n folder. For production, set DB_TYPE=postgresdb plus the DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST, _PORT, _DATABASE, _USER and _PASSWORD variables. Postgres handles concurrency, backups and scaling better, and queue mode needs it.

Set EXECUTIONS_MODE=queue. The main instance then receives triggers and webhooks and pushes execution jobs into Redis, using the Bull queue. Worker processes, started with the command 'n8n worker', pick up jobs and run them. You can add more workers to scale. Optional webhook processors ('n8n webhook') can take over incoming webhook load.

n8n encrypts stored credentials with N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY. If you don't set it, n8n generates one and saves it in the .n8n folder. In production, set it explicitly and back it up. Every main, worker and webhook process must use the same key, or credentials cannot be decrypted.

n8n's Git-based source control is a paid-plan feature (Enterprise and some Business tiers; check current plans). It links each instance to a Git branch, for example dev and prod, and you push and pull workflows, tags, variables and credential stubs. Credential secrets are never pushed. An instance can be marked protected so workflows cannot be edited there directly. On the free Community edition, use the CLI commands export:workflow and import:workflow with Git instead.

keyFacts: Item shape: an array of { json: {...}, binary: {...} }; the json key is required
Default port is 5678; the default database is SQLite; production should use DB_TYPE=postgresdb
Queue mode needs EXECUTIONS_MODE=queue, Redis (QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_HOST / QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_PORT) and Postgres
Workers start with 'n8n worker'; the default concurrency is 10 jobs per worker, changed with --concurrency
N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY must be identical on the main instance and all workers; losing it means losing access to saved credentials
Set WEBHOOK_URL to your public HTTPS address when behind a reverse proxy, or webhook URLs will show localhost
Error Trigger workflows fire only for automatic (production) executions, not manual test runs
On Error options: Stop Workflow (default), Continue, Continue (using error output)
Execution data pruning (EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE, EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE in hours) keeps the Postgres database from growing without limit
Source control pushes credential stubs only; you must recreate the secrets in each environment

example.caption: Minimal docker-compose for production queue mode: Postgres, Redis, a main instance and a worker sharing one encryption key
example.code:
x-n8n-env: &n8n-env
  DB_TYPE: postgresdb
  DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST: postgres
  DB_POSTGRESDB_DATABASE: n8n
  DB_POSTGRESDB_USER: n8n
  DB_POSTGRESDB_PASSWORD: ${PG_PASSWORD}
  EXECUTIONS_MODE: queue
  QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_HOST: redis
  N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY: ${N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY}
  GENERIC_TIMEZONE: Asia/Kolkata
  WEBHOOK_URL: https://n8n.example.in/
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    environment: { POSTGRES_USER: n8n, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${PG_PASSWORD}, POSTGRES_DB: n8n }
    volumes: [pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
  redis:
    image: redis:7
  n8n-main:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n
    environment: *n8n-env
    ports: ["5678:5678"]
    depends_on: [postgres, redis]
  n8n-worker:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n
    command: worker --concurrency=5
    environment: *n8n-env
    depends_on: [n8n-main]
volumes:
  pgdata:

pitfalls: Using different or auto-generated encryption keys on workers. The jobs then fail with credential decryption errors.
Running queue mode on SQLite, or keeping binary data in filesystem mode. Workers cannot share local files, so use database or external storage for binary data.
Expecting the error workflow to fire during manual testing. It only runs for production executions of active or triggered workflows.
Confusing Combine by Position with Combine by Matching Fields. Position pairs items by index, while matching joins them on a key such as email or order ID.
Forgetting WEBHOOK_URL behind Nginx or Caddy. Webhook and OAuth callback URLs then point to localhost:5678.
Assuming Git source control is available on the free Community edition. On Community, use CLI export/import, and recreate credentials in each environment.

workflow.title: From Level 2 course to a workflow running in production

steps.label: Complete Level 2 lessons
steps.detail: Work through data structures, data types, merging and splitting, error handling and the business-process lessons in your own n8n instance.

steps.label: Pass the knowledge check
steps.detail: Take the final Level 2 quiz to earn the badge, and review any lesson where you made mistakes.

steps.label: Provision production stack
steps.detail: Deploy n8n with Docker Compose using Postgres, Redis and a fixed N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY, behind HTTPS with WEBHOOK_URL set.

steps.label: Enable queue mode workers
steps.detail: Set EXECUTIONS_MODE=queue and start at least one 'n8n worker' process with the same environment variables.

steps.label: Promote the workflow
steps.detail: Push it from dev to the prod branch with source control, or use n8n export:workflow and import:workflow, then recreate its credentials.

steps.label: Attach error handling
steps.detail: Set an Error Trigger alert workflow in Workflow Settings and add Retry On Fail to nodes that call external APIs.

steps.label: Activate and monitor
steps.detail: Activate the workflow, confirm that executions appear and that workers are picking up jobs, and check that pruning is enabled.

project.title: n8n-order-intake-prod
project.summary: A production-style n8n stack (main instance, queue-mode worker, PostgreSQL, Redis) that runs an order-intake workflow: it splits order lines, computes totals, aggregates and merges data, then posts to a CRM with retries and an error output. docker-compose.yml and .env.example cover self-hosting, the two workflow JSON files cover Level 2 data handling and error workflows, deploy.sh imports them, and README.md explains the flow and the source-control and environments step.
project.run:
cp .env.example .env   # then set N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY and passwords
docker compose up -d
./scripts/deploy.sh
curl -X POST http://localhost:5678/webhook/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"orderId":"A1","customer":"Ravi","items":[{"sku":"PEN","qty":2,"price":50},{"sku":"BOOK","qty":1,"price":300}]}'

files.code:
# Production-style n8n: main + worker in queue mode, PostgreSQL, Redis
x-n8n-env: &n8n-env
  DB_TYPE: postgresdb                      # use PostgreSQL, not the default SQLite
  DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST: postgres
  DB_POSTGRESDB_PORT: 5432
  DB_POSTGRESDB_DATABASE: ${POSTGRES_DB}
  DB_POSTGRESDB_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER}
  DB_POSTGRESDB_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
  N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY: ${N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY} # same key on main AND workers, or credentials cannot be decrypted
  EXECUTIONS_MODE: queue                    # main puts jobs in Redis, workers run them
  QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_HOST: redis
  QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_PORT: 6379
  OFFLOAD_MANUAL_EXECUTIONS_TO_WORKERS: "true"
  GENERIC_TIMEZONE: ${GENERIC_TIMEZONE}
  N8N_HOST: ${N8N_HOST}
  N8N_PROTOCOL: ${N8N_PROTOCOL}
  WEBHOOK_URL: ${WEBHOOK_URL}               # public URL shown on Webhook nodes

services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    restart: always
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB}
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - pg_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER} -d ${POSTGRES_DB}"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    restart: always
    volumes:
      - redis_data:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10

  n8n:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:latest   # pin an exact version in real production
    restart: always
    ports:
      - "5678:5678"
    environment: *n8n-env
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n
      - ./workflows:/workflows:ro           # exported workflow JSON for import
    depends_on:
      postgres: { condition: service_healthy }
      redis: { condition: service_healthy }

  n8n-worker:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:latest   # must match the main instance version
    restart: always
    command: worker --concurrency=5         # each worker runs up to 5 jobs at once
    environment: *n8n-env
    depends_on:
      - n8n

volumes:
  pg_data:
  redis_data:
  n8n_data:

# Copy to .env and change every value before going live.
# Never commit the real .env to Git.

# PostgreSQL (n8n stores workflows, credentials and executions here)
POSTGRES_DB=n8n
POSTGRES_USER=n8n
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me-strong-password

# Encryption key for stored credentials.
# Generate once: openssl rand -hex 32
# Back it up safely. If you lose it, saved credentials cannot be decrypted.
# Use the SAME key on the main instance and every worker.
N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=replace-with-64-hex-characters

# Public address of this instance
N8N_HOST=localhost
N8N_PROTOCOL=http
WEBHOOK_URL=http://localhost:5678/

# Timezone used by Schedule Trigger and date expressions
GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata

{
  "id": "OrderIntakeWf001",
  "name": "Order Intake",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "a1", "name": "Order Webhook", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.webhook", "typeVersion": 2, "position": [0, 200],
      "webhookId": "orders-intake", "parameters": { "httpMethod": "POST", "path": "orders", "responseMode": "onReceived", "options": {} } },
    { "id": "a2", "name": "Split Out Lines", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.splitOut", "typeVersion": 1, "position": [220, 300],
      "parameters": { "fieldToSplitOut": "body.items", "options": {} } },
    { "id": "a3", "name": "Line Total", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.set", "typeVersion": 3.4, "position": [440, 300],
      "parameters": { "assignments": { "assignments": [
        { "id": "t1", "name": "lineTotal", "type": "number", "value": "={{ $json.qty * $json.price }}" } ] }, "options": {} } },
    { "id": "a4", "name": "Aggregate Totals", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.aggregate", "typeVersion": 1, "position": [660, 300],
      "parameters": { "fieldsToAggregate": { "fieldToAggregate": [ { "fieldToAggregate": "lineTotal" } ] }, "options": {} } },
    { "id": "a5", "name": "Merge Header + Totals", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.merge", "typeVersion": 3, "position": [880, 200],
      "parameters": { "mode": "combine", "combineBy": "combineByPosition", "options": {} } },
    { "id": "a6", "name": "Build Order", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.set", "typeVersion": 3.4, "position": [1100, 200],
      "parameters": { "assignments": { "assignments": [
        { "id": "b1", "name": "orderId", "type": "string", "value": "={{ $json.body.orderId }}" },
        { "id": "b2", "name": "customer", "type": "string", "value": "={{ $json.body.customer }}" },
        { "id": "b3", "name": "total", "type": "number", "value": "={{ $json.lineTotal.reduce((s, v) => s + v, 0) }}" } ] }, "options": {} } },
    { "id": "a7", "name": "Send to CRM", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.httpRequest", "typeVersion": 4.2, "position": [1320, 200],
      "retryOnFail": true, "maxTries": 3, "waitBetweenTries": 2000, "onError": "continueErrorOutput",
      "parameters": { "method": "POST", "url": "https://httpbin.org/post", "sendBody": true, "specifyBody": "json",
        "jsonBody": "={{ JSON.stringify($json) }}", "options": {} } },
    { "id": "a8", "name": "Mark Failed", "type": "n8n-nodes-base.set", "typeVersion": 3.4, "position": [1540, 300],
      "parameters": { "assignments": { "assignments": [
        { "id": "f1", "name": "status", "type": "string", "value": "crm_failed" },
        { "id": "f2", "name": "reason", "type": "string", "value": "={{ $json.error?.message }}" } ] }, "options": {} } }
  ],
  "connections": {
    "Order Webhook": { "main": [[ { "node": "Split Out Lines", "type": "main", "index": 0 }, { "node": "Merge Header + Totals", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ]] },
    "Split Out Lines": { "main": [[ { "node": "Line Total", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ]] },
    "Line Total": { "main": [[ { "node": "Aggregate Totals", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ]] },
    "Aggregate Totals": { "main": [[ { "node": "Merge Header + Totals", "type": "main", "index": 1 } ]] },
    "Merge Header + Totals": { "main": [[ { "node": "Build Order", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ]] },
    "Build Order": { "main": [[ { "node": "Send to CRM", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ]] },
    "Send to CRM": { "main": [[], [ { "node": "Mark Failed", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ]] }
  },
  "settings": { "executionOrder": "v1", "errorWorkflow": "ErrAlertWf000001" },
  "active": false
}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Import exported workflows into the running production instance.
# Workflows are stored in PostgreSQL, so workers see them immediately.
set -euo pipefail

# Wait until the main instance answers its health endpoint
until curl -sf http://localhost:5678/healthz > /dev/null; do
  echo "Waiting for n8n..."
  sleep 3
done

# Import the error workflow first, so its ID exists
# before Order Intake points to it in settings.errorWorkflow
docker compose exec -T n8n n8n import:workflow --input=/workflows/error-alert.json
docker compose exec -T n8n n8n import:workflow --input=/workflows/order-intake.json

# Confirm both workflows are in the database
docker compose exec -T n8n n8n list:workflow

echo "Imported. Open http://localhost:5678, open 'Order Intake' and activate/publish it."
echo "Then check worker logs: docker compose logs -f n8n-worker"

# n8n-order-intake-prod

Step 7 project: finish Level 2 ideas and run one workflow in production.

## What runs
- `n8n` (main): UI, API, receives webhooks, puts jobs on Redis.
- `n8n-worker`: takes jobs from Redis and executes them (queue mode).
- `postgres`: stores workflows, credentials (encrypted) and executions.
- `redis`: the job queue.

## Order Intake workflow (Level 2 concepts)
1. **Order Webhook** gets one item: an order with an `items` array.
2. **Split Out Lines** turns the array into one item per line.
3. **Line Total** runs once per item (n8n loops over items for you).
4. **Aggregate Totals** collects all `lineTotal` values back into one item.
5. **Merge Header + Totals** combines by position: input 1 = order header, input 2 = totals.
6. **Build Order** sums the totals with an expression.
7. **Send to CRM** retries 3 times; if it still fails, the **error output** goes to **Mark Failed**.

You need Loop Over Items only when you must control batches yourself, for example for rate limits.

## Error handling
- Node level: Retry On Fail plus On Error = Continue (using error output).
- Workflow level: `settings.errorWorkflow` points to **Error Alert**, which starts with an **Error Trigger**.
  It runs only for automatic (production) executions, not manual test runs.

## Production checklist
- Set a strong `N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY` and back it up. Main and worker must share it.
- Pin the image version. Main and workers must run the same version.
- Put HTTPS (reverse proxy) in front and set `WEBHOOK_URL` to the public URL.
- Add workers with `docker compose up -d --scale n8n-worker=3`.

## Version control and environments
- Here, workflows live as JSON in `workflows/` and are committed to Git.
- n8n's built-in Source control (Git-based, connecting dev and prod instances) is a paid
  Enterprise feature; check your plan. Credentials are not pushed with their secret values.
- Use a sub-workflow (Execute Workflow node) to reuse logic like Notify Team across workflows.

## Checkpoint
Level 2 badge earned, Order Intake active, and a curl test visible in Executions.

revision.examFocus: This step covers the n8n Course Level 2 knowledge check: data structures, Merge, splitting and looping, error handling and sub-workflows. It also covers the production self-hosting topics that interviews and real deployments test: Postgres, queue mode, encryption key, WEBHOOK_URL, pruning and source control. Level 2 questions usually show a workflow outcome, such as missing items, wrong pairing or a handler that did not fire, and ask which node, mode or setting explains or fixes it.

compare.difference: Position pairs item 1 with item 1, item 2 with item 2, by index. Matching Fields joins items whose key values are equal, such as email or order ID, no matter what order they arrive in.
compare.chooseA: Pick this when both inputs come from the same source in the same order and simply need to sit side by side.
compare.chooseB: Pick this when the inputs come from different systems, may be in different orders, or you need enrich, keep-matches or keep-non-matches behaviour.

compare.difference: Split Out turns one item that holds an array into many items. Aggregate does the reverse and collapses many items into one item that holds a list.
compare.chooseA: Pick this when an API returns one item with a nested list, such as line items, and you need to process each entry separately.
compare.chooseB: Pick this when you need a single item, for example one Slack message or one email summarising all rows.

compare.b: Node-level On Error: Continue (using error output)
compare.difference: The error workflow is a separate workflow that runs after a production execution fails, and it is mainly used for alerting. The error output keeps the run going and sends the failed items down a separate branch inside the same workflow.
compare.chooseA: Pick this for central alerting, for example notifying Slack or email with the workflow name and execution URL, across many workflows.
compare.chooseB: Pick this when one flaky node, such as an API call, should not stop the batch and failed items need their own handling, such as a retry or logging to a sheet.

compare.difference: In regular mode, one process both receives triggers and runs executions. In queue mode, the main instance only enqueues jobs in Redis, and any number of workers pick them up and run them.
compare.chooseA: Pick this for low-volume, single-server setups where simplicity matters more than scale.
compare.chooseB: Pick this when you need horizontal scaling, high webhook throughput, or long executions that must not block the editor.

compare.a: Git source control and environments (paid Enterprise feature)
compare.difference: Source control links instances to Git branches and supports push and pull from the UI. The CLI moves workflow JSON files with commands such as n8n export:workflow and n8n import:workflow. Both approaches carry credential references, not the working secrets.
compare.chooseA: Pick this when the licence includes it and the team needs dev-to-prod promotion with review through Git.
compare.chooseB: Pick this on self-hosted Community, where you script backups or promotion and recreate credentials in each target instance.

cues.cue: Items came out in the wrong pairs / data from customer A attached to customer B
cues.pick: Switch Merge from Combine by Position to Combine by Matching Fields on a unique key
cues.why: Index-based pairing breaks as soon as either input is sorted differently or has a missing row.

cues.cue: Process 500 records but the API allows only 10 per call / rate limit
cues.pick: Loop Over Items with a batch size, plus a Wait node inside the loop
cues.why: Most nodes already run once per item, so you add an explicit loop only when you must control batch size or pacing.

cues.cue: Alert the team whenever any production workflow fails
cues.pick: A dedicated workflow that starts with an Error Trigger, set as the Error Workflow in each workflow's settings
cues.why: One central handler avoids copying alert logic into every workflow.

cues.cue: Error workflow did not run while I tested in the editor
cues.pick: Expected behaviour; test by activating the workflow or triggering it for real
cues.why: Manual test runs never invoke the error workflow.

cues.cue: Jobs fail on workers with credential or decryption errors
cues.pick: Set the same N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY on the main instance and every worker
cues.why: Each process decrypts credentials with its own key, and a mismatched key cannot read the stored secrets.

cues.cue: Webhook URL or OAuth redirect shows localhost:5678 behind Nginx or Caddy
cues.pick: Set WEBHOOK_URL to the public HTTPS URL
cues.why: n8n cannot detect the address the proxy exposes, so you must tell it.

cues.cue: Database keeps growing / disk full on the n8n server
cues.pick: Enable execution data pruning with a sensible max age in hours
cues.why: Every stored execution's data stays in Postgres until it is pruned.

cues.cue: Reuse the same logic, such as customer lookup, in many workflows
cues.pick: A sub-workflow called with the Execute Sub-workflow node, started by the 'When Executed by Another Workflow' trigger
cues.why: One sub-workflow can be maintained in one place, and splitting work this way also lowers memory use per execution.

scenario.situation: A company self-hosts n8n with Docker behind Nginx. Volume has grown, so the engineer adds two worker containers and sets EXECUTIONS_MODE=queue with Redis. The instance still uses the default database, and the encryption key was never set explicitly. After the change, executions that use saved credentials fail on the workers, and some file-processing workflows cannot find their binary data. What is the correct fix?
reasoning: Queue mode needs a shared database. The default SQLite file lives inside one container, so the first fix is to migrate to PostgreSQL with DB_TYPE=postgresdb on all processes.

The credential failures point to the encryption key. With no explicit key, each container generated its own, so copy the main instance's existing key into N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY on every worker. Do not create a new key, or existing credentials become unreadable.
Binary data in filesystem mode is local to one container, and workers cannot see it. Move binary data to database or external storage.
Reject answers such as 'increase worker concurrency' or 'add more Redis memory'. They tune throughput but do not fix decryption errors or missing shared state.
Also confirm WEBHOOK_URL is set to the public HTTPS address, because the instance sits behind Nginx.
scenario.answer: Move the instance to PostgreSQL, set the original N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY identically on the main instance and all workers, and store binary data in the database or external storage instead of the filesystem. Queue mode only works when every process shares the same database, the same key and the same binary storage.

memoryAids: Queue mode needs 'P-R-K-B': Postgres, Redis, the same Key everywhere, and shared Binary storage.
Split Out = 1 → many; Aggregate = many → 1; Loop = many in controlled batches.
Position = 'line number'; Matching = 'ID card'. Use Matching whenever order cannot be trusted.
cheatSheet: Every node output is a list of items, and each item must have a json object; binary is optional.
Most nodes run once per input item automatically, so use Loop Over Items only for batching, pacing or nodes that need it.
Merge Append stacks both inputs; Combine joins them; Choose Branch passes on only one input.
Combine by Matching Fields can keep matches, non-matches or everything, so read the question for 'enrich' versus 'only matched'.
Default On Error is Stop Workflow; Continue passes the error on as data; Continue (using error output) adds a second, error branch.
Retry On Fail at node level handles transient API errors before any error handling kicks in.
Error Trigger gives you the workflow name, error message and execution details. Link it in Workflow Settings → Error Workflow.
Production setup: Postgres, explicit encryption key backed up safely, WEBHOOK_URL behind a proxy, and pruning enabled.
Start workers with 'n8n worker' and tune per-worker parallel jobs with --concurrency.
Never rotate or lose the encryption key casually, because every saved credential depends on it.
Moving workflows between environments never moves working secrets, so recreate credentials on each instance.
Git-based source control and environments are a paid feature; on Community, use CLI export/import.
selfCheck: I can predict how many items each node outputs after Split Out, Aggregate and each Merge mode.
I can choose between an error workflow, the error output and Retry On Fail for a given failure case.
I can list the environment variables a queue-mode deployment needs and explain why each must match across processes.
I can explain why SQLite and filesystem binary storage break queue mode.
I can move a workflow from dev to prod on Community edition and get its credentials working.
I have finished Level 2, earned the badge, and have one active workflow running with alerts on a production instance.

objective.question: You write a Code node that must return two records to the next node. Which return value matches the item structure n8n expects?
options: return { items: ['Asha', 'Ravi'] };
return 'Asha, Ravi';
return [{ binary: { name: 'Asha' } }, { binary: { name: 'Ravi' } }];
return [{ json: { name: 'Asha' } }, { json: { name: 'Ravi' } }];
objective.explanation: n8n passes data as an array of items, and each item is an object with a required json key and an optional binary key. A plain object, a string, or items with only binary data do not match this shape.

objective.question: A team installed n8n with default settings and now wants to move it to production. Which database does n8n use by default, and what should they set for production?
options: PostgreSQL by default; no change is needed
Redis by default; set DB_TYPE=postgres
SQLite by default; set DB_TYPE=postgresdb
MySQL by default; set DB_TYPE=sqlite
objective.explanation: n8n uses SQLite by default, and production setups should use PostgreSQL by setting DB_TYPE=postgresdb. Redis is the queue broker, not the database, and the value is postgresdb, not postgres.

objective.question: Your n8n instance runs behind an Nginx reverse proxy at https://flows.example.in. The Webhook node still shows URLs starting with http://localhost:5678. What is the correct fix?
options: Set WEBHOOK_URL to https://flows.example.in/
Enable queue mode so webhooks are routed through Redis
Use the test URL instead of the production URL
Change the n8n port from 5678 to 443
objective.explanation: Behind a reverse proxy, n8n cannot detect its public address, so you set WEBHOOK_URL to the public HTTPS address. Changing the port or enabling queue mode does not change the URL n8n shows, and test URLs have the same localhost problem.

objective.question: You created an error workflow that starts with an Error Trigger and linked it in the main workflow's settings. You click 'Execute workflow' on the main workflow, a node fails, but no alert arrives. What is the most likely reason?
options: Error workflows only work in queue mode
The failing node must be set to 'Continue' for the Error Trigger to fire
Error Trigger workflows fire only for automatic (production) executions, not manual test runs
The Error Trigger workflow must use a Webhook node as well
objective.explanation: Error workflows run only when an automatic execution fails, such as a trigger or webhook in an active workflow. Manual test runs do not fire them. Queue mode is not required, and setting 'Continue' would actually stop the workflow from failing.

objective.question: An HTTP Request node calls a CRM for 200 contacts. A few calls fail. You want the good items to carry on normally while the failed items go to a separate branch that logs them to a sheet. Which On Error setting should you use?
options: Continue
Continue (using error output)
Retry On Fail with 0 tries
Stop Workflow
objective.explanation: 'Continue (using error output)' adds an extra output so failed items can be routed to their own branch. 'Stop Workflow' halts everything, and 'Continue' passes the errors along the normal path without separating them.

objective.question: One branch returns customers with a customer_id field. Another branch returns orders that also have a customer_id field. You need each order enriched with the matching customer's name. Which Merge node configuration fits best?
options: Combine by Matching Fields on customer_id
Choose Branch
Combine by Position
Append
objective.explanation: Combining by matching fields joins items from both inputs where the key values are equal, like a database join. Append only stacks the lists. Combine by Position pairs items by their order, which is wrong when the lists are not aligned. Choose Branch outputs one input only.

objective.question: An API returns a single n8n item whose json contains an 'orders' array of 50 objects. The next node must act once per order. Which node should you add?
options: Split Out on the 'orders' field
Merge in Append mode
Loop Over Items with batch size 50
Aggregate on the 'orders' field
objective.explanation: Split Out turns a list field inside one item into separate items, one per element, so later nodes run once per order. Aggregate does the opposite. Merge needs two inputs. Loop Over Items batches existing items and does not split an array inside one item.

objective.question: A workflow has 30 items, one per new signup. You want to send one Slack message that lists all 30 email addresses. Which node prepares the data for this?
options: Loop Over Items
Error Trigger
Aggregate
Split Out
objective.explanation: Aggregate collects a field from many items into a list inside one item, so the Slack node runs only once. Split Out and Loop Over Items keep or create many items, and Error Trigger is only for error workflows.

objective.question: A partner API allows only 10 requests per minute. You have 500 items to send. Which design is the most reliable in n8n?
options: Use Loop Over Items with a batch size of 10 and add a Wait node before looping back
Turn on queue mode so workers spread the requests
Use Aggregate to combine the items into one request
Send all 500 items to the HTTP Request node at once and set On Error to Continue
objective.explanation: Loop Over Items processes items in batches, and a Wait node inside the loop controls the speed so you stay under the rate limit. Ignoring errors does not prevent throttling. Aggregating changes what the API receives. Queue mode spreads executions across workers, not requests inside one execution.

objective.question: You are enabling queue mode on a self-hosted n8n deployment. Which combination is required?
options: EXECUTIONS_MODE=queue and SQLite; Redis is optional
EXECUTIONS_MODE=workers and MySQL
EXECUTIONS_MODE=regular, a Redis instance, and SQLite
EXECUTIONS_MODE=queue, a Redis instance, and PostgreSQL as the database
objective.explanation: Queue mode needs EXECUTIONS_MODE=queue, Redis as the message broker (set with QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_HOST and QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_PORT), and PostgreSQL so the main instance and workers share one database. SQLite is not suitable, and 'workers' is not a valid mode value.

objective.question: You start a worker with 'n8n worker' and no extra flags. How many jobs can it run at the same time, and how do you change that?
options: 5 jobs; change it with EXECUTIONS_MODE
10 jobs; change it with --concurrency
Unlimited; change it with QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_PORT
1 job; change it with --workers
objective.explanation: By default each worker runs up to 10 jobs at once, and you change this with the --concurrency flag, for example 'n8n worker --concurrency=5'. The other flags and variables do not control worker concurrency.

objective.question: After you add two new workers in queue mode, executions that use saved credentials fail on those workers. The same workflows work on the main instance. What is the most likely cause?
options: The workers are not exposed on port 5678
WEBHOOK_URL is not set on the workers
Execution data pruning is turned off
The workers use a different N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY from the main instance
objective.explanation: Credentials are encrypted in the database with N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY, so every worker must have exactly the same key as the main instance to decrypt them. Ports, WEBHOOK_URL and pruning do not affect credential decryption.

objective.question: Your production Postgres database has grown very large because every execution is stored. Which settings keep it under control?
options: EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE=true and EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE set in hours
DB_TYPE=sqlite and WEBHOOK_URL
N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY rotation every week
EXECUTIONS_MODE=queue and --concurrency
objective.explanation: Execution data pruning deletes old execution records, and EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE sets how many hours to keep them. Queue mode settings, switching to SQLite or rotating the encryption key do not reduce stored execution data, and rotating the key would break credentials.

objective.question: You pull workflows from Git into a new production instance using n8n source control. The credentials appear by name, but nodes fail to authenticate. Why?
options: Source control pushes credential stubs only, so you must enter the secrets again in each environment
Credentials only sync when the workflow is active
Production instances cannot use credentials created through source control
Source control encrypts secrets with a different key on each pull
objective.explanation: Source control stores credential stubs (name, type and so on) but never the secret values, so each environment needs its own secrets. This is intentional, so that keys are not stored in Git and dev and prod can use different accounts.

objective.question: Five workflows all need the same 'validate and format a GST invoice' logic. What is the cleanest n8n approach?
options: Put the logic in a sub-workflow and call it with the Execute Workflow (Execute Sub-workflow) node
Use an Error Trigger to run the shared logic
Use the Merge node to share nodes between workflows
Copy the nodes into all five workflows
objective.explanation: A sub-workflow starts with the 'When Executed by Another Workflow' trigger and is called from other workflows, so the logic lives in one place. Copying nodes creates duplicates you must maintain. Merge only works inside one workflow, and Error Trigger is for failures.

objective.question: A workflow runs 'Get Customers' (5 items), then an HTTP Request node 'Lookup Plan' (5 items), then Slack. In the Slack node you need the name from the 'Get Customers' item that matches the current item. Which expression is correct?
options: {{ $('Get Customers').first().json.name }}
{{ $('Get Customers').all().json.name }}
{{ $json.name }}
{{ $('Get Customers').item.json.name }}
objective.explanation: .item uses item linking (paired items) to find the earlier item that matches the current one. $json only reads the immediate input, which is the HTTP response. first() always returns item 0, and all() returns an array that has no .json property.

objective.question: A Code node set to 'Run Once for All Items' receives 3 items with amount values 100, 200 and 300. What does it output?

code.code:
const total = $input.all().reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.json.amount, 0);
return [{ json: { total } }];

options: Three items, each with { total: 600 }
An error, because the Code node must return a plain object
Three items with totals 100, 300 and 600
One item: { total: 600 }
objective.explanation: In 'Run Once for All Items' mode the code runs once over every input item. It returns an array that holds one item object, so the output is a single item. Returning an array of { json } objects is the valid format.

objective.question: A parent workflow calls a sub-workflow with the Execute Workflow node and waits for it to finish. What data does the parent receive back?
options: Nothing, unless the sub-workflow ends with a Respond to Webhook node
The data from the sub-workflow's trigger node
The parent's input items, unchanged
The output of the last node that ran in the sub-workflow
objective.explanation: When the parent waits for completion, the sub-workflow returns the output of its last executed node to the parent. Respond to Webhook is only for webhook-triggered workflows. The trigger data is not what gets returned.

objective.question: In an error workflow that starts with an Error Trigger, you want the Slack alert to include a direct link to the failed execution. Which expression gives you that link?
options: {{ $json.workflow.url }}
{{ $json.error.link }}
{{ $execution.id }}
{{ $json.execution.url }}
objective.explanation: The Error Trigger output includes execution.url, execution.id, execution.error, execution.lastNodeExecuted and workflow.name. $execution.id is the ID of the error workflow's own run, not the failed one. The other two fields do not exist.

objective.question: A payment gateway sometimes returns HTTP 503 for a few seconds, and then the same request succeeds. You want the workflow to recover on its own without anyone stepping in. What should you configure?
options: Set On Error to 'Continue' and ignore the failed items
Wrap the node in Loop Over Items with a batch size of 1
Rely on the error workflow and re-run failed executions by hand
Turn on Retry On Fail on the HTTP Request node and set Max Tries and Wait Between Tries
objective.explanation: Retry On Fail handles short, transient errors by retrying the node after a wait. 'Continue' quietly drops the failed payments. An error workflow only alerts after the failure has already happened. Batching does nothing about 503 responses.

objective.question: Business rule: if an incoming invoice has a negative total, the execution must be marked as failed so that the linked error workflow fires. What should you add on the IF node's true branch?
options: A Set node that adds an 'error' field
A Respond to Webhook node that returns status 400
A No Operation node
A Stop and Error node with a clear error message
objective.explanation: Stop and Error deliberately fails the execution, and that triggers the error workflow. A Set node or a No Operation node lets the execution finish as successful. A 400 response tells the caller there is a problem, but the execution itself does not fail.

objective.question: A queue-mode deployment receives thousands of webhook calls per minute, and the main instance is overloaded. Which change scales webhook intake correctly?

code.code:
# main (editor, triggers, timers)
n8n start
# workers
n8n worker --concurrency=10
# option under consideration
n8n webhook

options: Raise concurrency on the main instance and remove the workers
Start the webhook processes with EXECUTIONS_MODE=regular
Send /webhook-test/* to the webhook processes and /webhook/* to the main
Run several 'n8n webhook' processes and have the load balancer send /webhook/* to them, while the main keeps the editor and /webhook-test/*
objective.explanation: Webhook processors accept production webhook calls and push them to Redis for workers to execute, so they must run in queue mode. Test webhooks stay on the main instance, so reversing the routes breaks production calls.

objective.question: You promote a workflow from dev to prod with source control. The CRM base URL differs per environment, and you must not edit the workflow after each pull. What is the best approach?
options: Put the URL in a Set node and keep a separate Git branch for each URL
Write the URL in the credential's description field
Hard-code the dev URL and edit it in prod after every pull
Create an n8n Variable on each instance with its own value, and reference it as {{ $vars.CRM_BASE_URL }}
objective.explanation: Variables are defined per instance and read with $vars, so the same workflow JSON works in every environment. Editing after each pull is error-prone and defeats source control. The other two options create drift or do not work at all.

objective.question: Loop Over Items has a batch size of 10 and receives 45 items. The loop output goes to an HTTP Request node, which connects back to Loop Over Items. What does the 'done' output emit?
options: An output after each batch, with 10 items each time
The original 45 items immediately, before any batch runs
Only the last batch of 5 items
One output after all batches finish, holding all 45 processed items combined
objective.explanation: The loop output sends batches of 10 until every item is processed. Only after that does 'done' fire, once, with the results of all iterations combined.

subjective.question: Explain how data flows between nodes in n8n. What does an item look like, and why does it matter when you write expressions or Code nodes?
subjective.answer: In n8n, data moves between nodes as an array of items. Each item is an object with a required json key, which holds the structured data, and an optional binary key for files such as PDFs or images. Most nodes run once for each item they receive, so ten input items usually mean ten operations. This matters in practice. In expressions, $json refers to the current item's json, so you must know whether a field sits at the top level or is nested inside an array. In a Code node, you must return an array of objects with a json key. Otherwise the next node gets data in the wrong shape or the node fails. Most data problems come from confusing 'one item containing a list' with 'many items'.
keyPoints: Data is an array of items
Each item has a required json key and an optional binary key
Most nodes run once per item
Code nodes must return [{ json: {...} }]
Know the difference between one item with a list and many items

subjective.question: Compare Split Out, Aggregate and Loop Over Items. Give a real use case for each.
subjective.answer: Split Out takes a list field inside one item and creates one item per element. For example, a Shopify-style API returns one item with an orders array, and Split Out gives you one item per order. Aggregate does the reverse. It collects a field from many items into a list inside a single item, for example to send one email summary of all new leads. Loop Over Items processes existing items in batches of a size you choose. It has a loop output and a done output. I use it when an API has a rate limit: batch size 10, call the API, add a Wait node, then loop back. Simply put, Split Out and Aggregate change the shape of the data, while Loop Over Items controls how many items are processed at a time.
keyPoints: Split Out: one item with a list becomes many items
Aggregate: many items become one item with a list
Loop Over Items: batching, with loop and done outputs
Use Loop Over Items with Wait for rate limits
Shape change versus pacing control

subjective.question: Describe the main Merge node modes and how you would choose between them.
subjective.answer: The Merge node joins data from two or more inputs. Append simply outputs the items from all inputs one after another. I use it when two sources produce the same kind of record, such as leads from two forms. Combine has several options. By Matching Fields joins items where a key is equal, like an SQL join on customer_id, and you can keep matches only or include unmatched items. By Position pairs the first item with the first, the second with the second, and so on. That is safe only when both lists are aligned. All Possible Combinations creates every pairing. The SQL Query mode lets you write a query over the inputs. Choose Branch outputs the data of one selected input, which is useful for waiting until both branches finish. I choose the mode based on whether a reliable shared key exists.
keyPoints: Append stacks the items
Combine by Matching Fields works like a join on a key
Combine by Position needs aligned lists
All Possible Combinations, SQL Query and Choose Branch
Choose based on whether a reliable key exists

subjective.question: What is the difference between node-level error handling and an error workflow? When would you use each?
subjective.answer: Node-level error handling is set on each node. The On Error setting has three options: Stop Workflow (the default), Continue, and Continue (using error output). You can also turn on Retry On Fail with a number of tries and a wait between them. I use this for expected, item-level problems, such as one bad record or a temporary API timeout. The failed item can go to its own branch for logging while the good items continue. An error workflow is a separate workflow that starts with the Error Trigger node and is linked in the main workflow's settings. It runs when an automatic execution fails and receives details such as the workflow name, the failed node, the error message and the execution URL. I use it for central alerting, for example a Slack or email alert to the on-call person. Good production workflows use both.
keyPoints: On Error options: Stop Workflow, Continue, Continue (using error output)
Retry On Fail for temporary failures
Error workflow starts with Error Trigger and is set in workflow settings
Error workflow is used for central alerting with execution details
Use both together

subjective.question: Your manager says the error alert workflow 'doesn't work' because nothing happened when they tested it. How do you explain this and test it properly?
subjective.answer: The Error Trigger fires only for automatic executions, meaning runs started by a trigger or a production webhook in an active workflow. When someone clicks 'Execute workflow' in the editor, that is a manual test run, so the error workflow does not fire. This is by design. To test it properly, I first check that the main workflow's settings point to the correct error workflow. Then I make a failure happen in a real execution. For example, I add a Stop And Error node, or point an HTTP Request at a bad URL, and activate the workflow with a schedule or webhook trigger. I trigger it, check the Executions list for the failed run, and confirm the alert arrives with the execution link. Then I remove the forced failure.
keyPoints: Error Trigger ignores manual test runs
Check the error workflow link in workflow settings
Force a failure with a Stop And Error node or a bad request
Trigger an automatic execution of the active workflow
Check the Executions list and the alert content

subjective.question: Why and how would you use sub-workflows in a business automation?
subjective.answer: Sub-workflows let me build a piece of logic once and call it from many workflows. The sub-workflow starts with the 'When Executed by Another Workflow' trigger. The parent workflow calls it with the Execute Workflow node, also called Execute Sub-workflow. The parent's items are passed in, and the output of the sub-workflow's last node comes back to the parent. The benefits are reuse, a single place to fix bugs, smaller workflows that are easier to read, and clear ownership. For example, 'create or update a customer in the CRM' can be one sub-workflow used by the website form, the payment flow and the support flow. I define the input fields clearly so callers know what to send. I also decide whether the parent should wait for the result or continue straight away.
keyPoints: The sub-workflow starts with the 'When Executed by Another Workflow' trigger
It is called with the Execute Workflow (Execute Sub-workflow) node
Data goes in, and the last node's output returns to the parent
Benefits: reuse, single place to fix bugs, readability
Define clear inputs; choose whether the parent waits

subjective.question: Why should a production n8n instance use PostgreSQL instead of the default SQLite, and which environment variables would you set?
subjective.answer: SQLite is a single file on the local disk. It is fine for learning but weak for production. It handles heavy concurrent writes poorly, it is harder to back up safely while running, and it cannot be shared between multiple processes, which queue mode needs. PostgreSQL is a proper database server. It handles concurrency, supports normal backup and restore tools, and is shared by the main instance and the workers. I set DB_TYPE=postgresdb, plus DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST, DB_POSTGRESDB_PORT, DB_POSTGRESDB_DATABASE, DB_POSTGRESDB_USER and DB_POSTGRESDB_PASSWORD. I keep the password in a secret store or Docker secret, not in the compose file in Git. I also turn on execution pruning and schedule regular database backups.
keyPoints: SQLite is a local file with weak concurrency
Queue mode needs a shared database
Set DB_TYPE=postgresdb and the DB_POSTGRESDB_* variables
Keep the database password out of Git
Back up regularly and turn on pruning

subjective.question: Explain n8n queue mode architecture: what each component does and why you would use it.
